    On ToonTwins, the unit of analysis is a pair of body plan and shape, which gives 18 units. On the animated animals, it is a motion group, which gives 21 units. We first average the folds and seeds within each unit. We then report means with 95 percent bootstrap confidence intervals [40] over 2,000 resamples of units. To compare two models, we use paired bootstrap and Wilcoxon signed-rank tests [41] over units and report Cohen’s d_z[42] as the paired effect size. The representation analysis in Section6.4 uses its own procedure, which we describe in that section, because its runs share test characters.

    6 Results

    We first test whether the pixel world model keeps the twin difference and then whether path prediction from the context recovers it. We then separate the parts of our model, test its body summary and its rendered frames, and repeat the main test on the animated animals and on unseen body plans.

    6.1 The tested pixel world model loses body-specific dynamics

    The pixel world model we tested has more parameters than our model (2.88 M against 1.62 M), but its decoded rollouts match the twins in only 0.27 to 0.30 of cases, where chance is 0.25, and recover only 14 to 25 percent of the true difference in jump height. Its IoU of 0.44 to 0.45 is lower than that of copying the first frame (0.50), and its frames are blurred, with a sharpness of 0.66 relative to the truth. This failure does not depend on the form of the command, because a variant that receives only the action type, without the effort or onset, matched the twins in 0.29 to 0.31 of cases.

    Fig.6 shows where the small amount of body information appears in the rollouts. Twin matching rises only during the flight phase of the jump and the run, peaks at 0.37 at step 9 with the contrastive body code and falls again afterwards. Replacing the code with the mean code or with a twin’s code brings it back to chance, so this small effect does come from the body code. The model also separates only the extreme profiles. Stiff and bouncy twins are matched in 0.52 and 0.51 of cases, but firm and soft twins in only 0.12 and 0.14, which is below chance. This is because the differences between the four predictions are small compared with the true differences, and only the extremes are sometimes ordered correctly.

    Fig.7 shows this for one twin set. The true peak heights of the four twins differ by about 4 to 5 pixels, while the four predicted height curves lie on top of each other. We see two likely sources of this failure, although our experiments do not separate them. First, the decoder appears to average over the possible futures, so the four twins collapse into one blurred body. Second, the training objective itself appears to discard body information. A path head trained on the frozen body code of the pixel model reaches a twin matching of 0.48 with the plain code, which is lower than with the same encoder at its random initial weights (0.55, p<0.001). With the contrastive code it reaches 0.50, which is also no better than the random encoder (p=0.084). A likely reason is that the silhouette measures of the context clips already carry body information, and a pixel objective has no reason to keep it, because the average motion already overlaps every twin well.

    6.2 Body dynamics can be recovered from other actions

    Predicting the motion path instead of pixels recovers most of the twin difference. Table2 compares all path models on the same folds and seeds, and Fig.8 shows one twin set.

    On new shapes, our model improves twin matching over the context attention baseline by 0.092 (95 percent CI 0.063 to 0.126, d_z=1.32, p<0.001) and over the body code by 0.184 (d_z=3.73, p<0.001). It also exceeds the model that receives the true profile label by 0.046 (p=0.012). This is because the context clips show how this exact shape moves, which the label does not. Swapping the contexts of twins drops twin matching to 0.044, below the chance level of 0.25, so the prediction follows the body information it receives. This test changes the context on purpose and does not prove that the model has identified the dynamics profile. Fine-tuning the model without body information on the context clips reaches only 0.281. The contrastive loss alone does not help the body code (0.672 against 0.675), so its gain on new shapes depends on the transformer (Section6.3). Every learned model ranks the four jump heights on new shapes with a Spearman correlation of 0.99 to 1.00.

    Two context clips already give most of the improvement (Fig.9). Our model reaches 0.586 with one clip and 0.795 with two clips, which is already above the context attention baseline with eight clips (0.767). With eight clips it reaches 0.859. A linear probe recovers the dynamics profile from our summary with 0.835 accuracy and the held-out action with 0.236 accuracy, close to the chance level of 0.20. The body code without the contrastive loss gives 0.655 and 0.760, so it stores which actions it has seen.

    Not every action carries information about the body (Fig.10). A context of turns alone leaves every model at chance (0.24 to 0.25), because turning is the one action that does not depend on the dynamics profile. Running, falling and jumping are the most informative context actions, with 0.81 to 0.87 for our model averaged over the query actions other than turn. Crouching is the least informative (0.67). Our model is better than the context attention baseline for every informative context action.

    The lead of our model is largest for the extreme profiles. It matches bouncy twins in 0.906 of cases and stiff twins in 0.863, against 0.767 and 0.748 for the context attention baseline. Fig.11 breaks twin matching down by body plan, query action and dynamics profile. Among the learned models, ours is best for every body plan, action and dynamics profile. Its largest gains over the context attention baseline are for limbless bodies (0.554 to 0.774), disjointed bodies (0.789 to 0.902), running (0.580 to 0.739) and falling (0.774 to 0.872). The profile label is better only for limbless and multilimb bodies and for jumping and crouching, where the motion depends on only one or two dynamics parameters, such as the jump gain or the crouch depth, so knowing the profile is enough.

    6.3 What each part of the model contributes

    Table2 does not include our model without the contrastive loss, so we retrained four models on the same folds and seeds to separate the parts of our model (Table3). We used 3 seeds for new shapes and for the animated animals and one seed for unseen body plans, so we treat the comparisons on unseen body plans as exploratory. The rerun reproduces the main results, with 0.857 against 0.859 for our model and 0.770 against 0.767 for the context attention baseline. The columns for the animated animals and unseen body plans are discussed in Sections6.6 and 6.7.

    On new shapes, giving the transformer a body token and a context encoder that does not see the query raises twin matching from 0.770 to 0.806 (difference 0.037, 95 percent CI 0.017 to 0.060, d_z=0.77, p<0.001). These two changes were made together, so their separate effects are not known. Adding the contrastive loss to the same architecture raises twin matching further to 0.857 (difference 0.050, CI 0.036 to 0.066, d_z=1.48, p<0.001). The contrastive loss gives more than half of the gain over the baseline, and this part cannot come from extra capacity, because the model without the loss has exactly the same parameters. Drawing the two contrastive sets from disjoint action types gives 0.838, which is lower than 0.857 (p<0.001) but still above the model without the loss (p<0.001), so the benefit of the loss does not depend on the two sets sharing action types.

    Fig.12 shows the same effect for each twin set. For several twin sets with a true spread of 2 to 3 pixels, the context attention baseline predicts a spread close to zero. Most of these cases disappear with the body token and the loss, and the correlation with the true spread rises from 0.93 to 0.95 and 0.96.

    6.4 The contrastive loss makes the summary more body-specific and less action-specific

    The contrastive loss makes the summaries of one character agree across different context actions and separates look-alike twins, but it reduces rather than removes the information about the observed actions. A probe on the query action cannot show this, so we measured it directly. For each held-out character, we computed ten summaries, each from four clips of one pair of actions, and compared summaries from pairs that share no action (Table4).

    Without the contrastive loss, the summaries of different characters stay close to each other. Two summaries of the same body have a cosine similarity of 0.987, but a body and its twin also reach 0.833. A linear probe recovers which pair of actions was observed in 0.626 of cases, where chance is 0.10. With the loss, two summaries of the same body from completely different actions stay similar (0.813), while twins drop to 0.248. The gap between the two grows from 0.154 to 0.564 (d_z=6.7, p<0.001 over 9 runs). The probe for the observed actions falls to 0.139 (95 percent CI 0.129 to 0.150). This is close to the chance level of 0.10 but above it, so the loss reduces this information without removing it.

    The runs share test characters, so we also resampled over the 12 twin sets of one run (fold 0, seed 0). This gives the same result, with a gap of 0.608 (95 percent CI 0.516 to 0.694) with the loss and 0.187 (0.114 to 0.277) without it, and the gap is larger with the loss for all 12 twin sets. Across the nine runs, it ranges from 0.51 to 0.64 with the loss and from 0.11 to 0.21 without it. A twin is picked out among its four look-alikes from actions that share nothing in 0.873 of cases, against 0.792 without the loss. Fig.13 shows the same result.

    We also ran the same probes on hand-made silhouette statistics with no learning, to check that the clips contain body information that can be recovered at all. For each clip, we took the maximum, minimum, mean and standard deviation of each of the nine measures and the mean absolute change between frames. We pooled these over the four clips of a context by their mean and maximum. A linear probe recovers the dynamics profile from these features in 0.506 of cases (95 percent CI 0.491 to 0.524), against 0.799 for our summary and a chance level of 0.25. However, the same features reveal the observed pair of actions in 0.999 of cases and pick out the correct twin in only 0.329 of cases (Table4), because they mix the body with the actions. In both cases, the feature scaler and the probe, a logistic regression with an L2 penalty (C=1), are fit on the training characters only, with no hyperparameter search.

    6.5 Path-guided rendering gives sharp frames that keep the difference

    Drawing the frames along the predicted path keeps both the image quality and the twin difference (Tables5 and 14).

    Our rendered frames improve IoU over the pixel world model by 0.413 (d_z=7.72, p<0.001) and twin matching by 0.604 (d_z=10.94, p<0.001). Against the context attention baseline, twin matching in the images rises by 0.081 (p<0.001). The model without body information also renders accurate frames (IoU 0.799), but it gives all four twins the same motion (third row of Fig.14). The gain in twin matching comes from the body information in the context and not from the renderer. The refiner adds 0.096 IoU and 0.168 twin matching over the warp alone. Running is the hardest action, because the warp moves the whole body and cannot swing the legs. Even so, our model matches running twins in 0.818 of cases.

    6.6 Animated animals

    To test whether the failure of the pixel world model on ToonTwins also holds for more complex bodies, we first trained it on these animals and asked it to roll out 8 frames of an action that is absent from the context, for held-out motion groups (Figs.15 and 16). We then measured how often the rollout is closer to the animal’s own true future than to the futures of other held-out animals performing the same action (chance 0.159). This chance level differs slightly from the 0.157 of the path models because this test used an earlier split and a different set of candidate animals. The score was 0.565 without body information, 0.573 with a body code and 0.545 with the contrastive body code, and neither body code differs significantly from no body information (p=0.45 and p=0.13). Repeating the last observed frame reached 0.580. The model does use the contrastive code, because replacing it with another animal’s code lowers the score by 0.101 (p<0.001), and a linear probe recovers the animal family from it with 0.565 accuracy (chance 0.20). The pixel model receives body information and reacts to it, but its rollouts do not improve and remain a blurred average body (Fig.16), as on ToonTwins. This test used the first grouping with 24 groups, in which an animal could share its animations with a training animal. This can only help the pixel model, which still showed no gain, so we did not repeat it.

    Our path model, in contrast, lowers the mean path error by 8.5 percent against the model without body information (95 percent CI 2.7 to 14.4), from 0.847 to 0.774 in standardized units (p=0.004). It identifies the animal from its own context in 0.324 of cases, where chance is 0.157 (Table6). The gain is uneven across queries. The error falls for 61 percent of them over all folds and seeds, and the percentage averaged over queries is only 5.0 (CI -3.4 to 12.0). Unlike on ToonTwins, more context lowers the error by less than 2 percent. With one, two or three other actions in the context, the error of our model is 0.787, 0.780 and 0.774, and the other models are similarly flat. A single other action of an animal already carries most of the body information that these models can use. Our model also has a lower error than the model that knows the animal family (0.810), although this difference is not significant (p=0.13).

    Our model beats the context attention baseline on identification (p=0.004) and on the gap between another animal’s context and its own (p<0.001), but its lower error is only borderline (p=0.046, Wilcoxon p=0.16). It matches the body code with the contrastive loss on error (p=0.52) and identification (p=0.88). The controlled rerun in Table3, which gives 8.1 percent for our model and 5.2 percent for the baseline, shows where the gain comes from. The body token and the query-free encoder do not help on these animals, and without the loss they give a slightly higher error than the baseline (p=0.049). Adding the contrastive loss lowers the error (p=0.003) and raises the identification of the animal from its own context from 0.153 to 0.296 (p<0.001). Drawing the two contrastive sets from disjoint action types gives 10.5 percent, slightly better than our model (p=0.047, Wilcoxon p=0.13). Most of the gain on these animals therefore comes from the contrastive loss and not from the transformer. Fig.17 breaks the error reduction down by action. The largest gains of our model are for jumping (12.5 percent) and running (11.9 percent), while attacking and standing idle become worse (by 8.6 and 6.2 percent).

    Fig.18 shows actual predictions of the seed-0 models. We chose typical cases, whose improvement over the model without body information is closest to the median, together with the best and the worst case, so that the figure does not show only successes. Across all 169 held-out pairs of animal and action in this seed, the path error was 3.02 px for our model, 3.08 px for the context attention baseline and 3.15 px without body information. Measured in pixels, our model improved on the model without body information in 63 percent of the cases of this seed. The gain was largest for canines (3.07 to 2.58 px), while for deer our model was worse than the model without body information (3.35 against 3.21 px). The boxes also show the main limit on these animals. Whole-body position and size are predicted well, but the differences between the models are small compared with the motion of the limbs, which a box does not describe.

    6.7 Unseen body plans remain hard

    When a whole body plan is held out, every learned model in the main comparison (Table2) drops to a twin matching between 0.389 and 0.436, and the profile label reaches 0.531. Our model (0.422) is not different from the context attention baseline (p=0.47) or the body code (p=0.20). The limbless body plan stays close to chance for all learned models, at 0.25 to 0.28 (Fig.19). For the multilimb body plan, the profile label reaches 0.71, while every learned model stays at or below 0.36. The context clips of known body plans do not show the models how a new kind of body responds to its dynamics profile. In rendered frames, our model also ranks the jump heights less reliably on unseen body plans, and it identifies the highest jumper in 0.59 of cases against 0.78 for the context attention baseline.

    The ablation suggests a reason, although it used one seed on this split and is exploratory (Tables3 and 4). On unseen body plans, the contrastive loss does not improve twin matching (0.409 and 0.375 against 0.418 without it) and lowers the jump gain from 0.64 to 0.49 and 0.38 (p<0.001). Two summaries of the same new body reach a cosine similarity of only 0.21, so the consistency learned on known body plans does not carry over to a new one. One possible explanation is that the loss learns distinctions within the body plans seen in training, rather than a summary that applies to unfamiliar structures. Testing this needs a wider range of body plans.

    7 Discussion and Limitations

    7.1 Pixel metrics and body dynamics

    Pixel error and IoU should not be used alone to judge whether a world model adapts to a character. In our tests, the pixel world model had an IoU only 0.05 below copying the first frame, while it recovered at most 25 percent of the twin difference. A test with look-alike bodies shows this gap directly and needs only a procedural generator. The two models we compared also differ in their output and their training objective. The pixel world model predicts frames through a latent state, while our model predicts a silhouette path that a separate renderer draws. Our results show a limitation of the pixel model we tested, not that path prediction is better than pixel-based world modeling in general. Within our experiments, a simple warp and a small refiner draw sharp frames once the path is predicted. With the true paths, the renderer reaches an IoU of 0.888, so most of the remaining error comes from the predicted path and not from drawing.

    7.2 The role of the contrastive loss

    The contrastive loss controls what the body summary stores. With the same architecture and parameters, it raised twin matching on new shapes from 0.806 to 0.857 and made the summary of one body agree across actions that share nothing (Section6.4). On the animated animals, it was the only part of our model that helped. However, it lowered the jump gain on unseen body plans in our single-seed comparison, so the weight λ of the loss may need a different value when the test contains new body plans.

    7.3 Known and new body plans

    For new shapes of known body plans, the model predicts body-specific motion well, and its summary of one body stays consistent across actions that share nothing. For body plans never seen in training, both prediction and consistency drop sharply (Section6.7). What the model learns is therefore bounded by the variety of body structures seen in training. Widening that variety, or describing a body by its parts so that new bodies can be built from known parts, is one possible next step.

    7.4 Limitations

    This study intentionally described each body by its whole silhouette, to isolate body-specific dynamics as the only experimental variable. Consequently, the renderer cannot move limbs independently, and running is the weakest action in rendered frames (twin matching 0.818). The model also does not transfer to unseen body plans, where the limbless body plan stays near chance. Both problems need a description of the parts of a body and how they move together.

    ToonTwins uses simple 2D characters at 64×64 pixels, and its dynamics profiles follow fixed rules in the generator. We did not test parameter values outside the four profiles used in training. Each profile also changes all eight parameters together, so our tests do not show which parameters the model uses to tell twins apart. The animal data contains only 32 animals in 21 motion groups, which limits the precision of these results, for example a 95 percent CI of 2.7 to 14.4 percent for the error reduction. The animals are also animations made by artists, so the gain shows an improvement on this subset and does not show transfer to natural animal video.

    We did not evaluate large pretrained video generation models, since adapting them to condition on a few clips of a specific character would require substantial changes. We predict only 15 future frames, so the accumulation of error over longer rollouts is not tested.

    8 Conclusion

    The latent pixel world model we tested kept at most 25 percent of the difference between look-alike bodies. A model that encodes the character’s other actions and predicts the motion path separated twins of new shapes in 85.9 percent of cases. Drawing frames along the predicted path kept this difference in the rendered frames (twin matching 0.904). More than half of the gain over a transformer baseline came from the contrastive loss, which made the summaries of one body agree across actions that share nothing. On 32 animated animals, the mean path error fell by 8.5 percent, and a simpler body code with the same loss gave a similar gain. These results suggest three points.

  • •

    World models for characters should be tested on look-alike characters that move differently, because pixel metrics do not show whether body dynamics are used.

  • •

    In our experiments, carrying body information through a predicted motion path kept it in the rendered frames, whereas the tested pixel model lost it.

  • •

    The body summary should be trained to depend as little as possible on which actions were observed.

    • The method does not transfer to body plans absent from training, and this transfer needs a wider range of body structures.

    Appendix A ToonTwins Parameters

    Table7 gives the default dynamics parameters of each body plan, and Table8 gives the multipliers of each dynamics profile. The value used for a character is the default of its body plan times the multiplier of its profile. Heights are in pixels of the 128×128 drawing canvas, which is downsampled to 64×64 pixels, and the turn rate does not depend on the profile.

    （参考文献见原文。）

item.title: 一张照片走一整个场景：Lyris 说「记忆」只能保住看过的，走远了会飘——得靠布局来锚 ｜ Lyris: Layout-Guided Long Video Generation with Persistent 3D Memory
item.description:
一句话：基于记忆的方法能保住已见内容，但一旦离开，相机就会偏离路径，文字提示能命名物体却无法放置它们。

要点：

  • 任务定义：从一张照片出发探索场景，需要生成一段长距离、相机可控的漫游，**远远超出被拍到的范围，且在回到原处时仍保持一致**
  • 两类方法的短板：**基于记忆**的视频生成能保住已见内容，但在视野之外没有锚点，于是相机偏离轨迹，而文字提示**只能命名物体、无法放置物体**；**布局条件**的方法提供了这种锚点与精确控制，但缺少长程记忆
  • Lyris 因此把两者接起来：**布局引导 + 持久 3D 记忆**，让「走远」与「回头一致」同时成立

为什么值得看：这是「状态外置」主线的又一次收敛：记忆负责「看过什么」，布局负责「没看过的地方该有什么」。引擎里的对应物就是场景图——你不可能只靠回放历史帧来维持一个开放世界。

中文摘要：仅凭一张照片探索场景，要求生成一段长距离、相机可控的漫游，既要远远超出原始拍摄范围，又要在返回时保持一致性。基于记忆的视频生成方法能保住已经看过的内容，但在视野之外没有锚点：相机会逐渐偏离路径，而文字提示虽然能命名物体，却无法规定它们的位置。布局条件的方法恰好提供了这种锚点与精确的空间控制，但缺少长程记忆。Lyris 因此把两者结合：用布局引导生成、用持久的 3D 记忆维持一致性，使「走远」与「回头仍然一致」这两件事同时成立。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-24

本期推送：2026-11-25

Lyris: Layout-Guided Long Video Generation with Persistent 3D Memory

Abstract

Exploring a scene from as little as a single photo requires generating a long, camera-controlled walkthrough that extends far beyond what was captured, yet remains consistent upon return. Memory-based video generation methods preserve what they have already seen, but have no anchor beyond it, where the camera drifts from its path and a text prompt can name objects but not place them. Layout-conditioned methods provide such an anchor and precise control over what appears where, but rely on layouts that are typically authored by hand. Both limitations arise because, beyond what was captured, nothing anchors the video model unless a human authors one. To overcome both, we propose Lyris, a long video generation framework that never leaves the video model without an anchor: a persistent point-cloud memory where the scene has been observed or generated, and a 3D layout that a vision-language model authors where it has not. Our key insight is that the interface between the two models can be surprisingly coarse. A layout of one labeled 3D box per object is simple enough for a vision-language model to author (and for a user to edit), yet expressive enough for a video model to follow once rendered along the camera path. We demonstrate walkthroughs of over three minutes and 50 meters from a single photo, passing through doorways into rooms it never shows. When evaluated on minute-long round trips across four datasets, Lyris outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a wide margin, reducing camera error by 3.8× and improving consistency upon return by 22% on average.

**footnotetext: Work done during an internship at NVIDIA.

1 Introduction

Virtual touring [61], content creation, and simulation for physical AI [62, 4] benefit from 3D environments that can be explored freely. Creating such environments from as little as a single photo requires generating a long, camera-controlled walkthrough beyond the captured view, passing through doorways and into unseen rooms. These regions must form a plausible extension of the observed scene and retain their layout and appearance when the camera returns.

Recent video generative models [60, 51, 52] can generate photorealistic clips from an image and a text prompt, but only seconds at a time. Memory-based methods extend them to long rollouts by conditioning each new chunk on the history, through compressed or retrieved past views [86, 41, 57, 29], learned implicit representations [88, 72], or explicitly reconstructed geometry [95, 12, 49]. This memory preserves what has already been seen but offers nothing beyond it. There, the camera path reaches the model only as a pose encoding [57, 90], a far weaker signal than rendered geometry [54, 10], and the camera drifts from its path as unseen regions accumulate. The content of the unseen regions is left to the text prompt, which can name objects and relate them coarsely, but cannot specify where they belong or how one space connects to the next. Layout-conditioned methods instead condition generation on an explicit scene layout, such as untextured geometry, object boxes, or maps [36, 5, 48], and offer precise control over the spatial arrangement of the objects. However, these methods take the layout as an input, typically authored by hand, which does not scale to open-ended exploration.

To overcome both limitations, we propose Lyris, a long video generation framework in which a vision-language model authors the layout of unseen regions before a video model generates them. Our key insight is that the interface between the two models can be surprisingly coarse: a 3D layout with one labeled bounding box per object [22, 80, 58] is simple enough for a vision-language model to author (and for a user to edit), yet expressive enough for a video model to follow. We fine-tune a pretrained video diffusion model to follow renderings of this layout, which specify what appears where and anchor the camera to its path, even in unseen regions. To remain consistent upon return, we reconstruct each generated chunk and write it into a persistent point-cloud memory, which conditions every subsequent chunk alongside the layout. The resulting loop between explicit 3D geometry and photorealistic video generation extends the walkthrough far beyond the photo, as the layout and the memory condition each chunk, and each generated chunk in turn extends the memory from which the next layout is planned.

We make the following contributions:

  • •

    We present Lyris, a long video generation framework that pairs a 3D layout of unseen regions planned by a vision-language model with a persistent 3D memory of existing ones, enabling consistent 3D world exploration from as little as a single image without human authoring.

  • •

    We demonstrate that the layout is crucial for camera control in unseen regions, and that rendering it into the target views is far more effective than stating it in the text prompt.

  • •

    We outperform state-of-the-art methods on minute-long round trips across four datasets, reducing camera error by 3.8× and improving consistency upon return by 22% on average.

    • 2 Related Work

    Camera-controlled video generation. Video diffusion models [28] generate photorealistic clips [8, 82, 73, 60] and increasingly accept multimodal conditions [56, 51, 52]. To control the viewpoint, existing methods inject per-frame camera poses [71] or dense Plücker ray embeddings [26, 77], often through dedicated conditioning branches [2, 1], and extend beyond single clips by conditioning each new clip on frames of the preceding one [27]. Geometry-guided approaches instead condition on point-cloud renderings at the target views [89, 54, 10, 87], couple implicit reconstruction of the input views with generation [39], or repair renderings of imperfect reconstructions [74, 14]. These methods guide generation where geometry has been observed, but leave the content of unobserved regions to the generative prior. SpatialCrafter [19] instead generates the geometry of these regions with a 3D generator conditioned on the input image alone, whereas Lyris lays them out as labeled boxes that a vision-language model can write and a user can edit.

    Scene memory for long video generation. To generate long videos, memory-based methods condition each new frame or chunk on previously observed or generated content. Many approaches compress this history into a limited token budget [92, 29, 11, 72] or retrieve its most relevant parts [86, 76, 41, 81]. However, the model must still infer how this history maps to the target view, which often fails under large viewpoint changes [57]. A second line of work addresses this by aligning the history with the target camera before generation [13, 57, 90, 88], or by maintaining scene geometry that is rendered into the target views [54, 75, 95, 94, 33, 12, 49, 59]. Although rendering aligns the memory with each target view, errors can accumulate in the geometry itself [94, 49, 59]. Other methods instead generate and simulate an editable latent 3D scene around the agent, albeit trained with ground-truth 3D supervision in a voxel game [24], or sample all views jointly in a geometry-native latent space [47]. Whatever its form, however, a memory of past frames preserves what has already been seen but offers nothing beyond it. There, the camera can only be conveyed through pose encodings [57, 90], which control it far less precisely than rendered geometry [54, 10]. The content, in turn, is left to the text prompt. Lyris also maintains an explicit point-cloud memory, but pairs it with a 3D layout of the objects that unseen regions should contain. Rendered into the same target views, this layout anchors the camera where the memory is empty and leaves the appearance of these objects, but no longer their placement, to the generative prior. As the generated views follow their requested cameras more closely, they also align more reliably with the memory, limiting the errors that accumulate in its geometry.

    Layout-conditioned generation. Scene structure is an effective control signal when it is available in advance. Generative renderers turn animated proxy meshes [9], 3D tracking videos [25], coarse geometry [36], or depth rendered by a game engine [50] into realistic or stylized video. Although some remain consistent even when a region is revisited [25, 50], they all require this structure to be modeled or captured beforehand. Looser controls ease this requirement by specifying mainly where content should appear, as boxes for images [6] or short video clips [66, 67, 5]. Layout-guided methods similarly generate entire indoor scenes from 3D layouts [18, 55, 78] and street scenes from road maps and object boxes [23, 48, 4, 52] or street and height maps [15]. However, these controls are typically authored by hand or taken from an existing scene or map, which does not scale to open-ended exploration. Lyris instead conditions on a coarse object layout that a vision-language model writes for unseen regions, along with a persistent memory that keeps revisited regions consistent.

    Language-driven scene planning. Large language and vision-language models have emerged as effective planners for visual content. Many systems use them to lay out 3D scenes [22, 80, 7, 43, 58, 91, 16], but these scenes inherit the synthetic appearance of the assets and engines that realize them. Other methods instead direct generative models through language, describing the content to generate next [85, 17] or iteratively refining prompts or plans for video generation [46, 79]. Although this avoids synthetic appearance, their plans remain natural language, which can name content but only coarsely describe where it belongs. Lyris bridges the two: a vision-language model authors a 3D layout of labeled boxes, and a video diffusion model turns it into a photorealistic video. Closest to our work, recent methods also guide video models with 3D boxes that a language model plans or programs [37, 64, 34]. However, these boxes direct individual objects and leave the scene around them to the video model, whereas ours lay out the scene beyond the capture. Concurrent to our work, AgiWorld [20] also plans unseen regions with a language-model agent, but conveys its layout through the text prompt, a strategy that we find far less effective than rendering the layout (Sec.4.4). CoDeR [21] instead re-creates the entire scene in code, which only approximates what the input image shows, whereas we keep the captured scene and lay out what lies beyond it.

    3 Method

    Given one or a few input views, a camera path, and an optional text description of what each part of the path should reveal, our goal is to generate a long video that follows the path far beyond the observed regions, while remaining consistent when the camera returns. Our solution is a chunk-wise autoregressive video model guided by a 3D layout of labeled object boxes, which a vision-language model plans for unseen regions, and by a persistent point-cloud memory and appearance references. We describe our object layouts in Sec.3.1, our scene memory in Sec.3.2, and our video model and its training in Sec.3.3. Figure2 illustrates our overall approach.

    3.1 Object Layouts

    Layout representation. We represent the layout as a set B={bᵢ} of labeled 3D bounding boxes, one per object, where each box bᵢ is parameterized by its center cᵢ∈ℝ³, size sᵢ∈ℝ³, rotation θᵢ about the gravity axis, and a text label. The boxes determine what unseen regions contain and where, and leave the shape and appearance of each object to the video model. As each box is tied to a single object, a user can also change what is generated by moving or relabeling boxes before generation (Fig.6).

    Planning. To let the layout build on what has already been generated, we use a vision-language model to plan the layout [22, 80, 58] of what each chunk will reveal right before it is generated (Fig.3). The planner receives the chunk’s start frame, the point-cloud memory, the boxes of earlier chunks, and the chunk’s cameras, and thus does not require the full camera path in advance. To keep the layout consistent with the existing scene, it first estimates a rectangular floor plan that encloses the memory’s points and the chunk’s cameras and fits boxes to the objects visible in the start frame (Fig.3a). It then determines which objects the chunk should reveal, following its description when one is given, and adds a box for each, placing it relative to the existing boxes and within the floor plan.

    Verification. To ensure that the layout is physically plausible and visible along the path, we verify the proposal with geometric checks (Fig.3c). The checks test whether each box is supported, lies within the floor plan and outside observed free space, does not collide with other boxes, is visible from the planned cameras, and satisfies the spatial relations of its description. We then let the model revise its proposal once, given the violations and renderings of the layout from above and from the planned cameras, and resolve the remaining violations with a deterministic repair (Fig.3b). We provide details in the supplement.

    Layout video and text prompt. We condition the video model on the layout through a layout video, which renders the boxes of objects yet to be generated from each chunk’s cameras ℂₖ. The layout video shows where each object belongs in every frame and anchors the camera to its path, even in unseen regions. To indicate what each box contains, we render it in a color unique to its label and name the object of each color in the text prompt (e.g., “the light violet box is a long table” in Fig.2).

    3.2 Scene Memory

    As the video model keeps no state across chunks, we maintain a scene memory of everything observed or generated so far, as a colored point cloud ℙ and a bank H of posed frames. We initialize it by reconstructing the input views [38, 69, 68].

    Memory video. To show the video model what the scene already contains, we render the point cloud ℙ from each chunk’s cameras ℂₖ, as in prior geometry-conditioned video models [54, 12, 95], and provide the resulting memory video as a reference video.

    Appearance references. As point renderings lack fine detail, we also provide a few frames of H as reference images. We select the frames whose views overlap the most with the chunk’s cameras, similar to Lyra2 [57], and provide details in the supplement.

    Memory update. To let later chunks build on what has been generated, we add each chunk to the memory once it is complete. We reconstruct a subset of its frames with Pi3X [69, 68] together with frames of the previous chunk, and align the reconstruction to the memory with a similarity transform fitted on these shared frames [63]. To keep misaligned geometry out of the memory, we accept the update only if the aligned cameras deviate from the requested ones by at most 15^∘ in rotation and a quarter of their spread in translation. We then add the new points to ℙ and the frames to H. A chunk that fails this test remains in the video but leaves the memory unchanged.

    Layout update. To keep the layout consistent with what has been generated, we then update it against the memory. We exclude the boxes of objects that the point cloud now shows in full from the layout video, and refit the boxes of partially generated objects to their points, so that the remainder of each object continues the part that exists. All other boxes remain as planned.

    3.3 Video Model

    Model. We start from a pretrained bidirectional video diffusion model (MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA [51]), freeze its VAE and Qwen3-VL encoder [3], and fine-tune its transformer with LoRA [30] via the original flow matching objective [45]. As the model natively supports reference images and videos, we provide the layout and memory videos as reference videos and the appearance references as reference images.

    Prefix frame. To maintain temporal coherence across chunks, each chunk starts from a prefix frame: an input view for the first chunk, and the last frame of the previous chunk for every other. The prefix frame also serves as an additional appearance reference. The supplement describes how we stabilize the transitions between chunks at inference.

    Camera embedding. The memory and layout videos convey the camera motion only where they show content. To provide camera control even when both are entirely empty, we encode the cameras ℂₖ as Plücker rays [26] and add them to the tokens of the target and reference frames via a linear layer in each transformer block. We zero-initialize these layers to ensure compatibility and stability with the pretrained initialization.

    Training. We construct training examples from captured clips of ScanNet++ [83] and DL3DV [44], treating each clip as one chunk and its first frame as the prefix frame. We render the memory video from geometry estimated from the input views instead of ground truth, so that the model must learn to handle the incomplete coverage and reconstruction artifacts that it encounters at inference. We derive the layout video from the 3D instance annotations of ScanNet++, using the boxes of objects visible beyond the first frame, and omit it for DL3DV clips, which provide no such annotations. We also drop the memory and layout videos independently with probability 0.2 each (and the text prompt with probability 0.1), so that a single model can generate from any subset of these conditions.

    4 Experiments

    As our goal is to extend captured scenes well beyond what was observed while remaining consistent upon return, we evaluate Lyris on long round-trip trajectories. We first give every method the same detailed description of what lies ahead, and assess how well each generates it (Sec.4.2). Exploring a new scene usually comes without such descriptions, so in Sec.4.3, we only provide the caption of the start frame, and we assess whether planning what lies ahead with a vision-language model is more effective than leaving it purely to the video model. We validate the contribution of individual components and measure how closely Lyris follows its layouts in Sec.4.4.

    4.1 Setup

    Implementation. We fine-tune MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA [51] with rank-32 LoRA on its attention and feed-forward layers, using 124-frame clips at 832×480 resolution from 9,926 DL3DV-10K [44] and 747 ScanNet++ v2 [83] scenes (the latter of which provide object annotations). We train on clips that start from one to five input views for 1,500 iterations using AdamW with a learning rate of 10⁻⁴ on 128 H100 GPUs. We then add clips that continue from a previous one for another 500 iterations (so that the model learns to build on its memory and retrieved references), and distill the resulting model into a few-step student via DMD2 [84]. We use MoGe-3 [38] to lift single frames, Pi3X [69, 68] to reconstruct multiple frames, GPT-6 to caption the training clips, and Claude Opus 5.5 to plan layouts. At test time, we retrieve three appearance references per chunk and sample with eight steps and no guidance. We provide more details in the supplement.

    Round trips. Each round trip follows the cameras of a real capture for up to 372 frames on the way out and retraces them on the way back, for a total of up to 744 frames, or about one minute of video at 12 fps. On average, the start frame observes only 29% of the pixels on the way out, leaving the rest to be generated, and the way back tests whether a method remembers what it generated there. In the directed setting (Sec.4.2), every method receives a detailed description of each 124-frame window of the path, written by GPT-6 from the captured video, and in the autonomous setting (Sec.4.3) only a caption of the start frame. All evaluation scenes are held out from training.

    Baselines. We compare Lyris to recent video generation methods that differ in how they leverage memory, namely AnyRecon [12], GEN3C [54], and Spatia [95], which condition on point-cloud renderings, Lyra2 [57], which instead establishes dense correspondences to history frames through per-frame geometry, and WorldCrafter [88], which queries an implicit 3D-aware memory. We also compare to SolarWM-H3 [32], a camera-controlled world model that builds on MiniMax-H3 as we do. All six baselines leave unseen regions directly to the video model. We run the official code of each method with its default settings and the same start frame, cameras, and text as Lyris (except for AnyRecon, whose official code uses an empty prompt).

    Metrics. We measure camera accuracy as the rotation and translation errors (RotErr, TransErr) between the input cameras and those that Depth Anything 3 (DA3) [42] recovers from the generated video, aligned at the first frame and up to scale, and report the imaging quality score of VBench [35] (Quality). As content generated in unseen regions need not match the ground truth, we compute PSNR, SSIM [70], and LPIPS [93] only over the pixels that the start frame observes, and measure consistency upon return as the DINOv2 [53] patch similarity between the two frames generated at each camera, over all revisited cameras (Revisit). As the descriptions of Sec.4.2 state what lies in unseen regions, we further report the fraction of the objects they name that a vision-language model finds in the generated video (Objects).

    4.2 Directed Layouts

    Datasets. We evaluate on ScanNet++ [83] and CA-1M [40] as real indoor captures with LiDAR depth and 3D object annotations, which we use in Sec.4.4 to measure how closely Lyris follows its layouts. We test on 20 held-out scenes of the former and the 20 longest landscape captures of the latter, which Lyris is not trained on. We provide additional results on DL3DV-Evaluation [44] (not overlapping with DL3DV-10K scenes) and from sparse input views in the supplement.

    Results. We summarize our results in Tab.1 and show a qualitative comparison in Fig.4. Lyris outperforms all baselines on every metric on both datasets, and follows the given cameras more than four times as accurately as the next-best method (SolarWM-H3). The baselines drift from the path once it leaves the start view, as their memory offers nothing to anchor the camera in unseen regions, whereas Lyris renders its layout there (Sec.4.4). Among the baselines, GEN3C best preserves the observed content through its explicit point cloud and WorldCrafter is the most consistent upon return through its implicit memory, but only our method achieves both by pairing a point cloud with retrieved appearance references.

    4.3 Autonomous Exploration

    Datasets. We evaluate on the ScanNet++ and CA-1M scenes of Sec.4.2 along with DL3DV-Evaluation [44] as a benchmark of diverse indoor and outdoor scenes, and SpatialVID [65] as in-the-wild videos that Lyris is not trained on. We again test on 20 scenes of each and provide additional details in the supplement.

    Results. We present quantitative results, using the same metrics as Tab.1, in Tab.2, and qualitative results in Fig.5. Lyris outperforms all baselines on every metric on all four datasets. Even without the descriptions of Sec.4.2, it outperforms every baseline that receives them on every metric (Tab.1), as its planner decides what lies ahead. Lyris also generalizes to the in-the-wild videos of SpatialVID, where it outperforms SolarWM-H3, which is trained on this dataset, on every metric. When the full camera path is available before generation, planning the layout for the whole path at once (Lyris w/ full path) further improves camera accuracy on CA-1M and SpatialVID, following the latter’s cameras more than three times as accurately as SolarWM-H3. Averaged over the six blocks of Tabs.1 and 2, Lyris reduces the rotation error of each block’s best baseline by 3.8× and improves on its Revisit by 22%.

    4.4 Ablation and Diagnostics

    Components. We ablate our design decisions by individually omitting the major components of our method: the layout, the memory’s point cloud, and the appearance references. We summarize our results in Tab.3. The layout is crucial, as omitting it increases the rotation error roughly three- to sevenfold and lowers consistency upon return, both with or without a description. Stating the layout only in the prompt, as the planner’s natural-language description of each chunk, instead of rendering it is far less effective, with a 2.8× higher rotation error. Omitting the memory’s point cloud degrades every metric, whereas omitting the appearance references mainly lowers consistency upon return. Lyris also remains ahead of all baselines in camera accuracy and consistency upon return with a smaller planner (Claude Haiku 5.5), an open-weight one (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next), or the smaller Cosmos3-Nano [52] as its video model. We provide these results in the supplement.

    Layout control. To test whether the generation follows its layout, we edit a plan and regenerate with the same inputs and seed (Fig.6). Moving a box moves its object and leaves its former place empty, and swapping two objects in the plan swaps them in the video, which lets a user edit the scene before it is generated. Over the round trips of Tab.1, we further measure the fraction of each box that the generated surface fills (adherence), for the objects that the start frame does not show (Tab.4). Lyris fills the boxes of its planned layout about a quarter more than when it generates without a layout. Given the annotated layout of the real scene instead, Lyris follows it as well, and its content covers more of the real objects than without a layout (Recall).

    Timing. Generating a 744-frame round trip takes about 28 minutes on a single H100 GPU, and planning its layout chunk by chunk adds a median of 10 minutes in the directed setting, for about 38 minutes end to end.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented Lyris, a long video generation framework that pairs a persistent point-cloud memory with a 3D layout that a vision-language model authors for unseen regions. The resulting loop preserves the existing scene while extending it according to the layout, and provides an explicit geometric interface for specifying what is generated. On minute-long round trips across four datasets, Lyris reduces the camera error of state-of-the-art methods by 3.8×.

    Limitations. Our method depends on the quality of the estimated geometry, as depth and alignment errors can accumulate in the memory and affect subsequent chunks. Our model still requires multiple steps of diffusion sampling and is not yet interactive.

    （参考文献见原文。）


    Supplementary Material

    We show videos of long walkthroughs, comparisons with the baselines, and layout edits on our project page: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/sil/projects/lyris/.

    Appendix A Additional Results

    A.1 Directed Round Trips on DL3DV

    We repeat the comparison of Tab.1 on the 20 indoor and outdoor DL3DV-Evaluation [44] scenes of Tab.2 and summarize our results in Tab.5. Lyris again outperforms all baselines on every metric, and follows the given cameras more than twice as accurately as the next-best method (WorldCrafter).

    A.2 Smaller and Open-Weight Planners

    We replace Claude Opus 5.5 with the smaller Claude Haiku 5.5 and with the open-weight Qwen3.8-Flash-Next111Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on Hugging Face, revision 812d96e1, served with vLLM at its released precision. on the directed CA-1M round trips of Tab.1, and summarize our results in Tab.6. With either planner, Lyris still outperforms all baselines on every metric of Tab.1, and follows the cameras roughly four times as accurately as the best of them. A stronger planner mainly produces a more complete layout, which places more of the described objects and satisfies more of their stated relations.

    A.3 Cosmos3-Nano as the Video Model

    To validate the effectiveness of our pipeline, we replace MiniMax-H3, whose transformer has 33B parameters, with the smaller Cosmos3-Nano [52], whose generator tower has 8B (Tab.7). We fully fine-tune this tower in the same two stages and on as many clips as Lyris (Tab.1), conditioning on the memory video, the layout video, and the appearance references, and distill it with DMD2. On the round trips of Tabs.1, 2 and 5, it still outperforms all baselines on every metric.

    A.4 Sparse Input Views

    Although our main experiments start from a single photo, Lyris also supports multiple posed views as input. We reconstruct these views into the initial point cloud of our scene memory and add them to its frame bank, so that each chunk can retrieve them as appearance references. To measure the impact of additional views, we generate the way out of the ScanNet++, DL3DV, and SpatialVID round trips of Tab.2 from one, three, or five views in the directed setting of Sec.4.2. We summarize our results in Tab.8 and show examples on our project page. Five views spread along the path improve PSNR over a single view by 2.5 to 3.8 dB on every dataset (and in each of the 60 scenes). Even when all five views lie within the first 40% of the path, PSNR over the remaining 60% (roughly 200 frames) still improves by more than 2 dB, as our persistent memory provides these views as conditioning for all subsequent chunks.

    A.5 Returns from a Different Viewpoint

    As our round trips retrace their cameras on the way back, we also evaluate consistency when each place is revisited from a different viewpoint. To do so, we shift each camera on the way back of the directed CA-1M round trips of Tab.1 by 0.5 to 1 m, while keeping it pointed at the same part of the scene. As no two frames then share a camera, we warp the most overlapping frame from the way out into each frame of the way back (using the depth and cameras that DA3 estimates from the generated video), and measure their DINOv2 similarity over the overlap. Lyris remains the most consistent method (Tab.9), with a similarity of 0.683 against 0.611 for the next-best method (SolarWM-H3).

    A.6 Consistency vs. Camera Accuracy

    As Revisit compares the two frames generated at each revisited camera, it also drops when a method deviates from the requested cameras. To disentangle consistency from camera accuracy, we recompute Revisit over only the frame pairs in which both frames have a rotation error of at most 5^∘, and summarize our results in Tab.10. Lyris remains the most consistent method in every block of Tabs.1 and 2 (0.76 to 0.83 against at most 0.73 for the baselines).

    A.7 Qualitative Ablation

    We illustrate the ablations of Tab.3 in Fig.7, at a camera that a directed CA-1M round trip visits on the way out and again on the way back. Lyris generates the same content upon return. Without the layout, the camera drifts from its path (with a rotation error of 93.9^∘ at this camera, against 2.0^∘ for Lyris) and views a different part of the scene. Without the memory’s point cloud (and thus with a blank memory video), the appearance references alone do not preserve the scene, and the content changes upon return. Conversely, the point cloud alone preserves the overall structure, but details change without the appearance references (e.g., the circled object that appears on the lid).

    A.8 Layout Editing

    As our layout consists of one labeled box per object, a user can directly edit it to control what Lyris generates. In unseen regions, the boxes determine what is generated and where, and moving, swapping, or adding them changes the content accordingly (Fig.6). In the existing scene, objects are also stored in our memory, which we thus edit along with the layout. As this memory is an explicit point cloud, we simply move an object’s points together with its box, and hide the points that a new box occludes. Although Lyris is trained only on static scenes, we find that moving a box over time also moves its object in the generated video (e.g., a chair sliding away from a wall or a ball rolling across the floor). We illustrate each of these edits on our project page.

    Appendix B Method Details

    B.1 Layout Planning

    Planning. We use Claude Opus 5.5 as our planner, although Lyris also outperforms all baselines with smaller and open-weight planners (Sec.A.2). As our layout only requires one labeled box per object, we simply query the planner with fixed prompts, without tools or fine-tuning. It first localizes each object visible in the start frame with a 2D bounding box, which we lift to 3D by fitting a box to the memory points within it. To place the objects that the chunk should reveal, we render the point-cloud memory and the fitted boxes from above and from four of the chunk’s cameras, overlaid with a metric grid so that the planner can specify each new box in metric coordinates (Fig.8). Similar to LayoutGPT [22], we retrieve two layouts with matching objects from the annotated ScanNet++ scenes of our training set as in-context examples, and provide median object sizes.

    Verification. We sample five proposals and verify each with the six geometric checks of Sec.3.1, whose criteria we list in Tab.11. We select the proposal with the fewest violations and let the planner revise it once, after which the deterministic repair resolves the remaining violations by displacing each flagged box as little as possible. Finally, we remove the placed boxes that are still not visible, collide with another box, or contradict a stated relation. The checks use the same tolerances for every scene and dataset. They are mainly for gross errors, and their exact values are not critical, as Lyris is robust to imprecise boxes. Even when we perturb the final boxes with Gaussian noise (standard deviations of up to 0.3 m, 25%, and 20^∘ in position, size, and orientation), the rotation error on the directed CA-1M round trips increases by less than 1^∘, and Lyris still outperforms all baselines on every metric of Tab.1.

    Autonomous setting. Given only a caption of the input view, the planner itself decides which objects each chunk should reveal, and writes the chunk’s description from the resulting layout. When the full camera path is available before generation (Lyris w/ full path in Tab.2), it instead plans the layout for the whole path at once, from the input views and the cameras of all chunks.

    B.2 Layout Rendering and Update

    Rendering. As the text prompt refers to each box by its color, we render the boxes of each training clip in perceptually distinct named colors, which we sample at random for each clip. As each training clip contains at most 12 boxes, we likewise render at most 12 boxes per chunk at inference, and sample a palette of 12 colors once per path. Each label thus retains its color across chunks, and a path with more than 12 labels reuses colors across chunks while keeping those within each chunk distinct.

    Update. As the memory video already shows what has been generated, the layout video prioritizes rendering only what has not. Before each subsequent chunk, we thus measure how much of each object the memory contains, as the fraction of its box’s pixels that are covered by memory points inside the box. Above 0.8, we consider the object fully generated and exclude its box. Between 0.1 and 0.8, we consider it partially generated and refit its box to the largest cluster of memory points around it, so that the remainder of the object continues the part that exists. As this cluster can include neighboring surfaces (e.g., the wall behind the object), we preserve the orientation of the box and allow each side to grow by at most 1.5×. Otherwise, the object is yet to be generated and its box remains as planned. When more than 12 boxes remain, we prioritize those planned in unseen regions over those fitted to visible objects, as the prefix frame already shows the latter.

    B.3 Reference Retrieval

    From the bank H of input views and previously generated frames, we retrieve up to three appearance references per chunk, selected to maximize their joint coverage of the chunk’s views. For each frame i in H, we project its estimated depth into every eighth camera of the chunk to obtain the set Vᵢ of pixels that it observes, with a depth test for occlusion. As each chunk already receives its prefix frame, we initialize the selection ℝ with it and greedily add the frame that maximizes the additional coverage,

    i^*=\underseti∉ℝ\arg\max|Vᵢ∖\bigcup_j∈ℝVⱼ|.

    		(1)

    Once no frame increases the coverage, we select the remaining references by the proximity of their cameras to the chunk’s. When a chunk returns close to the start of the path, we additionally include the first input view, so that the chunk is conditioned on the captured view itself.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：基于记忆的方法能保住已见内容，但一旦离开，相机就会偏离路径，文字提示能命名物体却无法放置它们。

要点：

  • 任务定义：从一张照片出发探索场景，需要生成一段长距离、相机可控的漫游，**远远超出被拍到的范围，且在回到原处时仍保持一致**
  • 两类方法的短板：**基于记忆**的视频生成能保住已见内容，但在视野之外没有锚点，于是相机偏离轨迹，而文字提示**只能命名物体、无法放置物体**；**布局条件**的方法提供了这种锚点与精确控制，但缺少长程记忆
  • Lyris 因此把两者接起来：**布局引导 + 持久 3D 记忆**，让「走远」与「回头一致」同时成立

为什么值得看：这是「状态外置」主线的又一次收敛：记忆负责「看过什么」，布局负责「没看过的地方该有什么」。引擎里的对应物就是场景图——你不可能只靠回放历史帧来维持一个开放世界。

中文摘要：仅凭一张照片探索场景，要求生成一段长距离、相机可控的漫游，既要远远超出原始拍摄范围，又要在返回时保持一致性。基于记忆的视频生成方法能保住已经看过的内容，但在视野之外没有锚点：相机会逐渐偏离路径，而文字提示虽然能命名物体，却无法规定它们的位置。布局条件的方法恰好提供了这种锚点与精确的空间控制，但缺少长程记忆。Lyris 因此把两者结合：用布局引导生成、用持久的 3D 记忆维持一致性，使「走远」与「回头仍然一致」这两件事同时成立。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-24

本期推送：2026-11-25

Lyris: Layout-Guided Long Video Generation with Persistent 3D Memory

Abstract

Exploring a scene from as little as a single photo requires generating a long, camera-controlled walkthrough that extends far beyond what was captured, yet remains consistent upon return. Memory-based video generation methods preserve what they have already seen, but have no anchor beyond it, where the camera drifts from its path and a text prompt can name objects but not place them. Layout-conditioned methods provide such an anchor and precise control over what appears where, but rely on layouts that are typically authored by hand. Both limitations arise because, beyond what was captured, nothing anchors the video model unless a human authors one. To overcome both, we propose Lyris, a long video generation framework that never leaves the video model without an anchor: a persistent point-cloud memory where the scene has been observed or generated, and a 3D layout that a vision-language model authors where it has not. Our key insight is that the interface between the two models can be surprisingly coarse. A layout of one labeled 3D box per object is simple enough for a vision-language model to author (and for a user to edit), yet expressive enough for a video model to follow once rendered along the camera path. We demonstrate walkthroughs of over three minutes and 50 meters from a single photo, passing through doorways into rooms it never shows. When evaluated on minute-long round trips across four datasets, Lyris outperforms state-of-the-art methods by a wide margin, reducing camera error by 3.8× and improving consistency upon return by 22% on average.

**footnotetext: Work done during an internship at NVIDIA.

1 Introduction

Virtual touring [61], content creation, and simulation for physical AI [62, 4] benefit from 3D environments that can be explored freely. Creating such environments from as little as a single photo requires generating a long, camera-controlled walkthrough beyond the captured view, passing through doorways and into unseen rooms. These regions must form a plausible extension of the observed scene and retain their layout and appearance when the camera returns.

Recent video generative models [60, 51, 52] can generate photorealistic clips from an image and a text prompt, but only seconds at a time. Memory-based methods extend them to long rollouts by conditioning each new chunk on the history, through compressed or retrieved past views [86, 41, 57, 29], learned implicit representations [88, 72], or explicitly reconstructed geometry [95, 12, 49]. This memory preserves what has already been seen but offers nothing beyond it. There, the camera path reaches the model only as a pose encoding [57, 90], a far weaker signal than rendered geometry [54, 10], and the camera drifts from its path as unseen regions accumulate. The content of the unseen regions is left to the text prompt, which can name objects and relate them coarsely, but cannot specify where they belong or how one space connects to the next. Layout-conditioned methods instead condition generation on an explicit scene layout, such as untextured geometry, object boxes, or maps [36, 5, 48], and offer precise control over the spatial arrangement of the objects. However, these methods take the layout as an input, typically authored by hand, which does not scale to open-ended exploration.

To overcome both limitations, we propose Lyris, a long video generation framework in which a vision-language model authors the layout of unseen regions before a video model generates them. Our key insight is that the interface between the two models can be surprisingly coarse: a 3D layout with one labeled bounding box per object [22, 80, 58] is simple enough for a vision-language model to author (and for a user to edit), yet expressive enough for a video model to follow. We fine-tune a pretrained video diffusion model to follow renderings of this layout, which specify what appears where and anchor the camera to its path, even in unseen regions. To remain consistent upon return, we reconstruct each generated chunk and write it into a persistent point-cloud memory, which conditions every subsequent chunk alongside the layout. The resulting loop between explicit 3D geometry and photorealistic video generation extends the walkthrough far beyond the photo, as the layout and the memory condition each chunk, and each generated chunk in turn extends the memory from which the next layout is planned.

We make the following contributions:

  • •

    We present Lyris, a long video generation framework that pairs a 3D layout of unseen regions planned by a vision-language model with a persistent 3D memory of existing ones, enabling consistent 3D world exploration from as little as a single image without human authoring.

  • •

    We demonstrate that the layout is crucial for camera control in unseen regions, and that rendering it into the target views is far more effective than stating it in the text prompt.

  • •

    We outperform state-of-the-art methods on minute-long round trips across four datasets, reducing camera error by 3.8× and improving consistency upon return by 22% on average.

    • 2 Related Work

    Camera-controlled video generation. Video diffusion models [28] generate photorealistic clips [8, 82, 73, 60] and increasingly accept multimodal conditions [56, 51, 52]. To control the viewpoint, existing methods inject per-frame camera poses [71] or dense Plücker ray embeddings [26, 77], often through dedicated conditioning branches [2, 1], and extend beyond single clips by conditioning each new clip on frames of the preceding one [27]. Geometry-guided approaches instead condition on point-cloud renderings at the target views [89, 54, 10, 87], couple implicit reconstruction of the input views with generation [39], or repair renderings of imperfect reconstructions [74, 14]. These methods guide generation where geometry has been observed, but leave the content of unobserved regions to the generative prior. SpatialCrafter [19] instead generates the geometry of these regions with a 3D generator conditioned on the input image alone, whereas Lyris lays them out as labeled boxes that a vision-language model can write and a user can edit.

    Scene memory for long video generation. To generate long videos, memory-based methods condition each new frame or chunk on previously observed or generated content. Many approaches compress this history into a limited token budget [92, 29, 11, 72] or retrieve its most relevant parts [86, 76, 41, 81]. However, the model must still infer how this history maps to the target view, which often fails under large viewpoint changes [57]. A second line of work addresses this by aligning the history with the target camera before generation [13, 57, 90, 88], or by maintaining scene geometry that is rendered into the target views [54, 75, 95, 94, 33, 12, 49, 59]. Although rendering aligns the memory with each target view, errors can accumulate in the geometry itself [94, 49, 59]. Other methods instead generate and simulate an editable latent 3D scene around the agent, albeit trained with ground-truth 3D supervision in a voxel game [24], or sample all views jointly in a geometry-native latent space [47]. Whatever its form, however, a memory of past frames preserves what has already been seen but offers nothing beyond it. There, the camera can only be conveyed through pose encodings [57, 90], which control it far less precisely than rendered geometry [54, 10]. The content, in turn, is left to the text prompt. Lyris also maintains an explicit point-cloud memory, but pairs it with a 3D layout of the objects that unseen regions should contain. Rendered into the same target views, this layout anchors the camera where the memory is empty and leaves the appearance of these objects, but no longer their placement, to the generative prior. As the generated views follow their requested cameras more closely, they also align more reliably with the memory, limiting the errors that accumulate in its geometry.

    Layout-conditioned generation. Scene structure is an effective control signal when it is available in advance. Generative renderers turn animated proxy meshes [9], 3D tracking videos [25], coarse geometry [36], or depth rendered by a game engine [50] into realistic or stylized video. Although some remain consistent even when a region is revisited [25, 50], they all require this structure to be modeled or captured beforehand. Looser controls ease this requirement by specifying mainly where content should appear, as boxes for images [6] or short video clips [66, 67, 5]. Layout-guided methods similarly generate entire indoor scenes from 3D layouts [18, 55, 78] and street scenes from road maps and object boxes [23, 48, 4, 52] or street and height maps [15]. However, these controls are typically authored by hand or taken from an existing scene or map, which does not scale to open-ended exploration. Lyris instead conditions on a coarse object layout that a vision-language model writes for unseen regions, along with a persistent memory that keeps revisited regions consistent.

    Language-driven scene planning. Large language and vision-language models have emerged as effective planners for visual content. Many systems use them to lay out 3D scenes [22, 80, 7, 43, 58, 91, 16], but these scenes inherit the synthetic appearance of the assets and engines that realize them. Other methods instead direct generative models through language, describing the content to generate next [85, 17] or iteratively refining prompts or plans for video generation [46, 79]. Although this avoids synthetic appearance, their plans remain natural language, which can name content but only coarsely describe where it belongs. Lyris bridges the two: a vision-language model authors a 3D layout of labeled boxes, and a video diffusion model turns it into a photorealistic video. Closest to our work, recent methods also guide video models with 3D boxes that a language model plans or programs [37, 64, 34]. However, these boxes direct individual objects and leave the scene around them to the video model, whereas ours lay out the scene beyond the capture. Concurrent to our work, AgiWorld [20] also plans unseen regions with a language-model agent, but conveys its layout through the text prompt, a strategy that we find far less effective than rendering the layout (Sec.4.4). CoDeR [21] instead re-creates the entire scene in code, which only approximates what the input image shows, whereas we keep the captured scene and lay out what lies beyond it.

    3 Method

    Given one or a few input views, a camera path, and an optional text description of what each part of the path should reveal, our goal is to generate a long video that follows the path far beyond the observed regions, while remaining consistent when the camera returns. Our solution is a chunk-wise autoregressive video model guided by a 3D layout of labeled object boxes, which a vision-language model plans for unseen regions, and by a persistent point-cloud memory and appearance references. We describe our object layouts in Sec.3.1, our scene memory in Sec.3.2, and our video model and its training in Sec.3.3. Figure2 illustrates our overall approach.

    3.1 Object Layouts

    Layout representation. We represent the layout as a set B={bᵢ} of labeled 3D bounding boxes, one per object, where each box bᵢ is parameterized by its center cᵢ∈ℝ³, size sᵢ∈ℝ³, rotation θᵢ about the gravity axis, and a text label. The boxes determine what unseen regions contain and where, and leave the shape and appearance of each object to the video model. As each box is tied to a single object, a user can also change what is generated by moving or relabeling boxes before generation (Fig.6).

    Planning. To let the layout build on what has already been generated, we use a vision-language model to plan the layout [22, 80, 58] of what each chunk will reveal right before it is generated (Fig.3). The planner receives the chunk’s start frame, the point-cloud memory, the boxes of earlier chunks, and the chunk’s cameras, and thus does not require the full camera path in advance. To keep the layout consistent with the existing scene, it first estimates a rectangular floor plan that encloses the memory’s points and the chunk’s cameras and fits boxes to the objects visible in the start frame (Fig.3a). It then determines which objects the chunk should reveal, following its description when one is given, and adds a box for each, placing it relative to the existing boxes and within the floor plan.

    Verification. To ensure that the layout is physically plausible and visible along the path, we verify the proposal with geometric checks (Fig.3c). The checks test whether each box is supported, lies within the floor plan and outside observed free space, does not collide with other boxes, is visible from the planned cameras, and satisfies the spatial relations of its description. We then let the model revise its proposal once, given the violations and renderings of the layout from above and from the planned cameras, and resolve the remaining violations with a deterministic repair (Fig.3b). We provide details in the supplement.

    Layout video and text prompt. We condition the video model on the layout through a layout video, which renders the boxes of objects yet to be generated from each chunk’s cameras ℂₖ. The layout video shows where each object belongs in every frame and anchors the camera to its path, even in unseen regions. To indicate what each box contains, we render it in a color unique to its label and name the object of each color in the text prompt (e.g., “the light violet box is a long table” in Fig.2).

    3.2 Scene Memory

    As the video model keeps no state across chunks, we maintain a scene memory of everything observed or generated so far, as a colored point cloud ℙ and a bank H of posed frames. We initialize it by reconstructing the input views [38, 69, 68].

    Memory video. To show the video model what the scene already contains, we render the point cloud ℙ from each chunk’s cameras ℂₖ, as in prior geometry-conditioned video models [54, 12, 95], and provide the resulting memory video as a reference video.

    Appearance references. As point renderings lack fine detail, we also provide a few frames of H as reference images. We select the frames whose views overlap the most with the chunk’s cameras, similar to Lyra2 [57], and provide details in the supplement.

    Memory update. To let later chunks build on what has been generated, we add each chunk to the memory once it is complete. We reconstruct a subset of its frames with Pi3X [69, 68] together with frames of the previous chunk, and align the reconstruction to the memory with a similarity transform fitted on these shared frames [63]. To keep misaligned geometry out of the memory, we accept the update only if the aligned cameras deviate from the requested ones by at most 15^∘ in rotation and a quarter of their spread in translation. We then add the new points to ℙ and the frames to H. A chunk that fails this test remains in the video but leaves the memory unchanged.

    Layout update. To keep the layout consistent with what has been generated, we then update it against the memory. We exclude the boxes of objects that the point cloud now shows in full from the layout video, and refit the boxes of partially generated objects to their points, so that the remainder of each object continues the part that exists. All other boxes remain as planned.

    3.3 Video Model

    Model. We start from a pretrained bidirectional video diffusion model (MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA [51]), freeze its VAE and Qwen3-VL encoder [3], and fine-tune its transformer with LoRA [30] via the original flow matching objective [45]. As the model natively supports reference images and videos, we provide the layout and memory videos as reference videos and the appearance references as reference images.

    Prefix frame. To maintain temporal coherence across chunks, each chunk starts from a prefix frame: an input view for the first chunk, and the last frame of the previous chunk for every other. The prefix frame also serves as an additional appearance reference. The supplement describes how we stabilize the transitions between chunks at inference.

    Camera embedding. The memory and layout videos convey the camera motion only where they show content. To provide camera control even when both are entirely empty, we encode the cameras ℂₖ as Plücker rays [26] and add them to the tokens of the target and reference frames via a linear layer in each transformer block. We zero-initialize these layers to ensure compatibility and stability with the pretrained initialization.

    Training. We construct training examples from captured clips of ScanNet++ [83] and DL3DV [44], treating each clip as one chunk and its first frame as the prefix frame. We render the memory video from geometry estimated from the input views instead of ground truth, so that the model must learn to handle the incomplete coverage and reconstruction artifacts that it encounters at inference. We derive the layout video from the 3D instance annotations of ScanNet++, using the boxes of objects visible beyond the first frame, and omit it for DL3DV clips, which provide no such annotations. We also drop the memory and layout videos independently with probability 0.2 each (and the text prompt with probability 0.1), so that a single model can generate from any subset of these conditions.

    4 Experiments

    As our goal is to extend captured scenes well beyond what was observed while remaining consistent upon return, we evaluate Lyris on long round-trip trajectories. We first give every method the same detailed description of what lies ahead, and assess how well each generates it (Sec.4.2). Exploring a new scene usually comes without such descriptions, so in Sec.4.3, we only provide the caption of the start frame, and we assess whether planning what lies ahead with a vision-language model is more effective than leaving it purely to the video model. We validate the contribution of individual components and measure how closely Lyris follows its layouts in Sec.4.4.

    4.1 Setup

    Implementation.
