We fine-tune MiniMax-H3 Ref2VA [51] with rank-32 LoRA on its attention and feed-forward layers, using 124-frame clips at 832×480 resolution from 9,926 DL3DV-10K [44] and 747 ScanNet++ v2 [83] scenes (the latter of which provide object annotations). We train on clips that start from one to five input views for 1,500 iterations using AdamW with a learning rate of 10⁻⁴ on 128 H100 GPUs. We then add clips that continue from a previous one for another 500 iterations (so that the model learns to build on its memory and retrieved references), and distill the resulting model into a few-step student via DMD2 [84]. We use MoGe-3 [38] to lift single frames, Pi3X [69, 68] to reconstruct multiple frames, GPT-6 to caption the training clips, and Claude Opus 5.5 to plan layouts. At test time, we retrieve three appearance references per chunk and sample with eight steps and no guidance. We provide more details in the supplement.

    Round trips. Each round trip follows the cameras of a real capture for up to 372 frames on the way out and retraces them on the way back, for a total of up to 744 frames, or about one minute of video at 12 fps. On average, the start frame observes only 29% of the pixels on the way out, leaving the rest to be generated, and the way back tests whether a method remembers what it generated there. In the directed setting (Sec.4.2), every method receives a detailed description of each 124-frame window of the path, written by GPT-6 from the captured video, and in the autonomous setting (Sec.4.3) only a caption of the start frame. All evaluation scenes are held out from training.

    Baselines. We compare Lyris to recent video generation methods that differ in how they leverage memory, namely AnyRecon [12], GEN3C [54], and Spatia [95], which condition on point-cloud renderings, Lyra2 [57], which instead establishes dense correspondences to history frames through per-frame geometry, and WorldCrafter [88], which queries an implicit 3D-aware memory. We also compare to SolarWM-H3 [32], a camera-controlled world model that builds on MiniMax-H3 as we do. All six baselines leave unseen regions directly to the video model. We run the official code of each method with its default settings and the same start frame, cameras, and text as Lyris (except for AnyRecon, whose official code uses an empty prompt).

    Metrics. We measure camera accuracy as the rotation and translation errors (RotErr, TransErr) between the input cameras and those that Depth Anything 3 (DA3) [42] recovers from the generated video, aligned at the first frame and up to scale, and report the imaging quality score of VBench [35] (Quality). As content generated in unseen regions need not match the ground truth, we compute PSNR, SSIM [70], and LPIPS [93] only over the pixels that the start frame observes, and measure consistency upon return as the DINOv2 [53] patch similarity between the two frames generated at each camera, over all revisited cameras (Revisit). As the descriptions of Sec.4.2 state what lies in unseen regions, we further report the fraction of the objects they name that a vision-language model finds in the generated video (Objects).

    4.2 Directed Layouts

    Datasets. We evaluate on ScanNet++ [83] and CA-1M [40] as real indoor captures with LiDAR depth and 3D object annotations, which we use in Sec.4.4 to measure how closely Lyris follows its layouts. We test on 20 held-out scenes of the former and the 20 longest landscape captures of the latter, which Lyris is not trained on. We provide additional results on DL3DV-Evaluation [44] (not overlapping with DL3DV-10K scenes) and from sparse input views in the supplement.

    Results. We summarize our results in Tab.1 and show a qualitative comparison in Fig.4. Lyris outperforms all baselines on every metric on both datasets, and follows the given cameras more than four times as accurately as the next-best method (SolarWM-H3). The baselines drift from the path once it leaves the start view, as their memory offers nothing to anchor the camera in unseen regions, whereas Lyris renders its layout there (Sec.4.4). Among the baselines, GEN3C best preserves the observed content through its explicit point cloud and WorldCrafter is the most consistent upon return through its implicit memory, but only our method achieves both by pairing a point cloud with retrieved appearance references.

    4.3 Autonomous Exploration

    Datasets. We evaluate on the ScanNet++ and CA-1M scenes of Sec.4.2 along with DL3DV-Evaluation [44] as a benchmark of diverse indoor and outdoor scenes, and SpatialVID [65] as in-the-wild videos that Lyris is not trained on. We again test on 20 scenes of each and provide additional details in the supplement.

    Results. We present quantitative results, using the same metrics as Tab.1, in Tab.2, and qualitative results in Fig.5. Lyris outperforms all baselines on every metric on all four datasets. Even without the descriptions of Sec.4.2, it outperforms every baseline that receives them on every metric (Tab.1), as its planner decides what lies ahead. Lyris also generalizes to the in-the-wild videos of SpatialVID, where it outperforms SolarWM-H3, which is trained on this dataset, on every metric. When the full camera path is available before generation, planning the layout for the whole path at once (Lyris w/ full path) further improves camera accuracy on CA-1M and SpatialVID, following the latter’s cameras more than three times as accurately as SolarWM-H3. Averaged over the six blocks of Tabs.1 and 2, Lyris reduces the rotation error of each block’s best baseline by 3.8× and improves on its Revisit by 22%.

    4.4 Ablation and Diagnostics

    Components. We ablate our design decisions by individually omitting the major components of our method: the layout, the memory’s point cloud, and the appearance references. We summarize our results in Tab.3. The layout is crucial, as omitting it increases the rotation error roughly three- to sevenfold and lowers consistency upon return, both with or without a description. Stating the layout only in the prompt, as the planner’s natural-language description of each chunk, instead of rendering it is far less effective, with a 2.8× higher rotation error. Omitting the memory’s point cloud degrades every metric, whereas omitting the appearance references mainly lowers consistency upon return. Lyris also remains ahead of all baselines in camera accuracy and consistency upon return with a smaller planner (Claude Haiku 5.5), an open-weight one (Qwen3.8-Flash-Next), or the smaller Cosmos3-Nano [52] as its video model. We provide these results in the supplement.

    Layout control. To test whether the generation follows its layout, we edit a plan and regenerate with the same inputs and seed (Fig.6). Moving a box moves its object and leaves its former place empty, and swapping two objects in the plan swaps them in the video, which lets a user edit the scene before it is generated. Over the round trips of Tab.1, we further measure the fraction of each box that the generated surface fills (adherence), for the objects that the start frame does not show (Tab.4). Lyris fills the boxes of its planned layout about a quarter more than when it generates without a layout. Given the annotated layout of the real scene instead, Lyris follows it as well, and its content covers more of the real objects than without a layout (Recall).

    Timing. Generating a 744-frame round trip takes about 28 minutes on a single H100 GPU, and planning its layout chunk by chunk adds a median of 10 minutes in the directed setting, for about 38 minutes end to end.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented Lyris, a long video generation framework that pairs a persistent point-cloud memory with a 3D layout that a vision-language model authors for unseen regions. The resulting loop preserves the existing scene while extending it according to the layout, and provides an explicit geometric interface for specifying what is generated. On minute-long round trips across four datasets, Lyris reduces the camera error of state-of-the-art methods by 3.8×.

    Limitations. Our method depends on the quality of the estimated geometry, as depth and alignment errors can accumulate in the memory and affect subsequent chunks. Our model still requires multiple steps of diffusion sampling and is not yet interactive.

    （参考文献见原文。）


    Supplementary Material

    We show videos of long walkthroughs, comparisons with the baselines, and layout edits on our project page: https://research.nvidia.com/labs/sil/projects/lyris/.

    Appendix A Additional Results

    A.1 Directed Round Trips on DL3DV

    We repeat the comparison of Tab.1 on the 20 indoor and outdoor DL3DV-Evaluation [44] scenes of Tab.2 and summarize our results in Tab.5. Lyris again outperforms all baselines on every metric, and follows the given cameras more than twice as accurately as the next-best method (WorldCrafter).

    A.2 Smaller and Open-Weight Planners

    We replace Claude Opus 5.5 with the smaller Claude Haiku 5.5 and with the open-weight Qwen3.8-Flash-Next111Qwen/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on Hugging Face, revision 812d96e1, served with vLLM at its released precision. on the directed CA-1M round trips of Tab.1, and summarize our results in Tab.6. With either planner, Lyris still outperforms all baselines on every metric of Tab.1, and follows the cameras roughly four times as accurately as the best of them. A stronger planner mainly produces a more complete layout, which places more of the described objects and satisfies more of their stated relations.

    A.3 Cosmos3-Nano as the Video Model

    To validate the effectiveness of our pipeline, we replace MiniMax-H3, whose transformer has 33B parameters, with the smaller Cosmos3-Nano [52], whose generator tower has 8B (Tab.7). We fully fine-tune this tower in the same two stages and on as many clips as Lyris (Tab.1), conditioning on the memory video, the layout video, and the appearance references, and distill it with DMD2. On the round trips of Tabs.1, 2 and 5, it still outperforms all baselines on every metric.

    A.4 Sparse Input Views

    Although our main experiments start from a single photo, Lyris also supports multiple posed views as input. We reconstruct these views into the initial point cloud of our scene memory and add them to its frame bank, so that each chunk can retrieve them as appearance references. To measure the impact of additional views, we generate the way out of the ScanNet++, DL3DV, and SpatialVID round trips of Tab.2 from one, three, or five views in the directed setting of Sec.4.2. We summarize our results in Tab.8 and show examples on our project page. Five views spread along the path improve PSNR over a single view by 2.5 to 3.8 dB on every dataset (and in each of the 60 scenes). Even when all five views lie within the first 40% of the path, PSNR over the remaining 60% (roughly 200 frames) still improves by more than 2 dB, as our persistent memory provides these views as conditioning for all subsequent chunks.

    A.5 Returns from a Different Viewpoint

    As our round trips retrace their cameras on the way back, we also evaluate consistency when each place is revisited from a different viewpoint. To do so, we shift each camera on the way back of the directed CA-1M round trips of Tab.1 by 0.5 to 1 m, while keeping it pointed at the same part of the scene. As no two frames then share a camera, we warp the most overlapping frame from the way out into each frame of the way back (using the depth and cameras that DA3 estimates from the generated video), and measure their DINOv2 similarity over the overlap. Lyris remains the most consistent method (Tab.9), with a similarity of 0.683 against 0.611 for the next-best method (SolarWM-H3).

    A.6 Consistency vs. Camera Accuracy

    As Revisit compares the two frames generated at each revisited camera, it also drops when a method deviates from the requested cameras. To disentangle consistency from camera accuracy, we recompute Revisit over only the frame pairs in which both frames have a rotation error of at most 5^∘, and summarize our results in Tab.10. Lyris remains the most consistent method in every block of Tabs.1 and 2 (0.76 to 0.83 against at most 0.73 for the baselines).

    A.7 Qualitative Ablation

    We illustrate the ablations of Tab.3 in Fig.7, at a camera that a directed CA-1M round trip visits on the way out and again on the way back. Lyris generates the same content upon return. Without the layout, the camera drifts from its path (with a rotation error of 93.9^∘ at this camera, against 2.0^∘ for Lyris) and views a different part of the scene. Without the memory’s point cloud (and thus with a blank memory video), the appearance references alone do not preserve the scene, and the content changes upon return. Conversely, the point cloud alone preserves the overall structure, but details change without the appearance references (e.g., the circled object that appears on the lid).

    A.8 Layout Editing

    As our layout consists of one labeled box per object, a user can directly edit it to control what Lyris generates. In unseen regions, the boxes determine what is generated and where, and moving, swapping, or adding them changes the content accordingly (Fig.6). In the existing scene, objects are also stored in our memory, which we thus edit along with the layout. As this memory is an explicit point cloud, we simply move an object’s points together with its box, and hide the points that a new box occludes. Although Lyris is trained only on static scenes, we find that moving a box over time also moves its object in the generated video (e.g., a chair sliding away from a wall or a ball rolling across the floor). We illustrate each of these edits on our project page.

    Appendix B Method Details

    B.1 Layout Planning

    Planning. We use Claude Opus 5.5 as our planner, although Lyris also outperforms all baselines with smaller and open-weight planners (Sec.A.2). As our layout only requires one labeled box per object, we simply query the planner with fixed prompts, without tools or fine-tuning. It first localizes each object visible in the start frame with a 2D bounding box, which we lift to 3D by fitting a box to the memory points within it. To place the objects that the chunk should reveal, we render the point-cloud memory and the fitted boxes from above and from four of the chunk’s cameras, overlaid with a metric grid so that the planner can specify each new box in metric coordinates (Fig.8). Similar to LayoutGPT [22], we retrieve two layouts with matching objects from the annotated ScanNet++ scenes of our training set as in-context examples, and provide median object sizes.

    Verification. We sample five proposals and verify each with the six geometric checks of Sec.3.1, whose criteria we list in Tab.11. We select the proposal with the fewest violations and let the planner revise it once, after which the deterministic repair resolves the remaining violations by displacing each flagged box as little as possible. Finally, we remove the placed boxes that are still not visible, collide with another box, or contradict a stated relation. The checks use the same tolerances for every scene and dataset. They are mainly for gross errors, and their exact values are not critical, as Lyris is robust to imprecise boxes. Even when we perturb the final boxes with Gaussian noise (standard deviations of up to 0.3 m, 25%, and 20^∘ in position, size, and orientation), the rotation error on the directed CA-1M round trips increases by less than 1^∘, and Lyris still outperforms all baselines on every metric of Tab.1.

    Autonomous setting. Given only a caption of the input view, the planner itself decides which objects each chunk should reveal, and writes the chunk’s description from the resulting layout. When the full camera path is available before generation (Lyris w/ full path in Tab.2), it instead plans the layout for the whole path at once, from the input views and the cameras of all chunks.

    B.2 Layout Rendering and Update

    Rendering. As the text prompt refers to each box by its color, we render the boxes of each training clip in perceptually distinct named colors, which we sample at random for each clip. As each training clip contains at most 12 boxes, we likewise render at most 12 boxes per chunk at inference, and sample a palette of 12 colors once per path. Each label thus retains its color across chunks, and a path with more than 12 labels reuses colors across chunks while keeping those within each chunk distinct.

    Update. As the memory video already shows what has been generated, the layout video prioritizes rendering only what has not. Before each subsequent chunk, we thus measure how much of each object the memory contains, as the fraction of its box’s pixels that are covered by memory points inside the box. Above 0.8, we consider the object fully generated and exclude its box. Between 0.1 and 0.8, we consider it partially generated and refit its box to the largest cluster of memory points around it, so that the remainder of the object continues the part that exists. As this cluster can include neighboring surfaces (e.g., the wall behind the object), we preserve the orientation of the box and allow each side to grow by at most 1.5×. Otherwise, the object is yet to be generated and its box remains as planned. When more than 12 boxes remain, we prioritize those planned in unseen regions over those fitted to visible objects, as the prefix frame already shows the latter.

    B.3 Reference Retrieval

    From the bank H of input views and previously generated frames, we retrieve up to three appearance references per chunk, selected to maximize their joint coverage of the chunk’s views. For each frame i in H, we project its estimated depth into every eighth camera of the chunk to obtain the set Vᵢ of pixels that it observes, with a depth test for occlusion. As each chunk already receives its prefix frame, we initialize the selection ℝ with it and greedily add the frame that maximizes the additional coverage,

    i^*=\underseti∉ℝ\arg\max|Vᵢ∖\bigcup_j∈ℝVⱼ|.

    		(1)

    Once no frame increases the coverage, we select the remaining references by the proximity of their cameras to the chunk’s. When a chunk returns close to the start of the path, we additionally include the first input view, so that the chunk is conditioned on the captured view itself.

item.title: CineAct：把「分支电影」做成可玩的——用户给目标、选做法，选择要一直延续下去 ｜ CineAct: Interaction-State Agents for Playable, Branching Film Generation
item.description:
一句话：现有长序列做法要么按预设剧本走，要么自回归续帧——画外状态丢了，幻觉越积越多。

要点：

  • 供给端的限制：MiniMax-H3 这类开放视频生成器每次只产出一段几秒到十几秒的短片
  • 两种现有延长方式各有代价：靠 **agentic 系统按预设剧本**推进，或**从上一段最后一帧自回归续写**——后者会**丢掉画外状态**并在多轮之后累积幻觉
  • CineAct 因此改成「交互状态」驱动：用户可以给出明确目标、选择如何完成，并让这个**选择的后果持续存在**，从而生成可玩、可分支的影片

为什么值得看：「选择要留下痕迹」是游戏与电影的分界。把交互状态显式建模，才可能让分支叙事不塌成「每次重开一段视频」——这与本周的持久状态主线完全同频。

中文摘要：像 MiniMax-H3 这样的开放视频生成器每次只能产出几秒到十几秒的短片。要合成更长的序列，现有方法要么依赖 agentic 系统按预设剧本推进，要么从上一段的最后一帧自回归续写——后者会丢失画外状态，并在多轮之后累积幻觉。结果是，用户仍然无法给出一个明确目标、自行选择如何完成它，并看到这个选择的后果持续下去。CineAct 因此提出以「交互状态」为核心的 agent 框架，用来生成可玩、可分支的影片：目标由用户给出，实现路径由用户选择，而选择的结果被持续保留。对互动叙事而言，这解决的是「分支一旦切换就重置」的根问题。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-24

本期推送：2026-11-25

CineAct: Interaction-State Agents for Playable, Branching Film Generation

Abstract

Open video generators such as MiniMax-H3 produce short clips of only several to a dozen seconds per run. To synthesize longer sequences, existing methods either rely on agentic systems following preset scripts, or roll out autoregressively from the previous clip’s last frame, losing off-screen states and accumulating hallucinations across turns. Consequently, users still cannot take an explicit goal, choose how to accomplish it, and see that choice persist across subsequent clips. We study goal-grounded interactive video generation, where one goal admits multiple valid approaches, the user’s chosen approach must be executed on screen, and its consequences must persist across clips. To this end, we propose CineAct, a state-first agentic framework in which language-model agents handle reasoning while frozen image and video generators serve purely as renderers. Before interaction, the Architect initializes the world as a spatial layout with cameras, an asset library, and a scene graph; at each turn, the system deduces the planned state change, generates a target end frame with an image generator and rigorously verifies it, and synthesizes intermediate motion with an FL2V model. We further introduce a multi-space benchmark covering two suites: long-horizon step execution and open-intent branching admissibility. Experiments show that explicit world-state modeling boosts multi-step rollout consistency over the pixel-only baseline (+11.4 automated, +23.1 human points) and raises paired branching success toward a shared goal by +30.8 points.

1 Introduction

Open video generators such as Wan [31], HunyuanVideo [16], CogVideoX [37], and Open-Sora [41], alongside models such as MiniMax-H3 [22], have made substantial progress in visual quality and motion realism, yet a single generation remains confined to short clips of several to a dozen seconds. To go beyond this limit and assemble complete long-form narratives, agentic director systems such as MovieAgent [34], ViMax [12], and MVAgent [17], together with node-based multimodal creative canvases, chain high-level scripts or keyframes into continuous multi-shot videos. In parallel, interactive video models such as Genie [2, 26], GameNGen [30], and WorldPlay [27] allow users to navigate through generated environments in real time via reactive controls. Recent work further explores combining the two lines: an agent plans the next action from a task goal, a video model renders it, and the system checks whether the action was completed on screen [15, 8, 36].

Yet how users interact with these systems, and how many routes they can take, remains tightly restricted. Agentic directors and creative canvases organize shots around a preset script; their review and resampling [12, 17] enforce a single storyboard, and turning them into interactive interfaces merely splits a fixed workflow into sequential clicks. Interactive video models support real-time camera navigation [11, 27], instruction following [28, 42], or object-level trajectory and action persistence [10, 35], yet they execute step-level controls without offering alternative task-level routes toward a goal. Conversely, goal-driven planning systems advance toward a task objective [15, 8, 36], but the planner autonomously determines the action sequence rather than letting the user choose among distinct valid approaches. In many domains, however, choosing the approach is the core interaction: trying alternative tools in skill training, valuing solution diversity as a key metric of engagement in playable games, testing task robustness across approaches in embodied evaluation, and leaving lasting traces in interactive narratives. Multiple valid paths toward a shared goal also provide an environment for agents to explore, compare action consequences, and accumulate verifiable experience toward policy learning and recursive self-improvement [32, 39, 24, 7]. We therefore study goal-grounded interactive video generation, supporting user-chosen routes toward a shared goal via menus, clicks, drags, or text, executing them visibly on screen, and preserving their consequences across turns (Fig. CineAct: Interaction-State Agents for Playable, Branching Film Generation).

While language agents can readily propose diverse alternative branches, existing video generators lack the physical grounding to execute them reliably. The core bottleneck is that current pipelines roll out autoregressively from the previous clip’s last frame alone, leaving the entire world state implicit in pixels. Relying solely on pixels creates three blind spots: the system lacks explicit preconditions to determine which actions are feasible and keep the goal reachable, cannot preserve object identities and states once entities leave the view or look-alike distractors appear, and has no geometric reference to align doorway directions and camera cuts across spaces. Thus, minor hallucinations compound over turns as removed items reappear, states revert on revisits, and characters take the wrong door, erasing distinctions between user choices.

To overcome these blind spots, we propose CineAct, a state-first agentic framework decoupling high-level world evolution from low-level pixel synthesis (Fig. 2): an explicit world state governs what exists and changes, while frozen image and video models render how it looks and moves. Addressing the three challenges above, CineAct maintains a spatial layout with cameras, an asset library, and a scene graph to constrain cross-space transitions, visual identity, and goal-reaching feasibility. At each turn, agents ground user input on this state to deduce a transition specification, synthesize and verify a target end frame to lock the endpoint, and condition an FL2V model under camera-geometry rules to render motion whose last frame refreshes Aₜ and seeds the next turn.

To evaluate this task systematically, we introduce a multi-space benchmark covering long-horizon step execution and branching admissibility. Across action, world-state, and spatial dimensions, we conduct controlled ablations, cross-backbone comparisons, counterfactual gating probes, paired branching tests, and an interface study. In multi-step rollouts, CineAct substantially improves overall consistency over the pixel-only baseline across both automated (+11.4 points) and blind human ratings (+23.1 points), with ablations confirming distinct gains from layout, assets, and scene graphs. Moreover, paired branching evaluations confirm that CineAct gates, executes, and preserves diverse user-chosen routes toward a shared goal (+30.8 points in paired branching success over Baseline).

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    Task formulation. We formalize goal-grounded interactive video generation, requiring the system to support multiple user-chosen routes toward a shared goal while jointly satisfying action validity, execution visibility, and cross-turn consequence persistence.

  • •

    State-first agentic framework. We propose CineAct, which decouples world-state reasoning from pixel synthesis. By maintaining explicit spatial layouts, dynamically refreshed asset libraries, and scene graphs, CineAct locks in post-action endpoints via pre-rendering target-frame verification and drives FL2V generation under camera-geometry rules.

  • •

    Benchmark and evaluation. We introduce a multi-space benchmark covering long-horizon step execution and branching admissibility across action, world-state, and spatial dimensions. Controlled ablations, backbone studies, and interface comparisons quantify each representation’s distinct contribution.

    • 2 Related Work

    Multi-shot video and agentic directors.

    Agentic director systems orchestrate multiple shots to synthesize coherent long-form videos from narrative scripts. Some simulate scriptwriting, storyboarding, and shooting via hierarchical chain-of-thought [34] or continuously monitor and refine narrative coherence with vision–language agents [12]. MVAgent [17] maintains a continuity memory and samples candidate continuations from a shared shot state; CineEvolve [40] co-evolves director and critic policies; and VideoGen-Agent [18] coordinates generation and verification tools through reinforcement learning. To support non-consecutive revisits to prior spaces, ATAS [33] compiles screenplays into bounded shot requests backed by explicit scene-geometry and event memories. Although these systems produce coherent multi-shot films, they remain organized around preset scripts rather than interactive user choices toward a task goal. We instead require every generated clip to respond directly to the user’s online choice across multiple viable routes.

    Controllable and interactive video generation.

    Interactive video models roll out frames in pixel space in response to control signals or online user inputs. Early work synthesizes interactive environments via unsupervised latent actions [2], exploration-driven data collection [26], or agent replay [30]. Subsequent streaming models enable frame-level keyboard-and-mouse control [11], maintain long-range geometric consistency by dynamically rebuilding context memory from past frames [27], or follow open-ended instruction prompts in game worlds [28]. Recent work advances to entity-level manipulation: Incantation [42] introduces per-entity language control with task-specific status tracking, WorldCraft [10] combines object selection and 2D drag trajectories with camera navigation to preserve object placements across off-screen revisits, and ActWorld [35] retains action-induced states such as opened doors and picked-up items via action-aware memory. In parallel, goal-driven systems such as CollabVR [15] and WorldGuide [8] couple step-level action planning with video execution verification toward a task goal. However, these approaches either execute step-level controls without checking multi-step goal reachability, or rely on an automated planner to dictate the next step without offering users alternative, equally valid routes toward a shared goal.

    Explicit world states and generative rendering.

    To curb hallucination accumulation in autoregressive rollouts, recent work decouples state logic and physical rules from neural pixel synthesis. PWM [14] compiles language into world programs and guides rendering with 3D bounding boxes and a trained spatial control branch; AgentGarten [7] constructs code-driven worlds for evolving agents; and GameDirector [20] and Code World Model [6] separate combat mechanics or executable code evolution from video rendering. For open-world interaction, Oneira [36] decomposes goals into dependency-ordered interactions over an object state table with LoRA-adapted rendering, while State World Models [4] combine a typed rule ledger and goal conditions with clay-scene camera rendering. Within single-clip synthesis, CausalMotion [43] and PhysPlan [23] steer inference using causal keyframes or sparse edits to a physical state graph, and SolarRenderer [9] injects structural videos through the backbone’s native reference pathway. While explicit state representations are well established, existing frameworks use them to execute predefined mechanics or a single decomposed plan, and several require training task-specific adapters or control branches [14, 6, 36, 20]. We instead pair frozen image and video generators with a spatial layout, a refreshed asset library, and a scene graph to deduce and validate multiple user-chosen routes toward a shared goal, using pre-rendering target-frame verification to lock in endpoints before FL2V synthesis.

    3 Problem Setting

    We formulate goal-grounded interactive video generation as a multi-turn, branchable conditional generation problem organized around a shared task goal. Let g be the global goal to achieve (e.g., “prepare a rest spot before dusk”) starting from an initial scene observation I₁. At turn t, the user provides an interaction input uₜ∈U via a menu selection, a click or drag trajectory on the frame, or free text. Conditioning on the current frame Iₜ and interaction history, the system resolves uₜ into a semantic action aₜ and synthesizes a video clip Vₜ, whose actual last frame Iₜ₊₁=Tail(Vₜ) serves as the starting frame of turn t+1. Interaction continues until g is accomplished, yielding a trajectory

    τ=(I₁,u₁,V₁,I₂,u₂,V₂,…,u_K,V_K).

    		(1)

    Unlike single-script video generation, a shared starting state or intermediate history (I₁,…,Iₜ) admits multiple valid routes {τ⁽ᵐ⁾} that reach the same goal g while leaving route-specific consequences in later frames.

    Consistency requirements.

    For a generated trajectory τ to support interactive play, it must jointly satisfy three consistency criteria across turns t∈{1,…,K}:

    (1) Action validity and process visibility. Each executed action aₜ must satisfy the physical preconditions P(aₜ) of the current scene while keeping the global goal g reachable in future turns. Moreover, the generated clip Vₜ must visibly realize the physical action process rather than merely teleporting to the end state:

    Vₜ⊨Δ(aₜ).

    		(2)

    (2) Entity identity and state persistence. Manipulated objects and characters must preserve their visual identity without vanishing, duplicating, or swapping across turns. Both the newly established holding or support states and the unaffected scene attributes K(aₜ) must persist across subsequent clips (when entities leave and re-enter view):

    Vₖ⊨K(aₜ), ∀ k≥t.

    		(3)

    (3) Cross-space geometric and camera continuity. When interactions span multiple connected spaces or revisit prior spaces, the character’s exit direction from the source space, entry portal side in the destination space, and camera viewpoint transitions must remain geometrically coherent across clips. Standard autoregressive rollouts condition only on the previous frame Iₜ, leaving all three constraints implicit in pixels. Below, we introduce CineAct to explicitly model and enforce these constraints using frozen renderers.

    4 CineAct: A State-First Agentic Framework for Interactive Film Generation

    Fig. 2 gives an overview of CineAct. The framework decouples high-level reasoning from low-level rendering. Reasoning tasks, namely intent parsing, validity checking, reachability search, and target-frame verification, are handled by language-model agents. Image and video generators act purely as physical renderers[9, 14]: they produce pixels under verified endpoint states and geometric constraints and take no part in deducing logical world state.

    4.1 Architect: World Initialization

    Before interaction begins, the language-model agent Architect constructs an interactive multi-space world around the global goal g and designs multiple valid routes (e.g., Fig. 2, top: carrying lantern L1 into cabin B or firewood W1 to camp C). To guarantee multi-route playability, the system verifies reachability during initialization so that at least two substantively distinct action sequences, differing in tools, strategy, or spatial path, can reach g from the start or shared mid-story decision points without redundant round trips. Architect then materializes this world into three complementary representations S₀=(L,A₀,G₀) (Fig. 2, top):

    (1) Spatial layout and cameras (L=(ℝ,ℙ,ℂ)). The layout represents the world as a 2D axis-aligned floor plan specifying rectangular space bounds r∈ℝ and shared-boundary portal segments D∈ℙ, together with one deterministic fixed camera ℂ per space (placed on a portal-free wall facing an exit). Geometric projection derives each portal’s on-screen side (left, right, or far wall) to constrain cross-space transitions and verify doorway placement.

    (2) Asset library (Aₜ). The asset library combines per-space visual memory (initialized from the opening renders and updated after each turn with the latest generated video tail of the visited space) with initial entity identity crops A₀(v) paired with unique identifiers and stable, location-free appearance descriptions. At each step, the system retrieves the destination-space memory and identity crops for action participants and off-screen actors while skipping characters already visible in Iₜ to prevent duplicate figures.

    (3) Scene graph (Gₜ=(Vₜ,𝔼ₜ)). Initialized as G₀, the scene graph tracks all in-view and off-screen entities Vₜ. Containment, support, and holding relations are deterministically derived from hierarchical ownership pointers alongside portability, carrying-capacity limits, and state attributes 𝔼ₜ (e.g., open/closed, lit/unlit). A symbolic transition engine checks preconditions and goal reachability over Gₜ, supplying valid action suggestions at each turn.

    4.2 Interpreter and Planner: Intent Grounding and State Deduction

    At turn t, the system presents feasible menu suggestions derived from Gₜ, while the user may select a menu option or issue open-ended input uₜ via clicks, drags, or free text. Given the current frame Iₜ, the asset library Aₜ, and Gₜ, the Interpreter grounds uₜ to specific scene entities, resolving it into a structured operation aₜ, an expected state change Δₜ, and invariance constraints (Fig. 2, bottom).

    The Planner then validates both in-plan choices and out-of-distribution (off-menu) operations using the symbolic transition engine over Gₜ. If aₜ matches a pre-verified branch, it advances directly; otherwise, the Planner checks physical preconditions P(aₜ), carrying capacity, and locality over Gₜ, deduces Gₜᵉˣᵖᵉᶜᵗᵉᵈ=Gₜ⊕Δₜ, and runs graph search to verify that the global goal g remains reachable from Gₜᵉˣᵖᵉᶜᵗᵉᵈ. Inputs that are physically impossible, ambiguous, or would render g unreachable are rejected before rendering. Validated actions advance the planned scene graph to Gₜ₊₁=Gₜᵉˣᵖᵉᶜᵗᵉᵈ (maintained separately from observed video frames) and deterministically diff (Gₜ,Gₜ₊₁) into an explicit transition specification:

    Specₜ=(V_operated,Δₜ,Vₖₑₚₜ,Cₜ),

    		(4)

    which details the operated instances, the modified relations, the instances that must remain untouched, and, for cross-space moves, the camera transition instruction Cₜ.

    4.3 Painter and Inspector: Verified Target-Frame Generation

    In first–last-frame (FL2V) video synthesis, the starting frame Iₜ is fixed, so securing an accurate target end frame Iₜ^⋆ provides reliable boundary anchors for rendering the motion in between. Given the transition specification, the Painter combines the planned changes, the layout L, and the asset library Aₜ into an image prompt and calls an image-editing model to generate a candidate target end frame Iₜ^⋆ depicting the intended post-action state, conditioned on the current frame Iₜ, the destination-space memory on cross-space moves, and the operated object’s identity crop (e.g., scene B and lantern L1 in Fig. 2).

    Between the Painter and the Director, the Inspector serves as a target-endpoint gatekeeper, using a vision–language model to verify each candidate target end frame item by item as pass, fail, or unclear before video rendering: whether it depicts the completed action, whether operated instances retain their identity, and whether non-target objects are unchanged; for cross-space moves, it also localizes doorways in the candidate frame and checks their screen sides against the geometric projections from L. Specifically, it verifies every entry of the transition specification, including the planned changes, held items, and must-keep instances (such as confirming in Fig. 2 that L1 remains the same held lantern and D1 appears on the left in B). A failed check returns its visual evidence to the Painter for regeneration (the feedback loop in Fig. 2, with at most three attempts per step). Once verified, Iₜ^⋆ is locked in and passed to the Director.

    4.4 Director: Geometry-Aware Process Rendering

    Given the current real frame Iₜ and the verified frame Iₜ^⋆, the Director synthesizes the transition in between. For interactions within a single space, the Director writes a motion description from Iₜ, Iₜ^⋆, and the action text, and renders the action in one fixed camera shot. For moves between spaces, it reads from L the camera orientation difference δ=(φ_d-φₛ)\bmod360^∘ between source rₛ and destination r_d, and combines it with the portal geometry to specify the on-screen exit and entry sides across two fixed shots joined by a cut. For instance, when adjacent spaces share the same camera heading (δ=0^∘ in Fig. 2), a character exiting through a doorway on the right naturally enters the next space from the left. Together with Iₜ and Iₜ^⋆, these instructions condition the FL2V video model to render a 10-second transition clip Vₜ. Once Vₜ is rendered, its actual last frame Iₜ₊₁=Tail(Vₜ) both seeds the next turn and updates the space memory in Aₜ₊₁ as the latest visual observation of the visited space (the feedback arrow to the next-turn panel in Fig. 2), preserving scene and object changes across subsequent turns and revisits.

    5 Benchmark

    Unlike existing video benchmarks that separately evaluate clip-level visual quality [13], prescribed multi-turn instruction adherence [38], disappear-and-reappear object recovery under occlusion [5], or paired counterfactual interventions [3, 21], we build an interactive benchmark that jointly evaluates multi-space execution consistency and pre-render branching admissibility toward a shared goal.

    5.1 Evaluation Suites

    Built on 40 natural long-horizon tasks authored with Hy4 [29] across diverse indoor, outdoor, and mixed scenes (10 each across 1–4 connected spaces), the benchmark comprises two suites: (1) Multi-Step Interactive Execution evaluates rollout consistency over these 40 multi-turn episodes. (2) Branching Admissibility evaluates pre-render proposal gating at their opening decision points across 571 truth-verified, player-phrased proposals: 237 valid routes and 334 disguised infeasible counterfactuals involving nonexistent places (n=80), nonexistent objects (n=80), or unsatisfied preconditions (n=174).

    5.2 Evaluation Metrics

    For Multi-Step Interactive Execution, we evaluate each step across Action, World State, and Spatial continuity. Automated Hy4 evaluation scores all ten items, while blind human raters annotate four core metrics: Action (action completion), State (object holding and support), Entry (destination and entry side), and Exit (exit doorway direction). Steps where lost camera framing hides the target are flagged separately as Unclear (Sec. 6.4); the full ten-item list and scoring rubric are detailed in the supplementary material (Supplementary Table S1).

    For Branching Admissibility, we primarily evaluate under an Open mode (admissible / inadmissible / unsure, where unsure counts as a failure), reporting the acceptance rate on valid proposals (Accept), rejection rate on infeasible ones (Reject), their mean (Balanced), and the Unsure rate. We also include a Forced binary control that disallows abstention to check whether high rejection relies on trivially refusing valid proposals.

    6 Experiments

    6.1 Experimental Setup

    Models and backbones.

    All high-level reasoning roles (Architect, Interpreter, Planner, Inspector, and the task authoring model) are served by the multimodal language model Hy4 [29]. For generative rendering, we cross-pair two image generators (Qwen-Image-2.1 [25] and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B [1]) with two frozen FL2V video backbones (MiniMax-H3 [22] and LTX-2.5 [19]) to synthesize 10-second transition clips and compare Baseline against CineAct across combinations. Blind human evaluation and the reference-to-video (Ref2V) interface comparison in Sec. 6.4 are conducted on Qwen-Image-2.1 + MiniMax-H3.

    Ablation settings.

    To isolate each explicit representation, we evaluate four cumulative settings under a shared cross-space room-memory policy (initial room render on first entry, own last video frame on revisits): Baseline (Direct rollout) receives only the current frame and a user instruction; +Layout adds the spatial layout L and camera transition rules; +Assets further adds entity identity crops and stable appearance descriptions from Aₜ; and CineAct (Full framework) adds the scene graph Gₜ with symbolic state deduction, deterministic state-change checklists, and target-frame checks. Without Gₜ, the first three settings bypass symbolic planning and synthesize frames directly from the action instruction and their allowed layout or asset inputs. All compared settings share identical frozen backbones, action sequences, initial frames, random seeds, and per-step compute budgets (at most three target-frame attempts and one video generation), rolling out autoregressively from their own generated video tails to isolate the contribution of explicit world modeling.

    6.2 Multi-Step Execution

    Table 1 and Fig. 3 summarize the stepwise ablations on Multi-Step Interactive Execution across all four backbone combinations (Hy4 ratings; full 10-item breakdowns in Supplementary Table S3) and blind human ratings by 10 raters on Qwen-Image-2.1 + MiniMax-H3:

  • •

    Layout and cameras (+Layout vs. Baseline): Adding spatial layout L and camera transition rules improves spatial and overall consistency across backbones, effectively resolving cross-space disorientation.

  • •

    Asset library (+Assets vs. +Layout): Introducing refreshed scene and instance references from Aₜ further boosts Action and World State under Qwen-Image-2.1, whereas lightweight FLUX.2 [klein] 4B [1] exhibits slight multi-reference editing variance before full CineAct recovers strongly.

  • •

    Scene graph and verification (CineAct vs. Baseline): Adding Gₜ, transition specifications, and target-frame checks achieves the highest consistency across all four backbone pairings, lifting Action, World State, and overall scores over Baseline (.862 overall on Qwen2.1 + H3, +11.4 points) and demonstrating strong cross-backbone generalization.

  • •

    Blind human evaluation (Fig. 3): Ten raters blindly scored 10 sampled stories on Qwen-Image-2.1 + MiniMax-H3 (40 anonymized story–setting units, 196 clips, 784 item ratings), corroborating the monotonic gain from .611 to .842 overall (+23.1 points) with best scores on every metric (Action .802, State .828, Entry/Exit 1.000).

    • Fig. 4(a–c) illustrates this stepwise progression on a four-room watering task: given the setup and route in (a), Baseline enters the wrong central arch toward the water room whereas +Layout takes the correct West door (b); after multiple room transitions, +Layout drops the items and +Assets holds both skins loose outside the basket, while CineAct keeps both packed inside the basket (c).

    6.3 Branching Admissibility

    Interactive video generation requires more than following a single fixed script: given a shared goal, a system must accommodate diverse player-proposed branches by admitting valid alternative routes while filtering out requests that violate world constraints. Across the opening decision points of all 40 stories, we evaluate 571 player-phrased proposals authored with Hy4 (237 valid goal-reaching approaches and 334 plausible-looking infeasible counterfactuals). Each ablation setting judges proposal admissibility solely from the opening frame, task goal, and its allowed prior information (L, A₀ containing initial views of all spaces and entity crops, or G₀) without generating video.

    As shown in Tables 2 and 3, pixel-only Baseline abstains (Unsure) on 80.0% of proposals under the Open mode (especially in multi-space scenes) and accepts only .080 of valid branches (.146 balanced accuracy). Even under the Forced control, Baseline achieves .970 rejection merely by refusing nearly all inputs, blocking 73.8% of valid routes (.262 acceptance). Across the three counterfactual categories (Table 3, where miss rate counts infeasible proposals answered either admissible or unsure), adding explicit representations progressively resolves each error type: +Layout substantially reduces misses on Nonexistent Place; +Assets sharply cuts Nonexistent Object misses and lowers overall abstention to 29.8%; and adding G₀ (CineAct) further drives down Broken Precondition misses, reducing abstention to 4.0% while achieving high acceptance and rejection across both Open (.887 balanced) and Forced (.905 balanced) modes. To evaluate paired execution, raters blindly score 13 multi-route stories (26 trajectories/method across 1–4 spaces; Table 4) on per-route and both-route goal completion, route-specific consequence preservation, and zero cross-leak or rollback (jointly counted as both succeed & distinct). From identical initial states, CineAct achieves 1.000 both-route goal completion (vs. .615) and .923 both succeed & distinct (.900 on 2–4 spaces, n=10, vs. .500).

    6.4 Interface Analysis: FL2V vs. Ref2V

    We compare our FL2V pipeline against Reference-to-Video (Ref2V), which conditions MiniMax-H3 directly on Iₜ and asset crops over the same 10 stories. On visually determinable items, Ref2V achieves comparable Baseline-to-CineAct gains under the 10-item Hy4 evaluation (.713→.875 vs. .733→.856 for FL2V). However, Ref2V leaves 26.0% (51/196) of object-holding/support (State) steps visually Unclear under human evaluation (vs. 0.0% for FL2V), which is unacceptable for multi-turn interaction. Specifically, as shown in Fig. 4(d), starting from the Shared input, FL2V anchors the room framing via the verified Target frame, so its output keeps both the held rag and the bucket and machinery in view (Scene retained); by contrast, Ref2V drifts into a close-up that crops out the bucket and surrounding room (View cropped), preventing users from inspecting or selecting them in subsequent turns (Supplementary Table S4).

    7 Limitations

    While CineAct improves multi-turn consistency and branching reliability, three trade-offs remain. First, skipping per-shot 3D reconstruction and fine-tuning keeps the pipeline lightweight and consistent, but limits each room to a fixed camera with cut transitions rather than continuous 3D camera motion. Second, sequential deduction, iterative verification, and 10-second FL2V synthesis yield turn-based rather than real-time streaming latency. Third, rooms and entities are fixed up front by Architect; adding new rooms on the fly, post-clip state re-sync, and streaming backbones is left to future work.

    8 Conclusion

    We formulated goal-grounded interactive video generation and presented CineAct, a state-first agentic framework that decouples high-level world-state reasoning from low-level pixel rendering. By maintaining explicit spatial layouts with cameras, dynamically refreshed asset libraries, and scene graphs, and by locking in post-action endpoints through pre-rendering target-frame verification, CineAct enables reliable multi-turn execution and pre-render gating of open-ended branching proposals. Experiments across multi-step execution, counterfactual branching admissibility, and interface comparisons validate each explicit representation’s specialized role.

    （参考文献见原文。）


    Supplementary Material

    Backbone Specifications

    All reasoning agents and automated evaluators run on the multimodal language model Hy4 [29]. For image editing, we use Qwen-Image-2.1 [25] and the distilled FLUX.2 [klein] 4B [1]. For video synthesis, both the FL2V and Ref2V interfaces of MiniMax-H3 [22] use the 8-step distilled variants, while LTX-2.5 [19] runs in full BF16 non-distilled two-stage mode (30 steps).

    System Representations and Execution Walkthrough

    Here we detail the three representations from Sec. 4 and summarize one execution turn in Algorithm 1. Fig. S6 shows a concrete example on the three-terrace seedling task: panels (a)–(d) give the layout L, initial views, scene graph G₁, and asset crops A₁, while panels (e)–(f) trace two rollouts. At each turn, the Planner checks preconditions on Gₜ, retrieves only the destination view and off-screen entity crops (Lines 4–5), verifies the target frame before rendering Vₜ (Lines 7–12), and writes Tail(Vₜ) back only to the visited terrace (Line 13).

  • •

    Spatial layout and cameras (L): Spaces are non-overlapping 2D axis-aligned rectangles with portals on shared walls, each observed by one fixed camera (65^∘ horizontal FOV, placed on a portal-free wall facing an exit). Geometric projection derives each doorway’s on-screen side (left, right, or far wall) for Painter/Director prompting and Inspector verification.

  • •

    Asset library (Aₜ): Combines per-space visual memory with static entity identity crops extracted at initialization. Only actual video tails Iₜ₊₁=Tail(Vₜ) (never intermediate target images Iₜ^⋆) update the visited space’s memory in Aₜ₊₁; conditioning uses the destination space’s latest memory plus crops for operated and off-screen entities, skipping actors already visible in Iₜ.

  • •

    Scene graph (Gₜ) and symbolic engine: Nodes store location/ownership pointers (in, on, held), portability, carrying capacity, and state attributes. Before rendering, the Planner checks preconditions and goal reachability via breadth-first search, advances the separate planned graph Gₜ₊₁, and deterministically diffs (Gₜ,Gₜ₊₁) into Specₜ.

    • Evaluation Metrics and Human–Automated Agreement

    Table S1 lists all ten per-step questions used in Multi-Step Interactive Execution, and Figs. S1–S2 show all six steps of the courtyard watering task across the four ablation settings. On the four shared items (Action, State, Entry, Exit) for Qwen-Image-2.1 + MiniMax-H3, Hy4 matches blind human ratings 73.0% of the time in binary agreement (64.4% exact three-tier) and follows the same ablation order as Table 1 and Fig. 3 of the main paper. Table S2 extends this blind human study to two LTX-2.5 pairings on the same 10 stories. CineAct ranks first under all three pairings (.842, .748, and .614; +23.1, +18.0, and +17.6 points over Baseline), matching the automated cross-backbone results in Table S3.
item.content:encoded:
一句话：现有长序列做法要么按预设剧本走，要么自回归续帧——画外状态丢了，幻觉越积越多。

要点：

  • 供给端的限制：MiniMax-H3 这类开放视频生成器每次只产出一段几秒到十几秒的短片
  • 两种现有延长方式各有代价：靠 **agentic 系统按预设剧本**推进，或**从上一段最后一帧自回归续写**——后者会**丢掉画外状态**并在多轮之后累积幻觉
  • CineAct 因此改成「交互状态」驱动：用户可以给出明确目标、选择如何完成，并让这个**选择的后果持续存在**，从而生成可玩、可分支的影片

为什么值得看：「选择要留下痕迹」是游戏与电影的分界。把交互状态显式建模，才可能让分支叙事不塌成「每次重开一段视频」——这与本周的持久状态主线完全同频。

中文摘要：像 MiniMax-H3 这样的开放视频生成器每次只能产出几秒到十几秒的短片。要合成更长的序列，现有方法要么依赖 agentic 系统按预设剧本推进，要么从上一段的最后一帧自回归续写——后者会丢失画外状态，并在多轮之后累积幻觉。结果是，用户仍然无法给出一个明确目标、自行选择如何完成它，并看到这个选择的后果持续下去。CineAct 因此提出以「交互状态」为核心的 agent 框架，用来生成可玩、可分支的影片：目标由用户给出，实现路径由用户选择，而选择的结果被持续保留。对互动叙事而言，这解决的是「分支一旦切换就重置」的根问题。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-24

本期推送：2026-11-25

CineAct: Interaction-State Agents for Playable, Branching Film Generation

Abstract

Open video generators such as MiniMax-H3 produce short clips of only several to a dozen seconds per run. To synthesize longer sequences, existing methods either rely on agentic systems following preset scripts, or roll out autoregressively from the previous clip’s last frame, losing off-screen states and accumulating hallucinations across turns. Consequently, users still cannot take an explicit goal, choose how to accomplish it, and see that choice persist across subsequent clips. We study goal-grounded interactive video generation, where one goal admits multiple valid approaches, the user’s chosen approach must be executed on screen, and its consequences must persist across clips. To this end, we propose CineAct, a state-first agentic framework in which language-model agents handle reasoning while frozen image and video generators serve purely as renderers. Before interaction, the Architect initializes the world as a spatial layout with cameras, an asset library, and a scene graph; at each turn, the system deduces the planned state change, generates a target end frame with an image generator and rigorously verifies it, and synthesizes intermediate motion with an FL2V model. We further introduce a multi-space benchmark covering two suites: long-horizon step execution and open-intent branching admissibility. Experiments show that explicit world-state modeling boosts multi-step rollout consistency over the pixel-only baseline (+11.4 automated, +23.1 human points) and raises paired branching success toward a shared goal by +30.8 points.

1 Introduction

Open video generators such as Wan [31], HunyuanVideo [16], CogVideoX [37], and Open-Sora [41], alongside models such as MiniMax-H3 [22], have made substantial progress in visual quality and motion realism, yet a single generation remains confined to short clips of several to a dozen seconds. To go beyond this limit and assemble complete long-form narratives, agentic director systems such as MovieAgent [34], ViMax [12], and MVAgent [17], together with node-based multimodal creative canvases, chain high-level scripts or keyframes into continuous multi-shot videos. In parallel, interactive video models such as Genie [2, 26], GameNGen [30], and WorldPlay [27] allow users to navigate through generated environments in real time via reactive controls. Recent work further explores combining the two lines: an agent plans the next action from a task goal, a video model renders it, and the system checks whether the action was completed on screen [15, 8, 36].

Yet how users interact with these systems, and how many routes they can take, remains tightly restricted. Agentic directors and creative canvases organize shots around a preset script; their review and resampling [12, 17] enforce a single storyboard, and turning them into interactive interfaces merely splits a fixed workflow into sequential clicks. Interactive video models support real-time camera navigation [11, 27], instruction following [28, 42], or object-level trajectory and action persistence [10, 35], yet they execute step-level controls without offering alternative task-level routes toward a goal. Conversely, goal-driven planning systems advance toward a task objective [15, 8, 36], but the planner autonomously determines the action sequence rather than letting the user choose among distinct valid approaches. In many domains, however, choosing the approach is the core interaction: trying alternative tools in skill training, valuing solution diversity as a key metric of engagement in playable games, testing task robustness across approaches in embodied evaluation, and leaving lasting traces in interactive narratives. Multiple valid paths toward a shared goal also provide an environment for agents to explore, compare action consequences, and accumulate verifiable experience toward policy learning and recursive self-improvement [32, 39, 24, 7]. We therefore study goal-grounded interactive video generation, supporting user-chosen routes toward a shared goal via menus, clicks, drags, or text, executing them visibly on screen, and preserving their consequences across turns (Fig. CineAct: Interaction-State Agents for Playable, Branching Film Generation).

While language agents can readily propose diverse alternative branches, existing video generators lack the physical grounding to execute them reliably. The core bottleneck is that current pipelines roll out autoregressively from the previous clip’s last frame alone, leaving the entire world state implicit in pixels. Relying solely on pixels creates three blind spots: the system lacks explicit preconditions to determine which actions are feasible and keep the goal reachable, cannot preserve object identities and states once entities leave the view or look-alike distractors appear, and has no geometric reference to align doorway directions and camera cuts across spaces. Thus, minor hallucinations compound over turns as removed items reappear, states revert on revisits, and characters take the wrong door, erasing distinctions between user choices.

To overcome these blind spots, we propose CineAct, a state-first agentic framework decoupling high-level world evolution from low-level pixel synthesis (Fig. 2): an explicit world state governs what exists and changes, while frozen image and video models render how it looks and moves. Addressing the three challenges above, CineAct maintains a spatial layout with cameras, an asset library, and a scene graph to constrain cross-space transitions, visual identity, and goal-reaching feasibility. At each turn, agents ground user input on this state to deduce a transition specification, synthesize and verify a target end frame to lock the endpoint, and condition an FL2V model under camera-geometry rules to render motion whose last frame refreshes Aₜ and seeds the next turn.

To evaluate this task systematically, we introduce a multi-space benchmark covering long-horizon step execution and branching admissibility. Across action, world-state, and spatial dimensions, we conduct controlled ablations, cross-backbone comparisons, counterfactual gating probes, paired branching tests, and an interface study. In multi-step rollouts, CineAct substantially improves overall consistency over the pixel-only baseline across both automated (+11.4 points) and blind human ratings (+23.1 points), with ablations confirming distinct gains from layout, assets, and scene graphs. Moreover, paired branching evaluations confirm that CineAct gates, executes, and preserves diverse user-chosen routes toward a shared goal (+30.8 points in paired branching success over Baseline).

Our contributions are threefold:

  • •

    Task formulation. We formalize goal-grounded interactive video generation, requiring the system to support multiple user-chosen routes toward a shared goal while jointly satisfying action validity, execution visibility, and cross-turn consequence persistence.

  • •

    State-first agentic framework. We propose CineAct, which decouples world-state reasoning from pixel synthesis. By maintaining explicit spatial layouts, dynamically refreshed asset libraries, and scene graphs, CineAct locks in post-action endpoints via pre-rendering target-frame verification and drives FL2V generation under camera-geometry rules.

  • •

    Benchmark and evaluation. We introduce a multi-space benchmark covering long-horizon step execution and branching admissibility across action, world-state, and spatial dimensions. Controlled ablations, backbone studies, and interface comparisons quantify each representation’s distinct contribution.

    • 2 Related Work

    Multi-shot video and agentic directors.

    Agentic director systems orchestrate multiple shots to synthesize coherent long-form videos from narrative scripts. Some simulate scriptwriting, storyboarding, and shooting via hierarchical chain-of-thought [34] or continuously monitor and refine narrative coherence with vision–language agents [12]. MVAgent [17] maintains a continuity memory and samples candidate continuations from a shared shot state; CineEvolve [40] co-evolves director and critic policies; and VideoGen-Agent [18] coordinates generation and verification tools through reinforcement learning. To support non-consecutive revisits to prior spaces, ATAS [33] compiles screenplays into bounded shot requests backed by explicit scene-geometry and event memories. Although these systems produce coherent multi-shot films, they remain organized around preset scripts rather than interactive user choices toward a task goal. We instead require every generated clip to respond directly to the user’s online choice across multiple viable routes.

    Controllable and interactive video generation.

    Interactive video models roll out frames in pixel space in response to control signals or online user inputs. Early work synthesizes interactive environments via unsupervised latent actions [2], exploration-driven data collection [26], or agent replay [30]. Subsequent streaming models enable frame-level keyboard-and-mouse control [11], maintain long-range geometric consistency by dynamically rebuilding context memory from past frames [27], or follow open-ended instruction prompts in game worlds [28]. Recent work advances to entity-level manipulation: Incantation [42] introduces per-entity language control with task-specific status tracking, WorldCraft [10] combines object selection and 2D drag trajectories with camera navigation to preserve object placements across off-screen revisits, and ActWorld [35] retains action-induced states such as opened doors and picked-up items via action-aware memory. In parallel, goal-driven systems such as CollabVR [15] and WorldGuide [8] couple step-level action planning with video execution verification toward a task goal. However, these approaches either execute step-level controls without checking multi-step goal reachability, or rely on an automated planner to dictate the next step without offering users alternative, equally valid routes toward a shared goal.

    Explicit world states and generative rendering.

    To curb hallucination accumulation in autoregressive rollouts, recent work decouples state logic and physical rules from neural pixel synthesis. PWM [14] compiles language into world programs and guides rendering with 3D bounding boxes and a trained spatial control branch; AgentGarten [7] constructs code-driven worlds for evolving agents; and GameDirector [20] and Code World Model [6] separate combat mechanics or executable code evolution from video rendering. For open-world interaction, Oneira [36] decomposes goals into dependency-ordered interactions over an object state table with LoRA-adapted rendering, while State World Models [4] combine a typed rule ledger and goal conditions with clay-scene camera rendering. Within single-clip synthesis, CausalMotion [43] and PhysPlan [23] steer inference using causal keyframes or sparse edits to a physical state graph, and SolarRenderer [9] injects structural videos through the backbone’s native reference pathway. While explicit state representations are well established, existing frameworks use them to execute predefined mechanics or a single decomposed plan, and several require training task-specific adapters or control branches [14, 6, 36, 20]. We instead pair frozen image and video generators with a spatial layout, a refreshed asset library, and a scene graph to deduce and validate multiple user-chosen routes toward a shared goal, using pre-rendering target-frame verification to lock in endpoints before FL2V synthesis.

    3 Problem Setting

    We formulate goal-grounded interactive video generation as a multi-turn, branchable conditional generation problem organized around a shared task goal. Let g be the global goal to achieve (e.g., “prepare a rest spot before dusk”) starting from an initial scene observation I₁. At turn t, the user provides an interaction input uₜ∈U via a menu selection, a click or drag trajectory on the frame, or free text. Conditioning on the current frame Iₜ and interaction history, the system resolves uₜ into a semantic action aₜ and synthesizes a video clip Vₜ, whose actual last frame Iₜ₊₁=Tail(Vₜ) serves as the starting frame of turn t+1. Interaction continues until g is accomplished, yielding a trajectory

    τ=(I₁,u₁,V₁,I₂,u₂,V₂,…,u_K,V_K).

    		(1)

    Unlike single-script video generation, a shared starting state or intermediate history (I₁,…,Iₜ) admits multiple valid routes {τ⁽ᵐ⁾} that reach the same goal g while leaving route-specific consequences in later frames.

    Consistency requirements.

    For a generated trajectory τ to support interactive play, it must jointly satisfy three consistency criteria across turns t∈{1,…,K}:

    (1) Action validity and process visibility. Each executed action aₜ must satisfy the physical preconditions P(aₜ) of the current scene while keeping the global goal g reachable in future turns. Moreover, the generated clip Vₜ must visibly realize the physical action process rather than merely teleporting to the end state:

    Vₜ⊨Δ(aₜ).

    		(2)

    (2) Entity identity and state persistence. Manipulated objects and characters must preserve their visual identity without vanishing, duplicating, or swapping across turns. Both the newly established holding or support states and the unaffected scene attributes K(aₜ) must persist across subsequent clips (when entities leave and re-enter view):

    Vₖ⊨K(aₜ), ∀ k≥t.

    		(3)

    (3) Cross-space geometric and camera continuity. When interactions span multiple connected spaces or revisit prior spaces, the character’s exit direction from the source space, entry portal side in the destination space, and camera viewpoint transitions must remain geometrically coherent across clips. Standard autoregressive rollouts condition only on the previous frame Iₜ, leaving all three constraints implicit in pixels. Below, we introduce CineAct to explicitly model and enforce these constraints using frozen renderers.

    4 CineAct: A State-First Agentic Framework for Interactive Film Generation

    Fig. 2 gives an overview of CineAct. The framework decouples high-level reasoning from low-level rendering. Reasoning tasks, namely intent parsing, validity checking, reachability search, and target-frame verification, are handled by language-model agents. Image and video generators act purely as physical renderers[9, 14]: they produce pixels under verified endpoint states and geometric constraints and take no part in deducing logical world state.

    4.1 Architect: World Initialization

    Before interaction begins, the language-model agent Architect constructs an interactive multi-space world around the global goal g and designs multiple valid routes (e.g., Fig. 2, top: carrying lantern L1 into cabin B or firewood W1 to camp C). To guarantee multi-route playability, the system verifies reachability during initialization so that at least two substantively distinct action sequences, differing in tools, strategy, or spatial path, can reach g from the start or shared mid-story decision points without redundant round trips. Architect then materializes this world into three complementary representations S₀=(L,A₀,G₀) (Fig. 2, top):

    (1) Spatial layout and cameras (L=(ℝ,ℙ,ℂ)). The layout represents the world as a 2D axis-aligned floor plan specifying rectangular space bounds r∈ℝ and shared-boundary portal segments D∈ℙ, together with one deterministic fixed camera ℂ per space (placed on a portal-free wall facing an exit). Geometric projection derives each portal’s on-screen side (left, right, or far wall) to constrain cross-space transitions and verify doorway placement.

    (2) Asset library (Aₜ). The asset library combines per-space visual memory (initialized from the opening renders and updated after each turn with the latest generated video tail of the visited space) with initial entity identity crops A₀(v) paired with unique identifiers and stable, location-free appearance descriptions. At each step, the system retrieves the destination-space memory and identity crops for action participants and off-screen actors while skipping characters already visible in Iₜ to prevent duplicate figures.

    (3) Scene graph (Gₜ=(Vₜ,𝔼ₜ)). Initialized as G₀, the scene graph tracks all in-view and off-screen entities Vₜ. Containment, support, and holding relations are deterministically derived from hierarchical ownership pointers alongside portability, carrying-capacity limits, and state attributes 𝔼ₜ (e.g., open/closed, lit/unlit). A symbolic transition engine checks preconditions and goal reachability over Gₜ, supplying valid action suggestions at each turn.

    4.2 Interpreter and Planner: Intent Grounding and State Deduction

    At turn t, the system presents feasible menu suggestions derived from Gₜ, while the user may select a menu option or issue open-ended input uₜ via clicks, drags, or free text. Given the current frame Iₜ, the asset library Aₜ, and Gₜ, the Interpreter grounds uₜ to specific scene entities, resolving it into a structured operation aₜ, an expected state change Δₜ, and invariance constraints (Fig. 2, bottom).

    The Planner then validates both in-plan choices and out-of-distribution (off-menu) operations using the symbolic transition engine over Gₜ. If aₜ matches a pre-verified branch, it advances directly; otherwise, the Planner checks physical preconditions P(aₜ), carrying capacity, and locality over Gₜ, deduces Gₜᵉˣᵖᵉᶜᵗᵉᵈ=Gₜ⊕Δₜ, and runs graph search to verify that the global goal g remains reachable from Gₜᵉˣᵖᵉᶜᵗᵉᵈ. Inputs that are physically impossible, ambiguous, or would render g unreachable are rejected before rendering. Validated actions advance the planned scene graph to Gₜ₊₁=Gₜᵉˣᵖᵉᶜᵗᵉᵈ (maintained separately from observed video frames) and deterministically diff (Gₜ,Gₜ₊₁) into an explicit transition specification:

    Specₜ=(V_operated,Δₜ,Vₖₑₚₜ,Cₜ),

    		(4)

    which details the operated instances, the modified relations, the instances that must remain untouched, and, for cross-space moves, the camera transition instruction Cₜ.

    4.3 Painter and Inspector: Verified Target-Frame Generation

    In first–last-frame (FL2V) video synthesis, the starting frame Iₜ is fixed, so securing an accurate target end frame Iₜ^⋆ provides reliable boundary anchors for rendering the motion in between. Given the transition specification, the Painter combines the planned changes, the layout L, and the asset library Aₜ into an image prompt and calls an image-editing model to generate a candidate target end frame Iₜ^⋆ depicting the intended post-action state, conditioned on the current frame Iₜ, the destination-space memory on cross-space moves, and the operated object’s identity crop (e.g., scene B and lantern L1 in Fig. 2).

    Between the Painter and the Director, the Inspector serves as a target-endpoint gatekeeper, using a vision–language model to verify each candidate target end frame item by item as pass, fail, or unclear before video rendering: whether it depicts the completed action, whether operated instances retain their identity, and whether non-target objects are unchanged; for cross-space moves, it also localizes doorways in the candidate frame and checks their screen sides against the geometric projections from L. Specifically, it verifies every entry of the transition specification, including the planned changes, held items, and must-keep instances (such as confirming in Fig. 2 that L1 remains the same held lantern and D1 appears on the left in B). A failed check returns its visual evidence to the Painter for regeneration (the feedback loop in Fig. 2, with at most three attempts per step). Once verified, Iₜ^⋆ is locked in and passed to the Director.

    4.4 Director: Geometry-Aware Process Rendering

    Given the current real frame Iₜ and the verified frame Iₜ^⋆, the Director synthesizes the transition in between. For interactions within a single space, the Director writes a motion description from Iₜ, Iₜ^⋆, and the action text, and renders the action in one fixed camera shot. For moves between spaces, it reads from L the camera orientation difference δ=(φ_d-φₛ)\bmod360^∘ between source rₛ and destination r_d, and combines it with the portal geometry to specify the on-screen exit and entry sides across two fixed shots joined by a cut. For instance, when adjacent spaces share the same camera heading (δ=0^∘ in Fig. 2), a character exiting through a doorway on the right naturally enters the next space from the left. Together with Iₜ and Iₜ^⋆, these instructions condition the FL2V video model to render a 10-second transition clip Vₜ. Once Vₜ is rendered, its actual last frame Iₜ₊₁=Tail(Vₜ) both seeds the next turn and updates the space memory in Aₜ₊₁ as the latest visual observation of the visited space (the feedback arrow to the next-turn panel in Fig. 2), preserving scene and object changes across subsequent turns and revisits.

    5 Benchmark

    Unlike existing video benchmarks that separately evaluate clip-level visual quality [13], prescribed multi-turn instruction adherence [38], disappear-and-reappear object recovery under occlusion [5], or paired counterfactual interventions [3, 21], we build an interactive benchmark that jointly evaluates multi-space execution consistency and pre-render branching admissibility toward a shared goal.

    5.1 Evaluation Suites

    Built on 40 natural long-horizon tasks authored with Hy4 [29] across diverse indoor, outdoor, and mixed scenes (10 each across 1–4 connected spaces), the benchmark comprises two suites: (1) Multi-Step Interactive Execution evaluates rollout consistency over these 40 multi-turn episodes. (2) Branching Admissibility evaluates pre-render proposal gating at their opening decision points across 571 truth-verified, player-phrased proposals: 237 valid routes and 334 disguised infeasible counterfactuals involving nonexistent places (n=80), nonexistent objects (n=80), or unsatisfied preconditions (n=174).

    5.2 Evaluation Metrics

    For Multi-Step Interactive Execution, we evaluate each step across Action, World State, and Spatial continuity. Automated Hy4 evaluation scores all ten items, while blind human raters annotate four core metrics: Action (action completion), State (object holding and support), Entry (destination and entry side), and Exit (exit doorway direction). Steps where lost camera framing hides the target are flagged separately as Unclear (Sec. 6.4); the full ten-item list and scoring rubric are detailed in the supplementary material (Supplementary Table S1).

    For Branching Admissibility, we primarily evaluate under an Open mode (admissible / inadmissible / unsure, where unsure counts as a failure), reporting the acceptance rate on valid proposals (Accept), rejection rate on infeasible ones (Reject), their mean (Balanced), and the Unsure rate. We also include a Forced binary control that disallows abstention to check whether high rejection relies on trivially refusing valid proposals.

    6 Experiments

    6.1 Experimental Setup

    Models and backbones.

    All high-level reasoning roles (Architect, Interpreter, Planner, Inspector, and the task authoring model) are served by the multimodal language model Hy4 [29]. For generative rendering, we cross-pair two image generators (Qwen-Image-2.1 [25] and FLUX.2 [klein] 4B [1]) with two frozen FL2V video backbones (MiniMax-H3 [22] and LTX-2.5 [19]) to synthesize 10-second transition clips and compare Baseline against CineAct across combinations. Blind human evaluation and the reference-to-video (Ref2V) interface comparison in Sec. 6.4 are conducted on Qwen-Image-2.1 + MiniMax-H3.

    Ablation settings.

    To isolate each explicit representation, we evaluate four cumulative settings under a shared cross-space room-memory policy (initial room render on first entry, own last video frame on revisits): Baseline (Direct rollout) receives only the current frame and a user instruction; +Layout adds the spatial layout L and camera transition rules; +Assets further adds entity identity crops and stable appearance descriptions from Aₜ; and CineAct (Full framework) adds the scene graph Gₜ with symbolic state deduction, deterministic state-change checklists, and target-frame checks. Without Gₜ, the first three settings bypass symbolic planning and synthesize frames directly from the action instruction and their allowed layout or asset inputs. All compared settings share identical frozen backbones, action sequences, initial frames, random seeds, and per-step compute budgets (at most three target-frame attempts and one video generation), rolling out autoregressively from their own generated video tails to isolate the contribution of explicit world modeling.

    6.2 Multi-Step Execution

    Table 1 and Fig. 3 summarize the stepwise ablations on Multi-Step Interactive Execution across all four backbone combinations (Hy4 ratings; full 10-item breakdowns in Supplementary Table S3) and blind human ratings by 10 raters on Qwen-Image-2.1 + MiniMax-H3:

  • •

    Layout and cameras (+Layout vs. Baseline): Adding spatial layout L and camera transition rules improves spatial and overall consistency across backbones, effectively resolving cross-space disorientation.

  • •
