    Asset library (+Assets vs. +Layout): Introducing refreshed scene and instance references from Aₜ further boosts Action and World State under Qwen-Image-2.1, whereas lightweight FLUX.2 [klein] 4B [1] exhibits slight multi-reference editing variance before full CineAct recovers strongly.

  • •

    Scene graph and verification (CineAct vs. Baseline): Adding Gₜ, transition specifications, and target-frame checks achieves the highest consistency across all four backbone pairings, lifting Action, World State, and overall scores over Baseline (.862 overall on Qwen2.1 + H3, +11.4 points) and demonstrating strong cross-backbone generalization.

  • •

    Blind human evaluation (Fig. 3): Ten raters blindly scored 10 sampled stories on Qwen-Image-2.1 + MiniMax-H3 (40 anonymized story–setting units, 196 clips, 784 item ratings), corroborating the monotonic gain from .611 to .842 overall (+23.1 points) with best scores on every metric (Action .802, State .828, Entry/Exit 1.000).

    • Fig. 4(a–c) illustrates this stepwise progression on a four-room watering task: given the setup and route in (a), Baseline enters the wrong central arch toward the water room whereas +Layout takes the correct West door (b); after multiple room transitions, +Layout drops the items and +Assets holds both skins loose outside the basket, while CineAct keeps both packed inside the basket (c).

    6.3 Branching Admissibility

    Interactive video generation requires more than following a single fixed script: given a shared goal, a system must accommodate diverse player-proposed branches by admitting valid alternative routes while filtering out requests that violate world constraints. Across the opening decision points of all 40 stories, we evaluate 571 player-phrased proposals authored with Hy4 (237 valid goal-reaching approaches and 334 plausible-looking infeasible counterfactuals). Each ablation setting judges proposal admissibility solely from the opening frame, task goal, and its allowed prior information (L, A₀ containing initial views of all spaces and entity crops, or G₀) without generating video.

    As shown in Tables 2 and 3, pixel-only Baseline abstains (Unsure) on 80.0% of proposals under the Open mode (especially in multi-space scenes) and accepts only .080 of valid branches (.146 balanced accuracy). Even under the Forced control, Baseline achieves .970 rejection merely by refusing nearly all inputs, blocking 73.8% of valid routes (.262 acceptance). Across the three counterfactual categories (Table 3, where miss rate counts infeasible proposals answered either admissible or unsure), adding explicit representations progressively resolves each error type: +Layout substantially reduces misses on Nonexistent Place; +Assets sharply cuts Nonexistent Object misses and lowers overall abstention to 29.8%; and adding G₀ (CineAct) further drives down Broken Precondition misses, reducing abstention to 4.0% while achieving high acceptance and rejection across both Open (.887 balanced) and Forced (.905 balanced) modes. To evaluate paired execution, raters blindly score 13 multi-route stories (26 trajectories/method across 1–4 spaces; Table 4) on per-route and both-route goal completion, route-specific consequence preservation, and zero cross-leak or rollback (jointly counted as both succeed & distinct). From identical initial states, CineAct achieves 1.000 both-route goal completion (vs. .615) and .923 both succeed & distinct (.900 on 2–4 spaces, n=10, vs. .500).

    6.4 Interface Analysis: FL2V vs. Ref2V

    We compare our FL2V pipeline against Reference-to-Video (Ref2V), which conditions MiniMax-H3 directly on Iₜ and asset crops over the same 10 stories. On visually determinable items, Ref2V achieves comparable Baseline-to-CineAct gains under the 10-item Hy4 evaluation (.713→.875 vs. .733→.856 for FL2V). However, Ref2V leaves 26.0% (51/196) of object-holding/support (State) steps visually Unclear under human evaluation (vs. 0.0% for FL2V), which is unacceptable for multi-turn interaction. Specifically, as shown in Fig. 4(d), starting from the Shared input, FL2V anchors the room framing via the verified Target frame, so its output keeps both the held rag and the bucket and machinery in view (Scene retained); by contrast, Ref2V drifts into a close-up that crops out the bucket and surrounding room (View cropped), preventing users from inspecting or selecting them in subsequent turns (Supplementary Table S4).

    7 Limitations

    While CineAct improves multi-turn consistency and branching reliability, three trade-offs remain. First, skipping per-shot 3D reconstruction and fine-tuning keeps the pipeline lightweight and consistent, but limits each room to a fixed camera with cut transitions rather than continuous 3D camera motion. Second, sequential deduction, iterative verification, and 10-second FL2V synthesis yield turn-based rather than real-time streaming latency. Third, rooms and entities are fixed up front by Architect; adding new rooms on the fly, post-clip state re-sync, and streaming backbones is left to future work.

    8 Conclusion

    We formulated goal-grounded interactive video generation and presented CineAct, a state-first agentic framework that decouples high-level world-state reasoning from low-level pixel rendering. By maintaining explicit spatial layouts with cameras, dynamically refreshed asset libraries, and scene graphs, and by locking in post-action endpoints through pre-rendering target-frame verification, CineAct enables reliable multi-turn execution and pre-render gating of open-ended branching proposals. Experiments across multi-step execution, counterfactual branching admissibility, and interface comparisons validate each explicit representation’s specialized role.

    （参考文献见原文。）


    Supplementary Material

    Backbone Specifications

    All reasoning agents and automated evaluators run on the multimodal language model Hy4 [29]. For image editing, we use Qwen-Image-2.1 [25] and the distilled FLUX.2 [klein] 4B [1]. For video synthesis, both the FL2V and Ref2V interfaces of MiniMax-H3 [22] use the 8-step distilled variants, while LTX-2.5 [19] runs in full BF16 non-distilled two-stage mode (30 steps).

    System Representations and Execution Walkthrough

    Here we detail the three representations from Sec. 4 and summarize one execution turn in Algorithm 1. Fig. S6 shows a concrete example on the three-terrace seedling task: panels (a)–(d) give the layout L, initial views, scene graph G₁, and asset crops A₁, while panels (e)–(f) trace two rollouts. At each turn, the Planner checks preconditions on Gₜ, retrieves only the destination view and off-screen entity crops (Lines 4–5), verifies the target frame before rendering Vₜ (Lines 7–12), and writes Tail(Vₜ) back only to the visited terrace (Line 13).

  • •

    Spatial layout and cameras (L): Spaces are non-overlapping 2D axis-aligned rectangles with portals on shared walls, each observed by one fixed camera (65^∘ horizontal FOV, placed on a portal-free wall facing an exit). Geometric projection derives each doorway’s on-screen side (left, right, or far wall) for Painter/Director prompting and Inspector verification.

  • •

    Asset library (Aₜ): Combines per-space visual memory with static entity identity crops extracted at initialization. Only actual video tails Iₜ₊₁=Tail(Vₜ) (never intermediate target images Iₜ^⋆) update the visited space’s memory in Aₜ₊₁; conditioning uses the destination space’s latest memory plus crops for operated and off-screen entities, skipping actors already visible in Iₜ.

  • •

    Scene graph (Gₜ) and symbolic engine: Nodes store location/ownership pointers (in, on, held), portability, carrying capacity, and state attributes. Before rendering, the Planner checks preconditions and goal reachability via breadth-first search, advances the separate planned graph Gₜ₊₁, and deterministically diffs (Gₜ,Gₜ₊₁) into Specₜ.

    • Evaluation Metrics and Human–Automated Agreement

    Table S1 lists all ten per-step questions used in Multi-Step Interactive Execution, and Figs. S1–S2 show all six steps of the courtyard watering task across the four ablation settings. On the four shared items (Action, State, Entry, Exit) for Qwen-Image-2.1 + MiniMax-H3, Hy4 matches blind human ratings 73.0% of the time in binary agreement (64.4% exact three-tier) and follows the same ablation order as Table 1 and Fig. 3 of the main paper. Table S2 extends this blind human study to two LTX-2.5 pairings on the same 10 stories. CineAct ranks first under all three pairings (.842, .748, and .614; +23.1, +18.0, and +17.6 points over Baseline), matching the automated cross-backbone results in Table S3.

item.title: 4D 占用预测的真正难点不是「预测变化」，而是「守住没变的」：这篇把未来分成三类再逐一处理 ｜ Write, Evolve, Read: Streaming Cameras into a Persistent World State for 4D Occupancy Forecasting
item.description:
一句话：几秒内场景几乎不变，大部分前方空间其实已经看过——但模型守不住它。

要点：

  • 观察角度很实用：4D 占用预测要预测几秒后的三维语义占用；而在几秒的时间尺度上，**场景本身变化很小、车在移动，因此前方大部分空间其实已经被看到过**
  • 作者因此把未来分成**不变、变化、未见**三类，并指出当前基于相机的世界模型在「不变」这一部分表现最差——它们**没能守住已经看到过的东西**，而不是没预测出会变化的部分
  • 做法是把流式相机输入**写入**一个持久的世界状态、让它**演化**，再从中**读出**预测（Write / Evolve / Read）

为什么值得看：这条给「持久状态」提供了一个可度量的失败模式：不是预测不准，而是记不住。把「不变/变化/未见」拆开评，等于告诉你该优化哪一块——这个方法学比结论更可迁移。

中文摘要：4D 占用预测的任务是预测数秒之后驾驶场景的三维语义占用。作者指出了一个容易被忽略的事实：在几秒的尺度上场景本身变化很小，主要是车在移动，因此前方大部分空间其实已经被看到过。据此他们把未来分为不变、变化与未见三类，并发现当前基于相机的世界模型在「不变」这一部分表现最差——它们的失败并不在于预测不准将要变化的部分，而在于没能守住已经看到过的内容。为此论文提出 Write / Evolve / Read 的做法：把流式相机输入写入一个持久的世界状态，让该状态持续演化，再从其中读出预测。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-24

本期推送：2026-11-25

Write, Evolve, Read: Streaming Cameras into
a Persistent World State for 4D Occupancy Forecasting

Abstract

4D occupancy forecasting predicts the 3D semantic occupancy of a driving scene seconds ahead. Over a few seconds, the scene changes little while the vehicle moves, so most of the space ahead has already been seen. Sorting the future into unchanged, changed, and unseen space, we find that current camera-based world models fall short on the unchanged part: they fail to hold on to what they have already seen, rather than to forecast what will change. We therefore make what the model has seen its state. PersistWorld streams camera frames into a persistent 3D world state anchored in the scene, writing each frame once instead of rebuilding the state from past frames. The state is learned end to end with the forecast, and an evolver predicts it at any queried time along the ego trajectory. On Occ3D-nuScenes, PersistWorld raises the IoU of the best camera-based world model by 19 points at 1–3 s and by 18 to 24 points up to 8 s, while running more than twice as fast.

Code: https://github.com/wangzian828/PersistWorld
Project: https://wangzian828.github.io/PersistWorld

1 Introduction

An autonomous vehicle must anticipate how the space around it will be occupied a few seconds ahead. Occupancy world models forecast future 3D semantic occupancy from past observations and the planned ego trajectory, and much of the work on them has gone into the forecasting itself: how to tokenize the scene, how to generate its future, and how to condition it on the ego trajectory [47, 11, 35, 26, 9]. Yet with cameras, the setting that matters in practice, they remain far less accurate than models given ground-truth occupancy [26, 6, 9]. Where do their errors lie?

Over a few seconds, a driving scene itself changes little, while the vehicle moves through it. Most of the space ahead of the vehicle has therefore already been seen by its cameras. We make this precise by sorting the future scene into three kinds of space (Figs.1 and 2): unchanged space, seen and still the same; changed space, seen but different by then; and unseen space, never seen. One second ahead, four fifths of the occupied future is unchanged space; changed space stays small, and unseen space grows only as the vehicle moves into regions it could not see.

Current camera-based world models lose much of exactly this part. SparseWorld-TC [9], the strongest of them, reaches an IoU of only 51.07 on unchanged space (Fig.1), where the scene as seen is already the answer. Its own estimate of the current frame, moved to the target time without any forecasting, already reaches 48.68 there, and the occupancy that STCOcc [25] predicts for two-stage methods reaches 46.31 (Sec.4.3). Where forecasting is actually needed, on changed and unseen space, SparseWorld-TC is far ahead of carrying the seen scene forward, with an IoU of 45.35 and 40.92 against 26.33 and 0. The shortfall of camera-based world models thus lies not in forecasting what will change but in holding on to what they have already seen, which models given ground-truth occupancy receive for free.

The same property of driving scenes also tells how to hold on to it: over a few seconds, the cameras view the same, largely unchanged scene from many positions. We therefore make what the model has seen its state: a 3D world state anchored in the scene, written directly from camera images and learned end to end with the forecast. The state stays in place as the vehicle moves, so the evidence that every frame provides about a place accumulates at one position. To forecast, an evolver predicts the features of the state at the queried time along the ego trajectory.

Holding what has been seen in a state also makes forecasting cheap. Since consecutive frames show nearly the same scene, the state is updated frame by frame as the images stream in: each new frame only adds its own evidence, as in streaming models that estimate the present scene [49, 32, 5] or keep a memory for forecasting [29]. Each image is thus processed once, and no separate perception network is needed, whereas sparse end-to-end models re-derive the scene from the image history for every forecast [7, 9] and two-stage methods first run a perception network [11, 35, 26, 6]. Since a forecast needs only a recent view of the surroundings, the state is reset periodically and keeps only the last few seconds of observation.

On Occ3D-nuScenes, our model raises the IoU and mIoU of the best camera-based world model by 19.13 and 3.32 at 1–3 s and runs more than twice as fast. Its IoU rises from 51.07 to 70.86 on unchanged space and from 40.92 to 62.71 on unseen space, and the same model leads by 18.19 to 24.41 IoU at every horizon up to 8 s. Our contributions are:

  • •

    An analysis that sorts the future scene into unchanged, changed, and unseen space, and shows that camera-based world models fall short in holding on to what they have already seen rather than in forecasting what will change.

  • •

    A camera-based occupancy world model that holds what it has seen in a 3D world state anchored in the scene, written from images, learned end to end with the forecast, updated as a stream, and reset periodically.

  • •

    State-of-the-art camera-based forecasting on Occ3D-nuScenes at 1–3 s and 1–8 s with a single model, which is also the fastest of the compared methods.

    • 2 Related Work

    Occupancy from cameras.

    Camera-based occupancy perception lifts image features into a 3D grid of semantic voxels, through view transformation into bird’s-eye-view or voxel features [21, 22], sparse queries [27, 38], or 3D Gaussians [14], and is evaluated on benchmarks such as Occ3D [37] and PanoBench [10]. Rendering-based methods add supervision along camera rays, rendering depth and semantics from the predicted volume [33, 13] or rendering both the prediction and the voxel labels and comparing them in the views or along the rays [3, 18]. We use the same kind of signal, predicting occupancy along each camera ray and supervising it with labels rendered from the ground-truth grid, so that the evidence of each image is written at the right depth along its rays. Temporal methods carry information across frames by propagating object queries [39] or fusing a long history through temporal stereo [34]; for occupancy, they evolve 3D Gaussians with ego and object motion [49], stream voxel features [32], or unify several temporal cues [5], and such a memory state can also be learned from multi-camera video as pre-training for perception and planning [30]. All these methods estimate the present scene, and every new frame corrects their state. Our state is also updated as a stream, but it is learned with the forecast and advanced to future times, where no new frame corrects it.

    Forecasting the future scene.

    Occupancy world models tokenize the scene and generate its future autoregressively or by diffusion [47, 40, 42, 43, 46, 11, 16, 41, 15, 26], warp the current scene to the future ego poses [6], add conditions [19, 12, 45], or separate ego motion from scene change [35]. They are commonly evaluated on Occ3D-nuScenes at 1, 2, and 3 s [47], and up to 8 s in later work [35, 9]. These models take occupancy as input; with cameras, they forecast from a separately trained perception network [22, 25], so what they forecast from is fixed before forecasting, and such chains degrade when errors enter upstream [48]. Camera-based end-to-end models learn the forecast from images [28, 44, 20, 31, 24]; some re-read the image history with sparse queries for every forecast [7, 9, 8], and some can be queried at any time [4, 1]. A persistent scene state has also been kept, but from bird’s-eye-view features [29]. PersistWorld holds what it has seen in a 3D world state written directly from images and updated as a stream, instead of re-deriving the scene for each forecast. Which parts of the future must be forecast has also been studied: aggregating past observations is a strong baseline [17], most occupied future voxels are static [35], and scene evolution has been split into static, moving, and newly observed parts [49, 2, 28]. We split the future by what the input frames have seen into unchanged, changed, and unseen space, and use the split to measure how each kind changes with the horizon and show that camera-based world models fall short on space they have already seen.

    3 Method

    Overview. PersistWorld holds what its cameras have seen in a world state S on a fixed 3D lattice and updates it as a stream, once per capture group. A capture group, which we also call a frame, is the surround-view images taken at one time, together with their camera parameters and the ego pose (Fig. 3). When a group arrives, the State Evolver carries S to its capture time (Sec. 3.3), the Visibility-aware State Writer writes the evidence of the new images into it (Sec. 3.2), and the Pose-queried Occupancy Reader decodes the current occupancy (Sec. 3.4). To forecast, the Evolver predicts the state at each queried time from S and the ego trajectory, and the Reader decodes occupancy in the queried ego frame. All components are trained end to end together with the image backbone (Secs. 3.5 and 3.6).

    3.1 World State

    The state lives on a lattice of 1.6 m cells anchored in the scene, so a cell keeps its address while the vehicle moves. The region queried at any time is the occupancy volume around the ego, 80×80×6.4 m on Occ3D, and spans 50×50×4 cells. Each cell stores a feature that packs the features of its 2×2×2 sub-cells of 0.8 m, together with the time of its estimate and the time of its last observation, which condition the Evolver (Sec. 3.3). Packing keeps attention in the Evolver over a compact lattice, while the Writer and Reader operate on the finer sub-cells; the Reader decodes each sub-cell into 2×2×2 voxels of 0.4 m (Sec. 3.4). The state is stored only where it has been written; an unwritten cell takes a learned initial feature of its ego-relative position.

    3.2 Visibility-aware State Writer

    Images are encoded by a DINOv3 ViT-B/16 [36] whose last blocks are fine-tuned, and key and value maps are projected from its feature map. Each capture group is encoded and written once, into the state that the Evolver has just carried to its capture time. For a sub-cell with center x, the Writer samples keys and values bilinearly at the projection of x into each camera, shifted by a small image-plane offset predicted from the sub-cell’s feature, and adds a learned camera embedding. Because the state is already at the capture time, the Writer only places what the new images show and needs no motion model; all motion is left to the Evolver.

    Ray-depth sections.

    All sub-cells along a pixel ray project to the same image location and sample the same feature, so projection alone cannot tell them apart. We split each patch ray into depth sections of 0.8 m and let a light head predict, for every patch, a distribution over the section that holds the first occupied surface, with one more bin for rays that hit no surface. For each sample, the section containing the sub-cell provides a geometry embedding that is added to the key and value, and the log-probability of that section is added as an attention bias, so evidence is weighted by how plausible it is that the sub-cell is the visible surface.

    Update.

    The sub-cell feature attends, with a single query, to its samples from all cameras and to a null token with zero key and value, which lets it take no evidence when no camera shows it. A gate from the prior and the candidate feature controls the residual update and is zero where no camera sees, so those keep the state carried by the Evolver.

    3.3 State Evolver

    The Evolver advances the state from the time of its estimate to a target time under the ego trajectory. It carries the state to the capture time before writing and predicts the state at each queried future time. Its inputs are the state in a window around the ego at the target time and the sequence of ego poses since the last reset (Sec. 3.6) up to the target pose. Motion tokens are formed from the relative SE(3) transforms between consecutive poses and the time steps; each cell attends only to the motion that follows its own estimate, and is conditioned on the age of its estimate and of its last observation. A context of the observed state, encoded by further axial blocks over all stored cells, is computed once per update of the state, shared by every advance from it, and added to the cell features before the residual blocks. Residual blocks, with adaptive layer normalization conditioned on these ages, each apply cross-attention to the motion tokens and self-attention along one lattice axis. The output is a change added to the state, scaled by the elapsed time, so that the Evolver is the identity when no time passes. Since the ego trajectory up to the target is an input, the same Evolver serves every horizon.

    3.4 Pose-queried Occupancy Reader

    The Reader unpacks the sub-cells and applies a local residual block of a depth-wise 3³ convolution and point-wise mixing, followed by a linear layer that predicts class logits for the 2×2×2 voxels of 0.4 m inside each sub-cell; the logits are resampled into the queried ego frame. The same Reader decodes the current occupancy right after writing and the future occupancy from the predicted states.

    3.5 Unified Occupancy Objective

    Each voxel is supervised with a focal score on the softmax probabilities p_c of its class distribution, applied to every class as a binary event. With the focal term f(q)=-(1-q)²\logq, a voxel with label y receives

    ℓ(p,y)=ω_y[a⁺_y f(p_y)+∑_c≠ya⁻_c f(1-p_c)],

    		(1)

    where the class weights follow the class priors π_c measured on the training set, a⁺_c∝π_c^-1/2 and a⁻_c∝(1-π_c)^-1/2 with a shared normalization constant, and ω_y=4 for free voxels and 1 otherwise. Classes absent from a scene still receive the negative term, so rare classes are supervised in every scene. The grid term L_grid(t) averages Eq. (1) over the voxels inside the target mask at time t.

    Grid and ray views.

    The ray-depth head of Sec. 3.2 predicts, for each patch ray, which section is occupied: it is a view of the same occupancy field along camera rays. We render the per-section occupancy of the current frame from the ground-truth grid and supervise the ray view with the same focal objective. The ray term L_ray averages Eq. (1) over the valid sections, separately from the grid term, so the two views have equal weight. The loss at a frame t₀ is

    L=(1)/(|K|)∑_k∈KL_grid(tₖ)+0.25(L_grid(t₀)+L_ray),

    		(2)

    where K is the set of supervised future horizons at that frame.

    Horizons.

    Each loss supervises 1, 2, and 3 s, plus one horizon drawn uniformly from the available ones in 4–8 s. A single model therefore serves all horizons from 1 to 8 s.

    3.6 Memory Span and Training

    Memory span.

    What a forecast needs from the past is a recent view of the surroundings, so the state holds only recent observations. We reset it to the initial state at the start of each scene and after every eight capture groups, the history length used by SparseWorld-TC, so it holds between one and eight capture groups. Each keyframe is answered with the state it holds at that moment.

    Training on streams.

    Training runs the model as at inference. A training segment is a run of up to eight consecutive capture groups of one scene, starting from the initial state; losses are placed at keyframes whose state depths, the number of capture groups written since the reset, are drawn uniformly from one to eight, so the model is trained at every depth it meets at inference. Gradients are truncated to the last two writes before each loss: the earlier writes run without gradient, so memory does not grow with the segment length. Each image is encoded once per segment.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Setup

    Dataset and metrics.

    Occ3D-nuScenes [37] provides 700 training and 150 validation scenes with 18-class labels at 0.4 m. Following SparseWorld-TC [9], a forecast uses at most the last eight capture groups and the ground-truth future ego poses. We forecast 1, 2, and 3 s ahead from every validation keyframe, which gives 6019 anchor keyframes with 5719, 5419, and 5119 targets at 1, 2, and 3 s. We report the intersection over union of occupied voxels, IoU, and its mean over the semantic classes, mIoU, inside the camera mask of the target frame. For long-horizon forecasting, we query the same model at every horizon from 1 to 8 s.

    Streaming evaluation.

    Our model processes each validation scene as a stream of keyframes, as it would run on a vehicle. Each capture group is written into the state once, and each keyframe is answered with the state at that moment, which holds one to eight capture groups (Sec.3.6). As in training, the state is reset at the start of each scene and after every eight capture groups.

    Implementation details.

    The state is written at every keyframe, 0.5 s apart. We train for 20 epochs with AdamW at a learning rate of 3×10⁻⁴; AppendixA gives the remaining settings.

    Baselines.

    Methods marked Occ GT forecast from the ground-truth occupancy, and camera-based methods forecast from images. Two-stage methods marked -STC forecast from the occupancy that STCOcc [25] predicts from the images. We measure the speed in frames per second, FPS, for every method with released code and weights on one A800 with batch size one, from the inputs on the GPU to the occupancy of the current frame and of 1, 2, and 3 s on the CPU. For two-stage methods, the time includes their perception network.

    4.2 Main Results

    Short-horizon forecasting.

    Tab.1 compares forecasts at 1, 2, and 3 s. Our model leads SparseWorld-TC, the strongest prior camera-based world model, at every horizon, and the lead grows with the horizon, from 18.19 to 20.14 IoU and from 3.04 to 3.63 mIoU. With future ego poses planned by BEV-Planner [23] instead of the ground truth, the lead widens to 22.63 IoU and 4.00 mIoU, so it does not rest on the ground-truth future poses; AppendixE gives the details. Two-stage methods are limited by their input: with ground-truth occupancy, GAST leads I2-World by 5.60 mIoU, but from the occupancy that STCOcc predicts, the two are within 0.75 mIoU and both fall below SparseWorld-TC (Sec.4.3). Our model is also the fastest of all methods with a measured speed, at 23.15 FPS (Fig.4), since it processes each image once and runs no separate perception network.

    Long-horizon forecasting.

    Tab.2 queries the model of Tab.1 at every horizon from 1 to 8 s. It leads SparseWorld-TC by 18.19 to 24.41 IoU at every horizon, and by 21.58 IoU and 4.21 mIoU on average over 1–8 s. The lead holds at 8 s, where most of the occupied future lies in space that no input frame saw (Fig.2), so the forecast does more than carry the seen scene forward: it also fills in unseen space.

    4.3 Three Kinds of Space

    Where forecasts fall short.

    We split the occupied future by the two questions of Sec.1, using the ground truth of the input frames. Unchanged space makes up 80.85% of it at 1 s and 34.87% at 8 s, unseen space grows from 14.39% to 62.06%, and changed space stays below 5% (Fig.2). Fig.5a scores the forecasts at 1–3 s on each kind. As a reference, copying the ground truth of the input frames forward with the ego poses scores 100 IoU on unchanged space, 26.33 on changed space, and 0 on unseen space. SparseWorld-TC does far better than this copy on changed and unseen space but reaches only 51.07 IoU on unchanged space, where the seen scene is already the answer. Our model reaches 70.86 there and 62.71 on unseen space, 19.79 and 21.79 above it.

    What is seen and what is forecast.

    To see what forecasting adds, we copy each model’s estimate of the current frame forward in the same way; for our model, this is Perception + warp in Fig.5a. On unchanged space, the copy already reaches 68.60 IoU for our model and 48.68 for SparseWorld-TC, close to their forecasts of 70.86 and 51.07, and the occupancy that STCOcc [25] predicts for two-stage methods reaches 46.31. Forecasting adds about as much there to both models, 2.26 and 2.39 IoU. Accuracy on unchanged space is thus decided before forecasting, and our lead there comes from how well the model holds on to what it has seen. On changed and unseen space, our forecast exceeds the copy by 4.46 and 37.48 IoU; this is what forecasting adds.

    Visibility.

    The state also keeps what has left the view of the cameras. Fig.5b splits the future by visibility at the last input frame. On space seen only in earlier frames, our model reaches 70.41 IoU, slightly above the 68.99 on space still in view, so what has left the view is not lost.

    4.4 Ablation Study

    Properties of the state.

    Tab.3 changes one property of the state at a time and scores each variant on the three kinds of space. The state must be anchored in the scene: with an ego-centric state, whose lattice moves with the vehicle and is resampled into the ego frame of every new capture group, as in temporal fusion of bird’s-eye-view features [21], the IoU falls by 3.86, most on unchanged space, by 4.38, and by 3.02 on unseen space, against 0.42 on changed space. Resampling the state at every capture group blurs what it has seen, and the extra resampling lowers the speed to 21.29 FPS. The image features must be learned: with the image encoder frozen, the mIoU falls by 4.07 and the IoU on unchanged space by 2.78. The Evolver is what completes unseen space: without it, the state is read unchanged at each target pose, and the IoU on unseen space falls by 12.22, against 3.66 and 2.43 on unchanged and changed space. Removing the depth conditioning or attention of the Writer, or the shared context of the Evolver, also lowers the accuracy of both the current frame and the forecasts, as the component ablations in AppendixC show.

    Streaming.

    Updating the state as a stream doubles the speed at nearly the same accuracy. Rebuilding the state for every query from the last eight capture groups reaches 29.26 mIoU and 67.97 IoU, against 28.72 and 67.82, but even with image features cached, every query then writes eight capture groups, and the speed nearly halves to 12.02 FPS.

    Input.

    The lead does not come from our image encoder. Writing the state from the occupancy that STCOcc [25] predicts, instead of from images, reaches 28.39 mIoU and 67.73 IoU, while GAST-STC reaches 24.70 and 42.47 from the same input. Copied forward, this input reaches only 46.31 IoU on unchanged space, and our state written from it reaches 72.06 there. The state combines the predictions of successive frames at fixed places in the scene, so it holds more of the seen scene than any single prediction. Running the perception network first, however, slows the model to 3.61 FPS, while a state learned end to end from images needs no separate perception network.

    Memory span.

    A forecast needs only the last few seconds of observation. We vary the reset period N of the state at evaluation, for the model trained with N=8 (Fig.6). The estimate of the current frame improves with every added capture group, from 61.14 IoU at N=1 to 68.99 at N=16, as the evidence of successive frames accumulates in the state. Forecasts at 1–3 s level off at N=8 and change by at most 0.15 IoU beyond it, and the 1–8 s average varies by at most 0.49. Resetting the state every eight capture groups thus costs no forecasting accuracy.

    4.5 Qualitative Results

    Fig.7 shows forecasts of our model and the ground truth in two scenes, at the current frame and 1, 2, and 3 s ahead. In scene (a), the vehicle drives along a construction zone with moving traffic and pedestrians; the buildings, vegetation, and sidewalks along the road stay in place in our forecasts up to 3 s, as in the ground truth, and the pedestrians on the right of the road remain in them. In scene (b), the vehicle crosses an intersection, and our forecast continues the road into space that no input frame observed. Comparisons with SparseWorld-TC on these and more scenes, forecasts from one state along two trajectories, and errors by distance and by dynamic and static classes are in AppendicesD, E and F.

    5 Conclusion

    Sorting the future scene into unchanged, changed, and unseen space shows that camera-based occupancy forecasting is limited first by how well models hold on to what they have already seen. PersistWorld holds it in a 3D world state anchored in the scene and updated as a stream, and an evolver predicts the state at any queried time along the ego trajectory. On Occ3D-nuScenes, this raises the IoU of the best camera-based world model by 19 points at 1–3 s and keeps the lead up to 8 s, at more than twice its speed.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix

    This appendix extends the experiments of Sec.4. AppendixA gives implementation details, AppendixB writes the state from occupancy instead of images, AppendixC removes components of the model one at a time, AppendixD breaks the forecasts down by class, distance, horizon, state depth, and ego motion, AppendixE forecasts along trajectories other than the ground truth, and AppendixF discusses more qualitative results. All results use the protocol of Sec.4.1 unless stated otherwise.

    Appendix A Implementation details

    Images are resized to 256×704 and, during training, augmented as in SparseWorld-TC [9] by random scaling, cropping, flipping, and photometric distortion. The last four blocks of DINOv3 are fine-tuned at one third of the base learning rate. The state has 384 channels; the Evolver has three residual blocks and three context blocks, and the Writer two attention layers. We train for 20 epochs with AdamW at a learning rate of 3×10⁻⁴, decayed to one third over the last four epochs, with gradients clipped at a norm of 5, on six A800 GPUs in about 15 hours.

    Appendix B Forecasting from occupancy

    Our model can be written from occupancy instead of images. For each new occupancy grid, the Writer reads the labels of the eight voxels covered by each sub-cell, embeds their class histogram, and applies a gated update to the state; the Evolver and Reader are unchanged. We train two such variants with the schedule of the main model. Both use the same streaming protocol as the camera model: each new grid is written once into the state, which is reset every eight keyframes and at scene changes, so a forecast uses one to eight keyframes since the last reset. PersistWorld-STC is written from the occupancy predicted by STCOcc [25], the perception network of the two-stage methods, and is scored inside the camera mask. PersistWorld-GT is written from the ground-truth occupancy and is scored on the full volume, as the Occ GT methods in Tab.1. Its 1–3 s evaluation uses 4519 anchors with at least 2 s of history and 3 s of future available in the scene; this selects the scored anchors and does not change the state reset schedule. Each block of Tab.4 also moves the input of the current frame to the target frame with the ego poses, which forecasts as if nothing changed.

    Occupancy-input forecasting.

    Using STCOcc predictions as the input source, PersistWorld-STC reaches 28.39 mIoU and 67.73 IoU on average, against 24.70 and 42.47 for GAST-STC, the strongest two-stage method. From the ground truth, PersistWorld-GT reaches 42.42 mIoU and 60.77 IoU, against 45.33 and 55.09 for GAST: it is the most accurate in geometry and third in semantics. PersistWorld-STC also exceeds the camera end-to-end baselines in Tab.1, while reaching similar accuracy to our camera model. Compared with copying only the current occupancy forward, the full model gains 30.11 IoU with STCOcc input and 7.93 with ground-truth input.

一句话：几秒内场景几乎不变，大部分前方空间其实已经看过——但模型守不住它。

要点：

  • 观察角度很实用：4D 占用预测要预测几秒后的三维语义占用；而在几秒的时间尺度上，**场景本身变化很小、车在移动，因此前方大部分空间其实已经被看到过**
  • 作者因此把未来分成**不变、变化、未见**三类，并指出当前基于相机的世界模型在「不变」这一部分表现最差——它们**没能守住已经看到过的东西**，而不是没预测出会变化的部分
  • 做法是把流式相机输入**写入**一个持久的世界状态、让它**演化**，再从中**读出**预测（Write / Evolve / Read）

为什么值得看：这条给「持久状态」提供了一个可度量的失败模式：不是预测不准，而是记不住。把「不变/变化/未见」拆开评，等于告诉你该优化哪一块——这个方法学比结论更可迁移。

中文摘要：4D 占用预测的任务是预测数秒之后驾驶场景的三维语义占用。作者指出了一个容易被忽略的事实：在几秒的尺度上场景本身变化很小，主要是车在移动，因此前方大部分空间其实已经被看到过。据此他们把未来分为不变、变化与未见三类，并发现当前基于相机的世界模型在「不变」这一部分表现最差——它们的失败并不在于预测不准将要变化的部分，而在于没能守住已经看到过的内容。为此论文提出 Write / Evolve / Read 的做法：把流式相机输入写入一个持久的世界状态，让该状态持续演化，再从其中读出预测。

主题：AI Native Engine

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-24

本期推送：2026-11-25

Write, Evolve, Read: Streaming Cameras into
a Persistent World State for 4D Occupancy Forecasting

Abstract

4D occupancy forecasting predicts the 3D semantic occupancy of a driving scene seconds ahead. Over a few seconds, the scene changes little while the vehicle moves, so most of the space ahead has already been seen. Sorting the future into unchanged, changed, and unseen space, we find that current camera-based world models fall short on the unchanged part: they fail to hold on to what they have already seen, rather than to forecast what will change. We therefore make what the model has seen its state. PersistWorld streams camera frames into a persistent 3D world state anchored in the scene, writing each frame once instead of rebuilding the state from past frames. The state is learned end to end with the forecast, and an evolver predicts it at any queried time along the ego trajectory. On Occ3D-nuScenes, PersistWorld raises the IoU of the best camera-based world model by 19 points at 1–3 s and by 18 to 24 points up to 8 s, while running more than twice as fast.

Code: https://github.com/wangzian828/PersistWorld
Project: https://wangzian828.github.io/PersistWorld

1 Introduction

An autonomous vehicle must anticipate how the space around it will be occupied a few seconds ahead. Occupancy world models forecast future 3D semantic occupancy from past observations and the planned ego trajectory, and much of the work on them has gone into the forecasting itself: how to tokenize the scene, how to generate its future, and how to condition it on the ego trajectory [47, 11, 35, 26, 9]. Yet with cameras, the setting that matters in practice, they remain far less accurate than models given ground-truth occupancy [26, 6, 9]. Where do their errors lie?

Over a few seconds, a driving scene itself changes little, while the vehicle moves through it. Most of the space ahead of the vehicle has therefore already been seen by its cameras. We make this precise by sorting the future scene into three kinds of space (Figs.1 and 2): unchanged space, seen and still the same; changed space, seen but different by then; and unseen space, never seen. One second ahead, four fifths of the occupied future is unchanged space; changed space stays small, and unseen space grows only as the vehicle moves into regions it could not see.

Current camera-based world models lose much of exactly this part. SparseWorld-TC [9], the strongest of them, reaches an IoU of only 51.07 on unchanged space (Fig.1), where the scene as seen is already the answer. Its own estimate of the current frame, moved to the target time without any forecasting, already reaches 48.68 there, and the occupancy that STCOcc [25] predicts for two-stage methods reaches 46.31 (Sec.4.3). Where forecasting is actually needed, on changed and unseen space, SparseWorld-TC is far ahead of carrying the seen scene forward, with an IoU of 45.35 and 40.92 against 26.33 and 0. The shortfall of camera-based world models thus lies not in forecasting what will change but in holding on to what they have already seen, which models given ground-truth occupancy receive for free.

The same property of driving scenes also tells how to hold on to it: over a few seconds, the cameras view the same, largely unchanged scene from many positions. We therefore make what the model has seen its state: a 3D world state anchored in the scene, written directly from camera images and learned end to end with the forecast. The state stays in place as the vehicle moves, so the evidence that every frame provides about a place accumulates at one position. To forecast, an evolver predicts the features of the state at the queried time along the ego trajectory.

Holding what has been seen in a state also makes forecasting cheap. Since consecutive frames show nearly the same scene, the state is updated frame by frame as the images stream in: each new frame only adds its own evidence, as in streaming models that estimate the present scene [49, 32, 5] or keep a memory for forecasting [29]. Each image is thus processed once, and no separate perception network is needed, whereas sparse end-to-end models re-derive the scene from the image history for every forecast [7, 9] and two-stage methods first run a perception network [11, 35, 26, 6]. Since a forecast needs only a recent view of the surroundings, the state is reset periodically and keeps only the last few seconds of observation.

On Occ3D-nuScenes, our model raises the IoU and mIoU of the best camera-based world model by 19.13 and 3.32 at 1–3 s and runs more than twice as fast. Its IoU rises from 51.07 to 70.86 on unchanged space and from 40.92 to 62.71 on unseen space, and the same model leads by 18.19 to 24.41 IoU at every horizon up to 8 s. Our contributions are:

  • •

    An analysis that sorts the future scene into unchanged, changed, and unseen space, and shows that camera-based world models fall short in holding on to what they have already seen rather than in forecasting what will change.

  • •

    A camera-based occupancy world model that holds what it has seen in a 3D world state anchored in the scene, written from images, learned end to end with the forecast, updated as a stream, and reset periodically.

  • •

    State-of-the-art camera-based forecasting on Occ3D-nuScenes at 1–3 s and 1–8 s with a single model, which is also the fastest of the compared methods.

    • 2 Related Work

    Occupancy from cameras.

    Camera-based occupancy perception lifts image features into a 3D grid of semantic voxels, through view transformation into bird’s-eye-view or voxel features [21, 22], sparse queries [27, 38], or 3D Gaussians [14], and is evaluated on benchmarks such as Occ3D [37] and PanoBench [10]. Rendering-based methods add supervision along camera rays, rendering depth and semantics from the predicted volume [33, 13] or rendering both the prediction and the voxel labels and comparing them in the views or along the rays [3, 18]. We use the same kind of signal, predicting occupancy along each camera ray and supervising it with labels rendered from the ground-truth grid, so that the evidence of each image is written at the right depth along its rays. Temporal methods carry information across frames by propagating object queries [39] or fusing a long history through temporal stereo [34]; for occupancy, they evolve 3D Gaussians with ego and object motion [49], stream voxel features [32], or unify several temporal cues [5], and such a memory state can also be learned from multi-camera video as pre-training for perception and planning [30]. All these methods estimate the present scene, and every new frame corrects their state. Our state is also updated as a stream, but it is learned with the forecast and advanced to future times, where no new frame corrects it.

    Forecasting the future scene.

    Occupancy world models tokenize the scene and generate its future autoregressively or by diffusion [47, 40, 42, 43, 46, 11, 16, 41, 15, 26], warp the current scene to the future ego poses [6], add conditions [19, 12, 45], or separate ego motion from scene change [35]. They are commonly evaluated on Occ3D-nuScenes at 1, 2, and 3 s [47], and up to 8 s in later work [35, 9]. These models take occupancy as input; with cameras, they forecast from a separately trained perception network [22, 25], so what they forecast from is fixed before forecasting, and such chains degrade when errors enter upstream [48]. Camera-based end-to-end models learn the forecast from images [28, 44, 20, 31, 24]; some re-read the image history with sparse queries for every forecast [7, 9, 8], and some can be queried at any time [4, 1]. A persistent scene state has also been kept, but from bird’s-eye-view features [29]. PersistWorld holds what it has seen in a 3D world state written directly from images and updated as a stream, instead of re-deriving the scene for each forecast. Which parts of the future must be forecast has also been studied: aggregating past observations is a strong baseline [17], most occupied future voxels are static [35], and scene evolution has been split into static, moving, and newly observed parts [49, 2, 28]. We split the future by what the input frames have seen into unchanged, changed, and unseen space, and use the split to measure how each kind changes with the horizon and show that camera-based world models fall short on space they have already seen.

    3 Method

    Overview. PersistWorld holds what its cameras have seen in a world state S on a fixed 3D lattice and updates it as a stream, once per capture group. A capture group, which we also call a frame, is the surround-view images taken at one time, together with their camera parameters and the ego pose (Fig. 3). When a group arrives, the State Evolver carries S to its capture time (Sec. 3.3), the Visibility-aware State Writer writes the evidence of the new images into it (Sec. 3.2), and the Pose-queried Occupancy Reader decodes the current occupancy (Sec. 3.4). To forecast, the Evolver predicts the state at each queried time from S and the ego trajectory, and the Reader decodes occupancy in the queried ego frame. All components are trained end to end together with the image backbone (Secs. 3.5 and 3.6).

    3.1 World State

    The state lives on a lattice of 1.6 m cells anchored in the scene, so a cell keeps its address while the vehicle moves. The region queried at any time is the occupancy volume around the ego, 80×80×6.4 m on Occ3D, and spans 50×50×4 cells. Each cell stores a feature that packs the features of its 2×2×2 sub-cells of 0.8 m, together with the time of its estimate and the time of its last observation, which condition the Evolver (Sec. 3.3). Packing keeps attention in the Evolver over a compact lattice, while the Writer and Reader operate on the finer sub-cells; the Reader decodes each sub-cell into 2×2×2 voxels of 0.4 m (Sec. 3.4). The state is stored only where it has been written; an unwritten cell takes a learned initial feature of its ego-relative position.

    3.2 Visibility-aware State Writer

    Images are encoded by a DINOv3 ViT-B/16 [36] whose last blocks are fine-tuned, and key and value maps are projected from its feature map. Each capture group is encoded and written once, into the state that the Evolver has just carried to its capture time. For a sub-cell with center x, the Writer samples keys and values bilinearly at the projection of x into each camera, shifted by a small image-plane offset predicted from the sub-cell’s feature, and adds a learned camera embedding. Because the state is already at the capture time, the Writer only places what the new images show and needs no motion model; all motion is left to the Evolver.

    Ray-depth sections.

    All sub-cells along a pixel ray project to the same image location and sample the same feature, so projection alone cannot tell them apart. We split each patch ray into depth sections of 0.8 m and let a light head predict, for every patch, a distribution over the section that holds the first occupied surface, with one more bin for rays that hit no surface. For each sample, the section containing the sub-cell provides a geometry embedding that is added to the key and value, and the log-probability of that section is added as an attention bias, so evidence is weighted by how plausible it is that the sub-cell is the visible surface.

    Update.

    The sub-cell feature attends, with a single query, to its samples from all cameras and to a null token with zero key and value, which lets it take no evidence when no camera shows it. A gate from the prior and the candidate feature controls the residual update and is zero where no camera sees, so those keep the state carried by the Evolver.

    3.3 State Evolver

    The Evolver advances the state from the time of its estimate to a target time under the ego trajectory. It carries the state to the capture time before writing and predicts the state at each queried future time. Its inputs are the state in a window around the ego at the target time and the sequence of ego poses since the last reset (Sec. 3.6) up to the target pose. Motion tokens are formed from the relative SE(3) transforms between consecutive poses and the time steps; each cell attends only to the motion that follows its own estimate, and is conditioned on the age of its estimate and of its last observation. A context of the observed state, encoded by further axial blocks over all stored cells, is computed once per update of the state, shared by every advance from it, and added to the cell features before the residual blocks. Residual blocks, with adaptive layer normalization conditioned on these ages, each apply cross-attention to the motion tokens and self-attention along one lattice axis. The output is a change added to the state, scaled by the elapsed time, so that the Evolver is the identity when no time passes. Since the ego trajectory up to the target is an input, the same Evolver serves every horizon.

    3.4 Pose-queried Occupancy Reader

    The Reader unpacks the sub-cells and applies a local residual block of a depth-wise 3³ convolution and point-wise mixing, followed by a linear layer that predicts class logits for the 2×2×2 voxels of 0.4 m inside each sub-cell; the logits are resampled into the queried ego frame. The same Reader decodes the current occupancy right after writing and the future occupancy from the predicted states.

    3.5 Unified Occupancy Objective

    Each voxel is supervised with a focal score on the softmax probabilities p_c of its class distribution, applied to every class as a binary event. With the focal term f(q)=-(1-q)²\logq, a voxel with label y receives

    ℓ(p,y)=ω_y[a⁺_y f(p_y)+∑_c≠ya⁻_c f(1-p_c)],

    		(1)

    where the class weights follow the class priors π_c measured on the training set, a⁺_c∝π_c^-1/2 and a⁻_c∝(1-π_c)^-1/2 with a shared normalization constant, and ω_y=4 for free voxels and 1 otherwise. Classes absent from a scene still receive the negative term, so rare classes are supervised in every scene. The grid term L_grid(t) averages Eq. (1) over the voxels inside the target mask at time t.

    Grid and ray views.

    The ray-depth head of Sec. 3.2 predicts, for each patch ray, which section is occupied: it is a view of the same occupancy field along camera rays. We render the per-section occupancy of the current frame from the ground-truth grid and supervise the ray view with the same focal objective. The ray term L_ray averages Eq. (1) over the valid sections, separately from the grid term, so the two views have equal weight. The loss at a frame t₀ is

    L=(1)/(|K|)∑_k∈KL_grid(tₖ)+0.25(L_grid(t₀)+L_ray),

    		(2)

    where K is the set of supervised future horizons at that frame.

    Horizons.

    Each loss supervises 1, 2, and 3 s, plus one horizon drawn uniformly from the available ones in 4–8 s. A single model therefore serves all horizons from 1 to 8 s.

    3.6 Memory Span and Training

    Memory span.

    What a forecast needs from the past is a recent view of the surroundings, so the state holds only recent observations. We reset it to the initial state at the start of each scene and after every eight capture groups, the history length used by SparseWorld-TC, so it holds between one and eight capture groups. Each keyframe is answered with the state it holds at that moment.

    Training on streams.

    Training runs the model as at inference. A training segment is a run of up to eight consecutive capture groups of one scene, starting from the initial state; losses are placed at keyframes whose state depths, the number of capture groups written since the reset, are drawn uniformly from one to eight, so the model is trained at every depth it meets at inference. Gradients are truncated to the last two writes before each loss: the earlier writes run without gradient, so memory does not grow with the segment length. Each image is encoded once per segment.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Setup

    Dataset and metrics.

    Occ3D-nuScenes [37] provides 700 training and 150 validation scenes with 18-class labels at 0.4 m. Following SparseWorld-TC [9], a forecast uses at most the last eight capture groups and the ground-truth future ego poses. We forecast 1, 2, and 3 s ahead from every validation keyframe, which gives 6019 anchor keyframes with 5719, 5419, and 5119 targets at 1, 2, and 3 s. We report the intersection over union of occupied voxels, IoU, and its mean over the semantic classes, mIoU, inside the camera mask of the target frame. For long-horizon forecasting, we query the same model at every horizon from 1 to 8 s.

    Streaming evaluation.

    Our model processes each validation scene as a stream of keyframes, as it would run on a vehicle. Each capture group is written into the state once, and each keyframe is answered with the state at that moment, which holds one to eight capture groups (Sec.3.6). As in training, the state is reset at the start of each scene and after every eight capture groups.

    Implementation details.

    The state is written at every keyframe, 0.5 s apart. We train for 20 epochs with AdamW at a learning rate of 3×10⁻⁴; AppendixA gives the remaining settings.

    Baselines.

    Methods marked Occ GT forecast from the ground-truth occupancy, and camera-based methods forecast from images. Two-stage methods marked -STC forecast from the occupancy that STCOcc [25] predicts from the images. We measure the speed in frames per second, FPS, for every method with released code and weights on one A800 with batch size one, from the inputs on the GPU to the occupancy of the current frame and of 1, 2, and 3 s on the CPU. For two-stage methods, the time includes their perception network.

    4.2 Main Results

    Short-horizon forecasting.

    Tab.1 compares forecasts at 1, 2, and 3 s. Our model leads SparseWorld-TC, the strongest prior camera-based world model, at every horizon, and the lead grows with the horizon, from 18.19 to 20.14 IoU and from 3.04 to 3.63 mIoU. With future ego poses planned by BEV-Planner [23] instead of the ground truth, the lead widens to 22.63 IoU and 4.00 mIoU, so it does not rest on the ground-truth future poses; AppendixE gives the details. Two-stage methods are limited by their input: with ground-truth occupancy, GAST leads I2-World by 5.60 mIoU, but from the occupancy that STCOcc predicts, the two are within 0.75 mIoU and both fall below SparseWorld-TC (Sec.4.3). Our model is also the fastest of all methods with a measured speed, at 23.15 FPS (Fig.4), since it processes each image once and runs no separate perception network.

    Long-horizon forecasting.

    Tab.2 queries the model of Tab.1 at every horizon from 1 to 8 s. It leads SparseWorld-TC by 18.19 to 24.41 IoU at every horizon, and by 21.58 IoU and 4.21 mIoU on average over 1–8 s. The lead holds at 8 s, where most of the occupied future lies in space that no input frame saw (Fig.2), so the forecast does more than carry the seen scene forward: it also fills in unseen space.

    4.3 Three Kinds of Space

    Where forecasts fall short.

    We split the occupied future by the two questions of Sec.1, using the ground truth of the input frames. Unchanged space makes up 80.85% of it at 1 s and 34.87% at 8 s, unseen space grows from 14.39% to 62.06%, and changed space stays below 5% (Fig.2). Fig.5a scores the forecasts at 1–3 s on each kind. As a reference, copying the ground truth of the input frames forward with the ego poses scores 100 IoU on unchanged space, 26.33 on changed space, and 0 on unseen space. SparseWorld-TC does far better than this copy on changed and unseen space but reaches only 51.07 IoU on unchanged space, where the seen scene is already the answer. Our model reaches 70.86 there and 62.71 on unseen space, 19.79 and 21.79 above it.

    What is seen and what is forecast.

    To see what forecasting adds, we copy each model’s estimate of the current frame forward in the same way; for our model, this is Perception + warp in Fig.5a. On unchanged space, the copy already reaches 68.60 IoU for our model and 48.68 for SparseWorld-TC, close to their forecasts of 70.86 and 51.07, and the occupancy that STCOcc [25] predicts for two-stage methods reaches 46.31. Forecasting adds about as much there to both models, 2.26 and 2.39 IoU. Accuracy on unchanged space is thus decided before forecasting, and our lead there comes from how well the model holds on to what it has seen. On changed and unseen space, our forecast exceeds the copy by 4.46 and 37.48 IoU; this is what forecasting adds.

    Visibility.

    The state also keeps what has left the view of the cameras. Fig.5b splits the future by visibility at the last input frame. On space seen only in earlier frames, our model reaches 70.41 IoU, slightly above the 68.99 on space still in view, so what has left the view is not lost.

    4.4 Ablation Study

    Properties of the state.

    Tab.3 changes one property of the state at a time and scores each variant on the three kinds of space. The state must be anchored in the scene: with an ego-centric state, whose lattice moves with the vehicle and is resampled into the ego frame of every new capture group, as in temporal fusion of bird’s-eye-view features [21], the IoU falls by 3.86, most on unchanged space, by 4.38, and by 3.02 on unseen space, against 0.42 on changed space. Resampling the state at every capture group blurs what it has seen, and the extra resampling lowers the speed to 21.29 FPS. The image features must be learned: with the image encoder frozen, the mIoU falls by 4.07 and the IoU on unchanged space by 2.78. The Evolver is what completes unseen space: without it, the state is read unchanged at each target pose, and the IoU on unseen space falls by 12.22, against 3.66 and 2.43 on unchanged and changed space. Removing the depth conditioning or attention of the Writer, or the shared context of the Evolver, also lowers the accuracy of both the current frame and the forecasts, as the component ablations in AppendixC show.

    Streaming.

    Updating the state as a stream doubles the speed at nearly the same accuracy. Rebuilding the state for every query from the last eight capture groups reaches 29.26 mIoU and 67.97 IoU, against 28.72 and 67.82, but even with image features cached, every query then writes eight capture groups, and the speed nearly halves to 12.02 FPS.

    Input.

    The lead does not come from our image encoder. Writing the state from the occupancy that STCOcc [25] predicts, instead of from images, reaches 28.39 mIoU and 67.73 IoU, while GAST-STC reaches 24.70 and 42.47 from the same input. Copied forward, this input reaches only 46.31 IoU on unchanged space, and our state written from it reaches 72.06 there. The state combines the predictions of successive frames at fixed places in the scene, so it holds more of the seen scene than any single prediction. Running the perception network first, however, slows the model to 3.61 FPS, while a state learned end to end from images needs no separate perception network.

    Memory span.

    A forecast needs only the last few seconds of observation. We vary the reset period N of the state at evaluation, for the model trained with N=8 (Fig.6). The estimate of the current frame improves with every added capture group, from 61.14 IoU at N=1 to 68.99 at N=16, as the evidence of successive frames accumulates in the state. Forecasts at 1–3 s level off at N=8 and change by at most 0.15 IoU beyond it, and the 1–8 s average varies by at most 0.49. Resetting the state every eight capture groups thus costs no forecasting accuracy.

    4.5 Qualitative Results

    Fig.7 shows forecasts of our model and the ground truth in two scenes, at the current frame and 1, 2, and 3 s ahead. In scene (a), the vehicle drives along a construction zone with moving traffic and pedestrians; the buildings, vegetation, and sidewalks along the road stay in place in our forecasts up to 3 s, as in the ground truth, and the pedestrians on the right of the road remain in them. In scene (b), the vehicle crosses an intersection, and our forecast continues the road into space that no input frame observed. Comparisons with SparseWorld-TC on these and more scenes, forecasts from one state along two trajectories, and errors by distance and by dynamic and static classes are in AppendicesD, E and F.

    5 Conclusion

    Sorting the future scene into unchanged, changed, and unseen space shows that camera-based occupancy forecasting is limited first by how well models hold on to what they have already seen. PersistWorld holds it in a 3D world state anchored in the scene and updated as a stream, and an evolver predicts the state at any queried time along the ego trajectory. On Occ3D-nuScenes, this raises the IoU of the best camera-based world model by 19 points at 1–3 s and keeps the lead up to 8 s, at more than twice its speed.

    （参考文献见原文。）

    Appendix

    This appendix extends the experiments of Sec.4. AppendixA gives implementation details, AppendixB writes the state from occupancy instead of images, AppendixC removes components of the model one at a time, AppendixD breaks the forecasts down by class, distance, horizon, state depth, and ego motion, AppendixE forecasts along trajectories other than the ground truth, and AppendixF discusses more qualitative results. All results use the protocol of Sec.4.1 unless stated otherwise.

    Appendix A Implementation details

    Images are resized to 256×704 and, during training, augmented as in SparseWorld-TC [9] by random scaling, cropping, flipping, and photometric distortion. The last four blocks of DINOv3 are fine-tuned at one third of the base learning rate. The state has 384 channels; the Evolver has three residual blocks and three context blocks, and the Writer two attention layers. We train for 20 epochs with AdamW at a learning rate of 3×10⁻⁴, decayed to one third over the last four epochs, with gradients clipped at a norm of 5, on six A800 GPUs in about 15 hours.

    Appendix B Forecasting from occupancy

    Our model can be written from occupancy instead of images. For each new occupancy grid, the Writer reads the labels of the eight voxels covered by each sub-cell, embeds their class histogram, and applies a gated update to the state; the Evolver and Reader are unchanged. We train two such variants with the schedule of the main model. Both use the same streaming protocol as the camera model: each new grid is written once into the state, which is reset every eight keyframes and at scene changes, so a forecast uses one to eight keyframes since the last reset. PersistWorld-STC is written from the occupancy predicted by STCOcc [25], the perception network of the two-stage methods, and is scored inside the camera mask. PersistWorld-GT is written from the ground-truth occupancy and is scored on the full volume, as the Occ GT methods in Tab.1. Its 1–3 s evaluation uses 4519 anchors with at least 2 s of history and 3 s of future available in the scene; this selects the scored anchors and does not change the state reset schedule. Each block of Tab.4 also moves the input of the current frame to the target frame with the ego poses, which forecasts as if nothing changed.

    Occupancy-input forecasting.

    Using STCOcc predictions as the input source, PersistWorld-STC reaches 28.39 mIoU and 67.73 IoU on average, against 24.70 and 42.47 for GAST-STC, the strongest two-stage method. From the ground truth, PersistWorld-GT reaches 42.42 mIoU and 60.77 IoU, against 45.33 and 55.09 for GAST: it is the most accurate in geometry and third in semantics. PersistWorld-STC also exceeds the camera end-to-end baselines in Tab.1, while reaching similar accuracy to our camera model. Compared with copying only the current occupancy forward, the full model gains 30.11 IoU with STCOcc input and 7.93 with ground-truth input.

item.title: NVIDIA 这月的游戏开发更新：Kimodo 进 UE 5.9 生成动作，DLSS 5 进 Dagor 引擎，还有 BVH 实时可视化 ｜ What’s New for Game Developers: AI Animation and RTX Tools
item.description:
一句话：一条新闻里塞了六个能直接改集成代码的东西。

要点：

  • **AI 动作生成进引擎**：NVIDIA **Kimodo** 成为第一个接入 **Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview「引导式动画框架」**的 AI 动作生成模型，动画师可以在 **Sequencer** 里用文字提示、样条路径与目标姿势直接生成角色动作
  • **DLSS 5 上真实游戏引擎**：Gaijin 把带 3D 引导神经渲染的 DLSS 5 接进 **Dagor Engine**（《战争雷霆》），并为此**调整色彩管理管线**——在 sRGB 空间评估该技术再映射回线性 HDR
  • 其余四项：In-Game Inferencing SDK 1.8（RTX Spark、llama.cpp/whisper.cpp、Parakeet ASR、Vulkan API）；RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2（ReSTIR DI 空间重采样的分层低差异采样）；**Real-Time BVH Viewer 1.0**（D3D12/Vulkan 实时光追加速结构可视化，可看 primitive ID 与追踪耗时热力图）；RTX Path Tracing 1.9（把 ReSTIR DI、SHaRC 辐射缓存与 DLSS Ray Reconstruction 串成九步示例，并加实时子采样与 GPU 侧加速结构实例生成）

为什么值得看：产品条目的价值在「能照抄的集成口径」：Sequencer 里生成动作、sRGB 评估再映回线性 HDR、BVH 可视化这三点都是工程团队明天就能试的；而 In-Game Inferencing SDK 的 Vulkan 支持意味着非 D3D 项目也能接本地 AI。

中文摘要：NVIDIA 这月的游戏开发更新里，有几项可以直接落进引擎。其一是 AI 动作生成：NVIDIA Kimodo 成为第一个接入 Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview「引导式动画框架」的 AI 动作生成模型，动画师可以在 Sequencer 中用文字提示、样条路径与目标姿势生成角色动作。其二是真实游戏对 DLSS 5 的接入：Gaijin 把带 3D 引导神经渲染的 DLSS 5 集成进《战争雷霆》的 Dagor Engine，并为此调整色彩管理管线——在 sRGB 空间评估该技术、再映射回线性 HDR。其余更新包括 In-Game Inferencing SDK 1.8（新增 RTX Spark 支持、llama.cpp 与 whisper.cpp 后端、Parakeet 语音识别与 Vulkan 优先级 API）、RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2（为 ReSTIR DI 空间重采样引入分层低差异采样）、Real-Time BVH Viewer 1.0（在独立窗口中实时可视化 D3D12/Vulkan 的加速结构，支持 primitive ID 与追踪耗时热力图），以及 RTX Path Tracing 1.9（把 ReSTIR DI、SHaRC 辐射缓存与 DLSS Ray Reconstruction 串成九步示例，并加入实时子采样与 GPU 侧加速结构实例生成）。

主题：AI Native Engine

  • Gaijin Entertainment integrated NVIDIA DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering into the Dagor Engine for War Thunder, adapting its color management pipeline to evaluate the technology in sRGB before post-processing and mapping results back to linear HDR.
  • NVIDIA Kimodo becomes the first AI motion-generation model integrated into Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview's guided animation framework, allowing animators to generate character motion inside Sequencer using text prompts, spline paths, and target poses.
  • The NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK 1.8 adds hardened RTX Spark platform support, updated llama.cpp and whisper.cpp backends, Parakeet automatic speech recognition through whisper.cpp, and Vulkan priority API integration.
  • NVIDIA RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2 introduces stratified low-discrepancy sampling for ReSTIR DI spatial resampling, a fallback sample feature, enhanced reservoir visualization, and RTX Spark support.
  • The new NVIDIA Real-Time BVH Viewer 1.0 displays live ray-tracing acceleration structures for D3D12 and Vulkan applications in a separate window with visualization modes for primitive IDs, trace time heatmaps, and geometry filters.
  • RTX Path Tracing 1.9 adds a nine-step introductory sample that progressively combines ReSTIR DI, SHaRC radiance caching, and DLSS Ray Reconstruction, plus performance optimizations including real-time subsampling and GPU-side acceleration-structure instance generation.

    • Next Steps

  • Read the War Thunder DLSS 5 developer interview for practical lessons on balancing lighting enhancements with art direction.
  • Explore the Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview release notes and Kimodo research project to understand the guided animation framework.
  • Download Nsight Graphics and Nsight Systems to analyze DLSS Frame Generation workloads and use agentic AI tooling for graphics development.

    This month’s NVIDIA game development updates help teams bring new graphics, animation, and local AI capabilities into their engines while balancing image quality, performance, and creative intent.

    This post covers:

  • Developer lessons from the War Thunder NVIDIA DLSS 5 integration
  • NVIDIA Kimodo animation generation in Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview
  • NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK 1.8 updates for RTX Spark, speech recognition, and Vulkan
  • NVIDIA RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2 and RTX Path Tracing 1.9 improvements for lighting, integration, and debugging
  • Nsight developer tools updates for Fall of 2026

    • How Gaijin raised War Thunder’s realism using NVIDIA DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering

    In an interview, Gaijin Entertainment shares how it integrated DLSS 5 with 3D-Guided Neural Rendering into War Thunder’s Dagor Engine while preserving the game’s established visual identity. The team explains how it adapted its color management pipeline to evaluate DLSS 5 in sRGB before post-processing and UI, then map the results back to linear HDR, saying “DLSS 5 delivers improved highlights and shadows while introducing a new level of microcontrast that we simply haven’t been able to achieve before. The result is a more natural, lifelike image, with finer detail and a stronger sense of realism.”

    The team also discusses tuning DLSS 5 against its reference look to preserve vehicle markings, surface wear, and material properties, as well as evaluating image quality and performance separately across air, ground, and naval combat. The interview offers developers practical lessons on balancing lighting and material enhancements with their game’s art direction, with ON/OFF comparisons highlighting rainy, overcast scenes.

    Read the full War Thunder interview.

    NVIDIA Kimodo is the first model in Unreal Engine 5.9’s guided animation framework

    Kimodo brings its animation research into Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview, which introduces a guided animation framework and a set of Sequencer tools that help animators work directly with AI motion-generation models. Kimodo is the first model integrated with it, enabling animators to generate character motion right inside Sequencer. The integration pairs GPU-accelerated motion generation with the familiar timeline editor workflow.

    Animators can describe a motion with a text prompt, draw a spline path for the character to follow, and set target poses at specific frames. The model generates motion that follows these constraints, so teams decide where characters move and how they pose at key moments, bringing creative control into the animation.

    Explore the Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview release notes and the Kimodo research project.

    NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK 1.8 expands platform and model support

    The NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK helps developers integrate NVIDIA ACE on-device. ACE is a suite of AI technologies designed to help middleware and game developers build knowledgeable, actionable, and conversational in-game characters. The SDK supports multiple inference backends across GPU and CPU hardware, giving teams a common interface for running AI alongside game graphics.

    Version 1.8 focuses on platform support and the inference components used in language and speech workflows. Key updates include:

  • RTX Spark: Hardened platform support for developers building applications
  • Updated inference backends: Newer llama.cpp and whisper.cpp versions
  • Expanded speech recognition: Support for the Parakeet automatic speech recognition (ASR) model through whisper.cpp
  • Vulkan integration: Added support for the Vulkan priority API
  • Additional bug fixes across the SDK.

    • Explore the NVIDIA In-Game Inferencing SDK.

    NVIDIA RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2 adds sampling improvements and reservoir debugging tools

    RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2 is available on GitHub with updates for developers integrating ReSTIR lighting into their renderers. The release adds new sampling options for ReSTIR DI, adds RTX Spark support, and expands the tools used to inspect lighting reservoirs.

    Release highlights include:

  • Stratified low-discrepancy sampling for ReSTIR DI spatial resampling
  • A fallback sample feature for ReSTIR DI
  • Enhanced reservoir visualization for direct illumination, global illumination, and path tracing, giving developers more ways to inspect the samples used by each technique
  • RTX Spark support
  • Updated Donut and NVRHI components, along with bug fixes

    • Explore the RTXDI SDK and samples on GitHub.

    NVIDIA Real-Time BVH Viewer 1.0 brings live acceleration structure inspection to D3D12 and Vulkan

    NVIDIA Real-Time BVH Viewer 1.0 is now available on GitHub. The utility shows ray tracing acceleration structures while a game or renderer is running. It helps developers understand TLAS and BLAS contents, validate acceleration structure updates, and debug geometry-related ray tracing issues.

    The viewer integrates at the graphics API level through Direct3D 12 and Vulkan libraries. Developers send acceleration structure builds, copies, queue submissions, and frame boundaries to the viewer, which displays the results in a separate window. Separate windows with its own camera allows it to inspect TLAS independently from the in-game camera.

    To inspect an existing title without changing its code, developers can use the included sampler. It attaches the viewer to a running D3D12 or Vulkan process and serves as an integration sample.

    Release highlights include:

  • Visualization modes for primitive, geometry, instance, and cluster IDs, BLAS addresses, instance masks and flags, and acceleration structure update state
  • Per-pixel trace time heatmaps that show which parts of a scene cost the most to trace
  • Support for various geometry filters: flags, types and ray culling
  • Support for Clustered geometry in D3D12
  • Vendor-agnostic integration with optional vendor-specific paths, plus builds for Windows x64 and RTX Spark

    • Access the BVH Viewer on github and download the v1.0.0 release.

    RTX Path Tracing 1.9 adds an introductory sample and SHaRC integration

    NVIDIA RTX Path Tracing 1.9 gives developers a more accessible starting point for adding ray-traced lighting and studying a real-time path tracing pipeline.

    The intro sample uses a hybrid deferred renderer to introduce lighting features one at a time across nine selectable steps. Developers can progress from image-based lighting and screen-space effects to ReSTIR DI, path-traced indirect lighting, and SHaRC radiance caching.

    SHaRC is also integrated into the main real-time path tracer and enabled by default, providing additional indirect-lighting information to DLSS Ray Reconstruction. Other updates include:

  • RTX Spark support
  • Performance optimizations including real-time subsampling, overlapping DLSS Ray Reconstruction with the next frame’s path tracing, and GPU-side acceleration-structure instance generation
  • Expanded NEE-AT light sampling support for up to two million lights and clustering of emissive triangles into light levels of detail
  • A new design document describing the real-time path tracing pipeline, plus updated dependencies, fixes, and rendering improvements

    • Read the RTX Path Tracing 1.9 release notes and explore the Intro Sample.

    RTX Global Illumination 2.9 adds improved diffuse GI sample and SER support

    Release highlights for NVIDIA RTX Global Illumination 2.9 include:

  • A new IndirectDiffuse sample introducing a deferred renderer that uses NRC or SHaRC for indirect diffuse illumination, complete with shadow mapping, sky lighting, and visualization modes
  • Shader Execution Reordering (SER) support for Direct3D 12 (Shader Model 6.9) and Vulkan, toggleable directly from the UI
  • Additional bug fixes and performance enhancements

    • NVIDIA Nsight Graphics and Nsight Systems Introduce DLSS-FG Support, Agentic AI Tooling

    Video 1. NVIDIA Nsight Graphics 2026.4 release spotlight, highlighting DLSS Frame Generation analysis and agentic AI tooling

    NVIDIA Nsight Graphics 2026.4 and Nsight Systems 2026.6 introduce support for analyzing applications using DLSS Frame Generation (DLSS-FG). When integrating DLSS Frame Generation and Multi-Frame Generation into a title, it is important to understand both the work submitted by the application and the pacing of the frames presented to players.

    In Nsight Graphics, GPU Trace now displays application and presented frames on separate timeline rows, while Graphics Capture preserves the DLSS-FG workload for inspection during capture and replay. Nsight Systems distinguishes generated frames from application frames and correlates them with CPU frame ranges. DLSS-FG support in both tools requires Streamline SDK 2.12 or newer.

    The new releases also introduce agentic AI tooling for graphics development. A new Nsight Graphics MCP server enables compatible AI agents to capture applications, inspect and debug captures, and analyze GPU traces. Nsight Systems includes skill files that guide AI agents in diagnosing CPU bottlenecks, frame stutter, and CPU-GPU synchronization overhead.

    Download Nsight Graphics and Nsight Systems.

要点：

  • **AI 动作生成进引擎**：NVIDIA **Kimodo** 成为第一个接入 **Unreal Engine 5.9 Preview「引导式动画框架」**的 AI 动作生成模型，动画师可以在 **Sequencer** 里用文字提示、样条路径与目标姿势直接生成角色动作
  • **DLSS 5 上真实游戏引擎**：Gaijin 把带 3D 引导神经渲染的 DLSS 5 接进 **Dagor Engine**（《战争雷霆》），并为此**调整色彩管理管线**——在 sRGB 空间评估该技术再映射回线性 HDR
  • 其余四项：In-Game Inferencing SDK 1.8（RTX Spark、llama.cpp/whisper.cpp、Parakeet ASR、Vulkan API）；RTX Dynamic Illumination 3.2（ReSTIR DI 空间重采样的分层低差异采样）；**Real-Time BVH Viewer 1.0**（D3D12/Vulkan 实时光追加速结构可视化，可看 primitive ID 与追踪耗时热力图）；RTX Path Tracing 1.9（把 ReSTIR DI、SHaRC 辐射缓存与 DLSS Ray Reconstruction 串成九步示例，并加实时子采样与 GPU 侧加速结构实例生成）

为什么值得看：产品条目的价值在「能照抄的集成口径」：Sequencer 里生成动作、sRGB 评估再映回线性 HDR、BVH 可视化这三点都是工程团队明天就能试的；而 In-Game Inferencing SDK 的 Vulkan 支持意味着非 D3D 项目也能接本地 AI。
