Appendix B Implementation Details

We provide additional implementation details of the forward simplification in Sec. 4.1 and the closed-form derivatives underlying the backward formulation in Sec. 4.3.

B.1 Cost Threshold and Budget Control

We initialize the pass-wise cost threshold τₚ (Sec. 4.1) at τ₁=10⁻⁴ and set τₚ₊₁=√10 τₚ. Within each pass, parallel collapse rounds continue until no edge chosen by independent-region selection (Sec. 3.2) satisfies Cₑ≤τₚ. Let |V| be the current vertex count. If a round selects more than |V|-K edges, we collapse only the |V|-K lowest-cost candidates so that the target budget K is not overshot.

B.2 Placement Branches and Fallbacks

Consider a collapse e=(i,j)∈𝔼ᵣ within a pass. We omit round superscripts when unambiguous: vᵢ,vⱼ denote the positions vᵢ⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾,vⱼ⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾ before the collapse, and Qₑ,vₑ denote Qₑ⁽ʳ⁾,vₑ⁽ʳ⁾. As in Eq. (1), Qₑ=Qᵢ⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾+Qⱼ⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾ has blocks Aₑ,bₑ,cₑ.

Regularized QEM placement.

We select the regularized QEM branch when

(μ_\min(Aₑ))/(μ_\max(Aₑ))>κ, κ=10⁻³,

(S3)

where μ_\min and μ_\max are the extremal eigenvalues of Aₑ; we additionally require μ_\max(Aₑ)>0. The merged vertex is then placed at

vₑ=-(Aₑ+λₑI)⁻¹bₑ, λₑ=η\maxₖ|(Aₑ)ₖₖ|, η=10⁻⁶.

(S4)

Edge-segment fallback.

When the regularized QEM branch is not selected, we instead minimize the collapse error Eₑ (Sec. 3.1) along the edge. With δ=vⱼ-vᵢ, segment placement is used when

δ^⊤Aₑδ>εₛ, εₛ=10⁻⁷,

(S5)

and is given by

α^⋆=-(δ^⊤(Aₑvᵢ+bₑ))/(δ^⊤Aₑδ),(S6)
γₑ=clamp(α^⋆,0,1),
vₑ=vᵢ+γₑδ.

Clamping keeps vₑ on the edge, at an endpoint when α^⋆∉[0,1].

Midpoint fallback.

If Eq. (S5) is also not satisfied, we use vₑ=\tfrac12(vᵢ+vⱼ).

For each collapse, the forward pass also records the discrete choices required by the backward pass: the placement branch, the segment clamp state (interior or either endpoint), and the diagonal index kₑ attaining the maximum in Eq. (S4). These choices are part of the collapse history σ (Sec. 4.2) and remain fixed during differentiation. Across ten reconstruction samples, regularized QEM, edge-segment, and midpoint placements account for 63.1%, 35.6%, and 1.3% of in-loop collapses, respectively.

B.3 Gradients through Vertex Placement

We derive the collapse-local VJPs for the placement branches in Sec. B.2, writing gₓ for the gradient of the loss with respect to x. Given the incoming position gradient g_vₑ=g_vₑ⁽ʳ⁾, each branch produces direct position gradients g_vᵢ,g_vⱼ and a quadric gradient Gₑ=(∂vₑ/∂Qₑ)^⊤g_vₑ. Writing G_A and G_b for the gradients with respect to the independent blocks Aₑ and bₑ, we represent the symmetric quadric gradient as

Gₑ=\beginbmatrixG_A&\tfrac12G_b \tfrac12G_b^⊤&0\endbmatrix.

(S7)

The factors \tfrac12 account for the two symmetric occurrences of bₑ in Qₑ, and the zero block reflects that cₑ does not affect the placement. Let sym(M)=\tfrac12(M+M^⊤) denote the symmetric part of a matrix.

Regularized QEM placement.

On this branch, Eq. (S3) and μ_\max(Aₑ)>0 imply Aₑ\succ0. Its diagonal entries are therefore positive, and the absolute value in λₑ can be dropped. Differentiating (Aₑ+λₑI)vₑ+bₑ=0 with the recorded kₑ fixed gives

dvₑ=-(Aₑ+λₑI)⁻¹(dAₑ vₑ+dλₑ vₑ+dbₑ), dλₑ=η (dAₑ)_kₑkₑ.

(S8)

With u=(Aₑ+λₑI)⁻¹g_vₑ, the VJP is

G_A=-sym(uvₑ^⊤)-η (u^⊤vₑ) e_kₑe_kₑ^⊤,(S9)
G_b=-u, g_vᵢ=g_vⱼ=0,

where e_kₑ is the kₑ-th unit vector. This branch propagates the placement gradient entirely through the quadrics, including the dependence of λₑ on Aₑ.

Edge-segment placement.

For an interior solution γₑ=α^⋆∈(0,1), let ρ=δ^⊤Aₑδ, zₑ=Aₑvₑ+bₑ, and

βₑ=-(δ^⊤g_vₑ)/(ρ), hₑ=g_vₑ+βₑAₑδ.

(S10)

Differentiating Eq. (S6) gives

g_vᵢ=(1-α^⋆) hₑ-βₑzₑ,g_vⱼ=α^⋆hₑ+βₑzₑ,(S11)
G_A=βₑsym(δvₑ^⊤),G_b=βₑδ.

If the solution is clamped to an endpoint, vₑ coincides with that endpoint and does not depend on Qₑ:

(g_vᵢ,g_vⱼ)=\begincases(g_vₑ,0),&γₑ=0, (0,g_vₑ),&γₑ=1,\endcases Gₑ=0.

(S12)

Midpoint placement.

For vₑ=\tfrac12(vᵢ+vⱼ),

g_vᵢ=g_vⱼ=\tfrac12g_vₑ, Gₑ=0.

(S13)

In all branches, Gₑ is the placement term of Eq. (7) and is added to the quadric gradients of both endpoints. The direct gradients g_vᵢ and g_vⱼ form the position part of the round-wise VJP g⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾=Jᵣ^⊤g⁽ʳ⁾.

B.4 Face-Quadric Derivatives

At the beginning of a pass, let f=(i,j,k)∈Fₚ₋₁ be a nondegenerate face. We write vᵢ,vⱼ,vₖ for its pass-input positions vᵢ⁽⁰⁾,vⱼ⁽⁰⁾,vₖ⁽⁰⁾ and define

\begingathereds=(vⱼ-vᵢ)×(vₖ-vᵢ), n_f=s/∥s∥, d_f=-n_f^⊤vᵢ, p_f=\beginbmatrixn_f d_f\endbmatrix, w_f=(∥s∥)/(2ā), K_f=w_fp_fp_f^⊤,\endgathered

(S14)

so that w_f=a_f/ā as in Sec. 4.1. From Eq. (8), the incoming face-quadric gradient is g_K_f=g_Qᵢ⁽⁰⁾+g_Qⱼ⁽⁰⁾+g_Qₖ⁽⁰⁾. Differentiating K_f gives

g_p_f=2w_fsym(g_K_f)p_f, g_w_f=p_f^⊤g_K_fp_f.

(S15)

We partition g_p_f=(g_n_f^⊤,g_d_f)^⊤ into normal and offset parts. Since d_f also depends on n_f, the total gradient on n_f is g̃_n_f=g_n_f-g_d_fvᵢ, and the gradient with respect to s is

gₛ=(1)/(∥s∥)(I-n_fn_f^⊤)g̃_n_f+(g_w_f)/(2ā)n_f.

(S16)

The face contributions to the vertex-position gradients follow from the cross product:

g_vⱼ^f=(vₖ-vᵢ)×gₛ,(S17)
g_vₖ^f=gₛ×(vⱼ-vᵢ),
g_vᵢ^f=-g_d_fn_f-g_vⱼ^f-g_vₖ^f.

Summing these contributions over incident faces and adding the direct position gradients g_vᵢ⁽⁰⁾ yields the pass-input gradient in Eq. (8). As in Sec. 4.1, ā is held fixed during differentiation. Under a fixed collapse history, uniformly scaling all quadrics leaves the vertex placement unchanged in every branch.

Appendix C Additional Method Analysis

We further analyze the forward simplifier, the fixed-history backward pass, and iterative optimization. Unless stated otherwise, we follow the low-poly mesh reconstruction setup of Sec. 5.1 and use the same 79 shapes. We report squared Chamfer distance (CD) scaled by 10⁵.

C.1 Forward Simplifier

C.1.1 Component Ablation

We evaluate the contributions of area-weighted face quadrics, the cost-threshold schedule, and pass-wise quadric recomputation by removing each component from our forward simplifier. All variants simplify the original meshes of the same 79 shapes (33,228 vertices on average) to K=1000 without optimization. Base denotes our parallel QEM-based edge-collapse simplifier without these three improvements. As shown in Table S1, Base yields higher mean CD (1.879 vs. 1.774) and lower F1 (0.196 vs. 0.215) than sequential QEM, reflecting the quality–efficiency trade-off of parallel edge collapse. Our complete forward simplifier reduces mean CD to 1.250, while removing any component increases CD and decreases F1. Fig. S1 illustrates the qualitative effects of these components.

C.1.2 Comparison with Other Simplification Operators

Table S2 compares our forward simplifier with QEM, vertex clustering, and PaMO on the same 79 original meshes at K=1000 without optimization. These methods exhibit different trade-offs: vertex clustering is fast but introduces substantial geometric error due to spatial quantization, while PaMO ensures intersection-free outputs at higher computational cost. Sequential QEM achieves better geometric fidelity than both but requires considerably more time than ours. Our forward simplifier achieves the lowest CD, the highest F1 and NC, and the shortest simplification time (7.5 ms) among the evaluated methods, while maintaining SI and SR at levels comparable to QEM. This balance of approximation quality and efficiency makes it suitable for repeated application within gradient-based optimization.

C.2 Backward

C.2.1 Pass Count and Quadric Reduction-Forest Efficiency

Our factorized backward substantially reduces computation within each pass by propagating quadric gradients through the reduction forest, allowing face quadrics to be differentiated only once per pass across multiple collapse rounds. As shown in Table S3, even at K=250, simplification requires only 4.3 passes on average despite 101.3 collapse rounds. In contrast, recomputing quadrics after every round requires repeated face-quadric differentiation. Our pass-wise approach consequently achieves 5.5–8.8× faster backward execution, demonstrating the efficiency of reusing quadrics across collapse rounds. Note that the every-round variant still computes collapse-local VJPs in parallel, as described in Sec. 4.3.

C.2.2 Backward Work

The quadric reduction-forest formulation in Sec. 4.3 performs constant-size updates per collapse and differentiates each pass-input face once, yielding work proportional to W=∑ₚ(∑ᵣ₌₁^Rₚ|𝔼ᵣ|+|Fₚ₋₁|). Here, Rₚ denotes the number of collapse rounds in pass p, and the pass index of 𝔼ᵣ is omitted for brevity. As shown in Table S4, our launched GPU threads remain near 2.05–2.25 per unit of W across the tested input sizes. In contrast, an autograd replay of the same recorded history launches 501–772 threads per unit of W, while the normalized direct face-derivative count ∑ₑ|Fₑ|/W increases from 5.40 to 21.95. This increase reflects repeated differentiation of the same face-quadric contributions accumulated in vertex quadrics across successive collapses. These results support the linear-work structure of our factorized backward and demonstrate how the quadric reduction forest avoids redundant face-level differentiation across collapse rounds.

C.2.3 Gradient Correctness

We validate the factorized CUDA backward pass of DiffSimp against a PyTorch autograd replay of the same recorded collapse history. We randomly select ten of the 79 original meshes and perform a single forward and backward evaluation per mesh at K=1000, without optimization. For each mesh, we define a random linear loss on the simplified vertex positions. Let G and G_AD64 denote the input-vertex gradients computed by our double-precision CUDA backward and double-precision PyTorch autograd, respectively. We measure the relative L₂ error ∥G-G_AD64∥₂/∥G_AD64∥₂ over flattened vertex gradients. The mean and maximum relative L₂ errors are 4.7×10⁻¹² and 2.5×10⁻¹¹, respectively, demonstrating near-exact numerical agreement between our CUDA backward and the autograd reference.

C.3 Iterative Optimization

C.3.1 Training Loss Curves

Fig. S2 compares the training losses of DiffSimp and the unsimplified reference in low-poly mesh reconstruction (Sec. 5.1) and inverse rendering (Sec. 5.2). With T=5000, the warmup (t_w=0.2T) and budget-reduction (tᵣ=0.45T) schedules divide training into warmup (0–1000), ramp (1000–3250), and hold (3250–5000) phases. Both methods optimize the same dense geometry during warmup. During the ramp, our training loss increases as the vertex budget progressively decreases. Once the target budget is reached, our training loss continues to decrease throughout the hold phase, exhibiting a clear convergence trend despite repeated simplification during optimization.

C.3.2 Post-Simplification Fine-Tuning

An alternative is to simplify the dense reconstruction once and then optimize the simplified mesh with fixed connectivity. To construct this baseline, we apply our forward simplifier as post-processing and refine the resulting vertex positions for 2,000 additional iterations using Large Steps with its multi-view reconstruction objective described in Sec. A.1. Table S5 shows that, even after these additional 2,000 iterations, post-simplification fine-tuning fails to match the in-loop output of DiffSimp in both CD and F1 across all tested vertex budgets. The gaps in both metrics increase under tighter budgets, with the largest differences at K=500.

要点：

  • 现状的断层：可微网格提取让基于梯度的三维几何优化成为可能，但**紧凑网格通常靠后处理简化得到**，于是**简化引入的误差被留在了上游优化之外**
  • DiffSimp 是一个**免训练、可即插即用**的可微网格简化层，建立在基于 QEM 的**并行边折叠**之上
  • 效果是让已有几何优化管线可以在**目标就是低模**的情况下直接优化，而不是先做高模再事后压缩

为什么值得看：LOD 与低模是游戏资产的基本要求，而「先高模再简化」的流程永远学不到简化会损失什么。把简化做成可微层，等于把 LOD 纳入优化目标——这对做程序化资产或可微建模的团队是结构性的改进。

中文摘要：可微网格提取让基于梯度的三维几何优化成为可能，但紧凑网格通常是通过后处理简化得到的，于是简化引入的误差被留在了上游优化之外。DiffSimp 提出一个免训练、可直接替换的可微网格简化层，它建立在基于二次误差度量（QEM）的并行边折叠之上，使现有的几何优化管线能够在「目标本身就是低模」的前提下直接进行优化，而不必先生成高模再做压缩。对游戏资产管线而言，这意味着 LOD 的代价第一次能被优化过程感知。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.GR（English）

原文发布：2026-11-24

本期推送：2026-11-25

DiffSimp: Differentiable Mesh Simplification for
Gradient-Based Low-Poly Modeling

Abstract

Differentiable mesh extraction enables gradient-based optimization of detailed 3D geometry across diverse tasks. However, compact meshes are commonly obtained through post-processing simplification, leaving simplification-induced errors outside upstream optimization. We introduce DiffSimp, a training-free, drop-in differentiable mesh simplification layer built on QEM-based parallel edge collapse, enabling existing geometry optimization pipelines to optimize their final simplified meshes. We formulate simplification under a fixed collapse history as a locally differentiable collapse map, enabling gradient propagation without relaxing discrete collapse decisions. We combine fast, high-quality parallel simplification with a factorized backward formulation that exploits differentiable vertex quadrics and quadric reduction forests for efficient gradient propagation. Experiments on low-poly mesh reconstruction and inverse rendering demonstrate improved fidelity over post-processing simplification, with additional gains from gradient propagation that increase under tighter vertex budgets. DiffSimp supports diverse geometry optimization frontends, with 1.00–1.25× the end-to-end runtime of unsimplified baselines in evaluated pipelines.

1 Introduction

Triangle meshes remain a fundamental surface representation across computer graphics, 3D vision, and robotics. Recent advances in differentiable mesh extraction [44, 46, 47, 1, 56] have enabled gradient-based geometry optimization by propagating gradients from mesh-based objectives upstream, supporting inverse rendering [35, 24, 59], scene reconstruction [19, 10], and generative 3D modeling [13, 57, 2]. However, these pipelines often produce dense meshes to capture fine geometric structures, while downstream applications may require compact meshes.

A straightforward way to obtain compact meshes is to reduce the resolution of differentiable mesh extraction, but this limits the recovery of fine geometric details during optimization. Instead, a common strategy is to reconstruct or generate sufficiently detailed meshes, followed by post-processing simplification to meet downstream complexity requirements. Among mesh simplification methods, quadric error metric (QEM) edge collapse [17, 16] has become a practical off-the-shelf choice [27, 31]. It naturally adapts mesh complexity to local geometry, enabling aggressive simplification while limiting geometric approximation error, without requiring separate iterative fitting as in variational approaches [9, 58] or pretrained simplification models [42]. These advantages have made QEM a common post-processing step in modern 3D pipelines [52, 55, 7, 15].

However, post-processing mesh simplification decouples geometry optimization from the final simplified mesh. While differentiable mesh extraction enables gradient propagation from mesh-based objectives upstream, these objectives are typically evaluated on detailed intermediate meshes rather than the simplified meshes ultimately deployed. This mismatch becomes particularly consequential under aggressive simplification, where even QEM can introduce substantial geometric distortion as fine structures are approximated by increasingly coarse meshes. These simplification-induced errors provide no gradient signal to the upstream optimizer, preventing it from directly compensating for them to improve the final deployed mesh.

To address this optimization–deployment mismatch, we seek to integrate mesh simplification as a differentiable layer into gradient-based geometry optimization pipelines. For practical integration, we identify three design priorities. First, the layer should be training-free and mesh-native, independent of learned simplification priors and specific upstream representations, enabling its use across diverse pipelines and downstream objectives. Second, high forward simplification quality must be maintained. At less restrictive budgets, simplification typically introduces smaller geometric errors, leaving limited room for gradient-based compensation and making forward quality particularly important. Under tighter budgets, high-quality forward simplification and gradient-based compensation become complementary in preserving geometric fidelity. Third, efficient forward and backward execution is essential, as simplification must be performed at every optimization iteration.

To meet these priorities, we introduce DiffSimp, a training-free, drop-in differentiable mesh simplification layer built on QEM-based parallel edge collapse, enabling existing gradient-based geometry optimization pipelines to optimize through their simplified meshes. Although discrete edge-collapse decisions prevent global differentiability, we exploit the recorded collapse history to express simplification as a locally differentiable collapse map, enabling gradient propagation without relaxing these decisions. To achieve fast, high-quality forward simplification, we extend the parallel edge-collapse scheme of PaMO [38], improving simplification quality while retaining efficient execution. For efficient backward propagation, we propose a factorized differentiation scheme that treats vertex quadrics as differentiable intermediates, enabling parallel collapse-local vector–Jacobian products (VJPs), and exploits the quadric reduction-forest structure to avoid redundant face-level differentiation. We implement both operations in CUDA and introduce a progressive vertex-budget schedule for integration into iterative optimization.

Experiments on low-poly mesh reconstruction and inverse rendering demonstrate that optimizing through DiffSimp improves the fidelity of final simplified meshes over post-processing in both tasks. We also show that gradient propagation provides additional gains that increase under tighter vertex budgets, as upstream optimization compensates for simplification-induced errors. We further demonstrate compatibility with diverse existing gradient-based geometry optimization pipelines. These improvements are achieved with only 1.00–1.25× the end-to-end optimization time of the corresponding unsimplified pipelines.

2 Related Work

2.1 Gradient-Based Mesh Optimization

Differentiable mesh extraction [44, 21, 20, 46, 47, 56, 1] and differentiable mesh representations [43, 49, 50] enable upstream gradient propagation from mesh-based objectives, supporting diverse downstream applications [35, 59, 37, 19, 10, 13, 57]. However, extracted mesh complexity remains tied to the underlying extraction structure. Even adaptive extraction methods [47, 1] adjust spatial sampling and extraction structures rather than performing aggressive, geometry-adaptive mesh simplification. Gradient-based low-poly mesh optimization has also been explored through geometry and appearance refinement [23, 7], joint base-mesh and displacement optimization [11], and adaptive remeshing or topology updates [39, 14, 12]. However, these approaches either optimize compact meshes from given or reconstructed geometry without propagating gradients through simplification to upstream representations, or adapt mesh connectivity within dedicated optimization pipelines. In contrast, our reusable differentiable mesh simplification layer propagates gradients from objectives on aggressively simplified meshes to upstream representations without redesigning existing optimization pipelines.

2.2 Mesh Simplification

Mesh simplification has been extensively studied through vertex clustering [45], variational approximation [9, 58], remeshing [53, 54, 6], and iterative edge collapse [25, 30]. These training-free, mesh-native methods are widely used as post-processing in modern 3D pipelines. Among these, quadric error metric (QEM) edge collapse [17, 16] has become a standard approach to mesh simplification. To overcome the computational cost of sequential greedy edge collapse, parallel methods [40, 38] accelerate simplification while maintaining competitive geometric quality, albeit with some loss relative to sequential QEM. However, these methods do not propagate gradients through collapse operations, leaving simplification largely as post-processing in gradient-based pipelines. Building on PaMO [38], we combine the geometric adaptivity of QEM and the efficiency of parallel execution with fixed-history differentiation, enabling their use in gradient-based optimization. We further improve parallel simplification quality to better preserve geometric fidelity under aggressive simplification while retaining efficient execution.

2.3 Learning-Based Low-Poly Modeling

Learning-based approaches to mesh reduction and low-poly modeling include task-driven mesh pooling [22], learned simplification operators [42], learned geometric representations [33], progressive mesh representations [3, 5, 28], and generative mesh priors [29, 48, 4, 32, 51]. While these approaches support mesh reduction and low-poly modeling, they also depend on learned parameters and training distributions. Notably, Neural Mesh Simplification [42] enables differentiable simplification through learned vertex sampling and connectivity prediction, but remains dependent on a pretrained network. In contrast, our training-free differentiable layer retains the geometric adaptivity of QEM without relying on learned simplification priors.

3 Preliminaries

3.1 Quadric Error Metrics for Edge Collapse

Quadric error metric (QEM) simplification [17, 16] iteratively simplifies a triangle mesh through successive edge collapses. Let M⁽⁰⁾=(V⁽⁰⁾,F⁽⁰⁾) denote an input triangle mesh with vertices V⁽⁰⁾={vᵢ⁽⁰⁾}ᵢ₌₁^N, vᵢ⁽⁰⁾∈ℝ³, and faces F⁽⁰⁾. The simplification proceeds as M⁽⁰⁾\xrightarrow𝔼₁⋯\xrightarrow𝔼_RM^(R), where 𝔼ᵣ denotes the set of edges collapsed in round r. In classical sequential QEM, each round greedily collapses the minimum-cost edge e=(i,j), merging its endpoints vᵢ and vⱼ into vₑ, updating mesh connectivity and neighboring edge costs.

Before the first round, each face f∈F⁽⁰⁾ defines a face quadric K_f=w_fp_fp_f^⊤∈ℝ^4×4, where p_f=(n_f^⊤,d_f)^⊤ represents the supporting plane of face f, with unit normal n_f and offset d_f, and w_f is its weight. Each vertex vᵢ is assigned a vertex quadric Qᵢ=∑_f\niiK_f over its incident faces. To evaluate the collapse error for an edge e=(i,j), we first combine the vertex quadrics of its endpoints:

Qₑ=Qᵢ+Qⱼ=\beginbmatrixAₑ&bₑ bₑ^⊤&cₑ\endbmatrix,

(1)

where Aₑ∈ℝ^3×3, bₑ∈ℝ³, and cₑ∈ℝ. The collapse error at position v is Eₑ(v)=ṽ^⊤Qₑṽ, where ṽ=(v^⊤,1)^⊤. When Aₑ is sufficiently well-conditioned, the optimal placement is vₑ=\arg\min_v∈ℝ³Eₑ(v)=-Aₑ⁻¹bₑ; otherwise, an edge-segment minimizer or midpoint fallback is used. The collapse cost is Cₑ=Eₑ(vₑ). Collapsing edge e then updates its endpoint positions and vertex quadrics as (vᵢ,Qᵢ),(vⱼ,Qⱼ)↦(vₑ,Qₑ).

3.2 Parallel Edge Collapse

Parallel edge collapse contracts multiple non-conflicting edges in a single round. PaMO [38] enables this through independent-region selection. For each edge e=(i,j), let ℕ₁(e)=ℕ₁(vᵢ)∪ℕ₁(vⱼ) denote its 1-ring face neighborhood, where ℕ₁(vᵢ) contains the faces incident to vᵢ. Each edge propagates its collapse cost Cₑ to all faces in ℕ₁(e), and each face selects a single minimum-cost candidate. An edge e is selected if it is the minimum-cost candidate at every face in ℕ₁(e). Since collapsing e only modifies mesh geometry and topology within ℕ₁(e), this neighborhood defines its independent region. As each face selects a single candidate, the independent regions are face-disjoint, enabling conflict-free parallel collapses. In each round, selected edges satisfying Cₑ≤τ are collapsed simultaneously, where τ is the cost threshold. While improving efficiency, parallel execution may compromise approximation quality relative to sequential QEM simplification.

4 Method

We introduce DiffSimp (Fig. 1), a differentiable mesh simplification layer built on QEM-based parallel edge collapse. Given an upstream mesh generator parameterized by θ, let M_θ=(V_θ,F_θ) denote its output mesh. We formulate the optimization objective as

\min_θ L(S_K(M_θ)),

(2)

where S_K denotes the forward simplification operator of DiffSimp with a target vertex budget K.

4.1 Forward Simplification

For forward simplification, we extend the parallel edge-collapse scheme in Sec. 3.2, using the QEM placement, collapse cost, and quadric update rules from Sec. 3.1. To improve simplification quality while retaining the efficiency of parallel execution, we progressively increase the cost threshold across simplification passes until reaching the target vertex budget K. Each pass p performs parallel collapse rounds under a cost threshold τₚ until no further edges can be collapsed. If the target budget K is not reached, the threshold is increased to τₚ₊₁. Following memoryless simplification [30, 26], we recompute face and vertex quadrics at the beginning of each pass to reflect updated mesh geometry. We also use area-weighted face quadrics K_f=w_fp_fp_f^⊤, with w_f=a_f/ā, where a_f is the face area and ā is the mean face area at the beginning of each pass.111 The normalization by ā is omitted from differentiation, as uniform quadric scaling does not affect vertex placement. For numerical stability, we use the regularized QEM placement vₑ=-(Aₑ+λₑI)⁻¹bₑ for well-conditioned Aₑ, where λₑ=η\maxₖ|(Aₑ)ₖₖ| and η is a small coefficient. Otherwise, an edge-segment or midpoint fallback is used, yielding three possible placement branches.

4.2 Fixed-History Differentiation

Edge collapse involves discrete edge selections and connectivity updates, making the overall simplification process not globally differentiable. However, given a fixed collapse history, the output connectivity is determined, while the output vertex positions are obtained from the input vertex positions through a locally differentiable map. We exploit this distinction by preserving discrete edge selections and connectivity updates during forward simplification, while differentiating the resulting geometry in backward.

Let M⁽⁰⁾=M_θ, and let σ(V⁽⁰⁾,F⁽⁰⁾) denote the discrete collapse history, recording the collapsed edge sets {𝔼ᵣ}ᵣ₌₁^R, pass boundaries, surviving and removed endpoint indices, and the placement branch of each collapse. With σ fixed, vertex placement, quadric addition, and pass-wise quadric recomputation compose into a locally differentiable collapse mapℂ_σ:V⁽⁰⁾↦V^(R). We can therefore express the forward simplification operator as

S_K(M⁽⁰⁾)=M^(R)=(ℂ_σ(V⁽⁰⁾),F^(R)).

(3)

Substituting Eq. (3) into Eq. (2), the loss becomes L(ℂ_σ(V_θ),F^(R)). Where σ remains unchanged, F^(R) is fixed, and differentiating the loss through the output vertex positions yields

∇_θL(S_K(M_θ))=((∂V_θ)/(∂θ))^⊤((∂ℂ_σ(V_θ))/(∂V_θ))^⊤∇_V^(R)L.(4)

The collapse-map Jacobian (∂ℂ_σ(V_θ))/(∂V_θ) captures dependencies across successive collapses, allowing gradients to reach input vertices removed during simplification.

4.3 Factorized Parallel Differentiation

Efficient evaluation of the VJP ((∂ℂ_σ(V_θ))/(∂V_θ))^⊤∇_V^(R)L in Eq. (4) requires handling geometric dependencies in the collapse-map Jacobian, both within each round and across successive rounds. Within a round, the independent regions {ℕ₁(e)}_e∈𝔼ᵣ are face-disjoint but may share neighboring vertices, inducing overlapping dependencies through face quadrics. Across rounds, collapses depend on previously updated vertex positions and accumulated vertex quadrics. We address these dependencies by treating vertex quadrics as differentiable intermediate variables, separating each collapse from its underlying face geometry. This allows gradients for multiple collapses within a round to be computed in parallel. Across rounds, vertex quadric gradients are propagated through additive quadric merges along a reduction forest, avoiding redundant differentiation.

Let P denote the number of simplification passes, Vₚ the output vertex positions of pass p with V₀=V⁽⁰⁾=V_θ, and Q the collection of vertex quadrics Qᵢ. At the beginning of pass p, the vertex quadrics Qₚ₋₁ are recomputed from the input geometry Vₚ₋₁. For pass p with Rₚ collapse rounds, we use local round indices and omit the pass index. Let X⁽ʳ⁾=(V⁽ʳ⁾,Q⁽ʳ⁾) denote the state after round r, initialized as X⁽⁰⁾=(Vₚ₋₁,Qₚ₋₁), and let Jᵣ=∂X⁽ʳ⁾/∂X⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾ be its round-wise Jacobian. The Jacobian of pass p factorizes as

Dₚ:=(∂Vₚ)/(∂Vₚ₋₁)=\beginbmatrixI&0\endbmatrixJ_Rₚ⋯J₁\beginbmatrixI \dfrac∂Qₚ₋₁∂Vₚ₋₁\endbmatrix,

(5)

where the leftmost factor selects the output vertex positions, and the rightmost factor differentiates the pass initialization, including quadric recomputation. The full collapse-map Jacobian is then (∂ℂ_σ(V_θ))/(∂V_θ)=D_P⋯D₁.

Parallel Jacobian Structure.

For e=(i,j)∈𝔼ᵣ within pass p, let Jₑ⁽ʳ⁾ denote the Jacobian of the collapse update (vᵢ⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾,Qᵢ⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾,vⱼ⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾,Qⱼ⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾)↦(vₑ⁽ʳ⁾,Qₑ⁽ʳ⁾). Since the face-derived geometric contributions to each collapse are accumulated in its endpoint quadrics, treating these quadrics as differentiable intermediate variables confines Jₑ⁽ʳ⁾ to its two endpoint states. As the collapsed edges have face-disjoint regions ℕ₁(e) and hence disjoint endpoints, the round-wise Jacobian separates into independent collapse-local blocks:

Jᵣ=(\bigoplus_e∈𝔼ᵣJₑ⁽ʳ⁾)⊕I,

(6)

up to permutations, where ⊕ denotes the matrix direct sum and I is the identity block for unchanged vertex states. Consequently, the round-wise VJP decomposes into independent collapse-local VJPs, evaluated in parallel without conflicting writes to endpoint gradients.

Quadric Reduction-Forest Backpropagation.

While the round-wise Jacobians enable parallel local differentiation, accumulated vertex quadrics retain dependencies across successive collapses. Since vertex quadrics are merged additively, the recorded merge history forms a reduction forest whose leaves are the initial vertex quadrics. We propagate quadric gradients backward through this forest, deferring face-level differentiation until its leaves are reached. This avoids repeatedly differentiating the contributing face geometry at each collapse.

Let g⁽ʳ⁾=∇_X⁽ʳ⁾L denote the gradient with respect to the state after round r. Since the loss depends on the terminal state X^(Rₚ) only through Vₚ, we initialize g^(Rₚ)=(∇_VₚL,0) and apply g⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾=Jᵣ^⊤g⁽ʳ⁾ in reverse round order. Placement derivatives generate quadric gradients that are propagated through earlier merges. For e=(i,j)∈𝔼ᵣ, let g_vₑ⁽ʳ⁾ and g_Qₑ⁽ʳ⁾ denote the incoming gradients at its merged position and quadric. Since Qₑ⁽ʳ⁾=Qᵢ⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾+Qⱼ⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾, both input vertex quadrics receive identical gradients:

g_Qᵢ⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾=g_Qⱼ⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾=g_Qₑ⁽ʳ⁾+((∂vₑ⁽ʳ⁾)/(∂Qₑ⁽ʳ⁾))^⊤g_vₑ⁽ʳ⁾.

(7)

The first term carries quadric gradients from subsequent collapses, while the second adds the contribution from the current vertex placement.

Propagating gradients through the merge history yields g⁽⁰⁾, the gradient with respect to Vₚ₋₁ and Qₚ₋₁ treated as independent state inputs. We then differentiate the quadric recomputation for this pass to obtain the full gradient with respect to the input geometry. Since Qᵢ⁽⁰⁾=∑_f\niiK_f,

g_K_f=∑_i∈fg_Qᵢ⁽⁰⁾,(8)
∇_vᵢ⁽⁰⁾L=g_vᵢ⁽⁰⁾+∑_f\nii((∂K_f)/(∂vᵢ⁽⁰⁾))^⊤g_K_f.

This combines direct position gradients with deferred quadric-induced gradients, yielding the pass-wise VJP Dₚ^⊤∇_VₚL=∇_Vₚ₋₁L. Applying these pass-wise VJPs in reverse pass order yields the full collapse-map VJP in Eq. (4), including differentiation through quadric recomputation at each pass boundary.

Within each pass, each collapse requires a constant-size local backward update, and each initial face is differentiated only once. These backward updates therefore require O(∑ᵣ₌₁^Rₚ|𝔼ᵣ|+|Fₚ₋₁|) work, where Fₚ₋₁ is the input face set of pass p. Even when retaining only 0.5% of the input vertices, simplification takes about four passes on average. Our CUDA implementation performs these updates without constructing per-collapse PyTorch autograd graphs [41]. The placement derivatives used to propagate position gradients are provided in Appendix B.

4.4 Integration into Gradient-Based Optimization

Applying aggressive simplification before the underlying geometry is sufficiently optimized, or abruptly imposing the target vertex budget, can cause substantial geometric changes and destabilize optimization. We therefore introduce a progressive vertex-budget schedule for integrating simplification into gradient-based geometry optimization. Let t index optimization iterations and Nₜ=|V_θ|=|V⁽⁰⁾| denote the input vertex count at iteration t. With warmup duration t_w and budget-reduction duration tᵣ, we define

sₜ=\begincases0,&t

(9)

The vertex budget at iteration t is

Kₜ=round(Nₜ^1-sₜK^sₜ),

(10)

where round(·) denotes rounding to the nearest integer. After warmup, the vertex budget is interpolated in log space from Nₜ to K, followed by optimization at the target budget. At each iteration, we apply S_Kₜ to the current mesh.

Although the collapse history may change between optimization iterations, we empirically demonstrate that differentiating the collapse map under each realized history supports effective optimization (Sec. 5.3).

5 Experiments

We evaluate DiffSimp on low-poly mesh reconstruction and inverse rendering. In both tasks, we follow the progressive vertex-budget schedule in Sec. 4.4, with warmup duration t_w=0.2T and budget-reduction duration tᵣ=0.45T, where T is the total number of optimization iterations. All experiments are conducted on a single RTX 5090. For detailed experimental settings, see Appendix A.

5.1 Low-Poly Mesh Reconstruction

Experimental Setup.

We use 79 shapes from Myles et al. [36], excluding non-watertight and very thin shapes [47]. Our base reconstruction pipeline optimizes FlexiCubes [47] at grid resolution n=128 for 5,000 iterations on shapes normalized to fit within [-0.9,0.9]³, using multi-view silhouette, depth, and normal supervision. Baselines include low-resolution FlexiCubes (Low-res), using the finest per-shape grid with at most K vertices, and representative mesh simplification methods applied to the base reconstructions: QEM [17] (MeshLab [8]), PaMO [38], and vertex clustering [45], along with the remeshing method ACVD [53]. We also compare against CWF [58], which optimizes simplified geometry, and TriFlow [29], a learning-based method. Unlike post-processing, we integrate DiffSimp into the base pipeline to optimize through the simplified mesh.

We evaluate the largest connected component to exclude disconnected interior geometry unseen by image-based supervision [1]. We report squared Chamfer distance (CD) and F1 (10⁻³ threshold) using 10⁶ surface samples, along with normal consistency (NC), self-intersection rate (SI), and sliver-triangle rate (SR). CD is scaled by 10⁵, and SR is the percentage of triangles with minimum angle below 1^∘.

Comparison with Low-Poly Modeling Methods.

Table 1 and Fig. 2 compare low-poly modeling methods at K=1000. Our method outperforms all baselines in CD, F1, and NC, while maintaining SI and SR comparable to those of QEM. These results demonstrate the effectiveness of optimizing through simplification over both direct low-resolution reconstruction and post-processing simplification. We further evaluate reconstruction across vertex budgets K∈{2000,1500,1000,500,250} at n=128, keeping the remaining settings unchanged. To distinguish the contributions of forward simplification and differentiation, we also evaluate our forward operator as post-processing (Ours, fwd. only). As shown in Table 2 and Fig. 3, differentiating through simplification consistently improves reconstruction fidelity over the forward-only variant. At larger budgets, most of the improvement over QEM comes from the forward simplifier, since simplification-induced errors are small and leave little for gradients to correct. Under tighter budgets, these errors grow and gradients compensate for more of them, so the absolute CD gain from differentiation increases from 0.05 at K=2000 to 1.34 at K=250.

Integration across Geometry Optimization Pipelines.

We evaluate DiffSimp beyond FlexiCubes by replacing FlexiCubes with DiffMC [56], integrating it into the separate tetrahedral reconstruction pipeline of DMTet [46], and applying it to Large Steps [37], which optimizes explicit meshes through differential coordinates without isosurface extraction. All three use the same multi-view supervision as the base reconstruction pipeline. We use K=1000 (n=128 for DMTet and DiffMC) and the 42 genus-zero shapes for Large Steps. Table 3 shows that DiffSimp outperforms all baselines in both CD and F1 across the three pipelines. These results demonstrate that optimizing through simplification consistently improves low-poly reconstruction across different gradient-based geometry optimization pipelines, extending beyond isosurface extraction to explicit mesh optimization.

5.2 Inverse Rendering

Experimental Setup.

We use nvdiffrec [35] as our base inverse-rendering pipeline, with FlexiCubes as the geometry frontend. We evaluate eight NeRF-synthetic scenes [34]. Stage 1 optimizes geometry, materials, and lighting, followed by UV parameterization and texture baking. Stage 2 jointly refines vertex positions and UV textures with fixed connectivity for 5,000 iterations. We integrate DiffSimp into Stage 1 geometry optimization while retaining the same Stage 2. At K=2000, we compare against low-resolution FlexiCubes (Low-res), QEM [17], and our forward-only variant. Low-res directly optimizes a coarse grid, whereas QEM and Ours (fwd. only) simplify the geometry after Stage 1 optimization but before texture baking. All three undergo the same Stage 2 refinement as our method. We additionally compare with texture-aware QEM (TQEM) [18] and appearance-driven simplification (ADS) [23], which operate on the final textured reference. ADS further refines the TQEM-initialized mesh to match the reference. We report PSNR, SSIM, and LPIPS on held-out views.

Rendering Fidelity after Simplification.

As shown in Table 4, after Stage 1, DiffSimp is only 1.32 dB below the dense reference while retaining just 3.9% of its vertices. As illustrated in Fig. 4, our method better preserves fine structures both after Stage 1 and after the full run. It outperforms both post-processing QEM and our forward-only variant, demonstrating that the gains extend beyond improvements in the forward simplifier alone. These advantages persist after the shared Stage 2 refinement. Our method also outperforms TQEM and ADS across all rendering metrics, indicating that appearance-aware post-processing does not match the fidelity achieved by optimizing upstream geometry through differentiable simplification. These results demonstrate that optimizing through simplification enables upstream geometry to compensate for simplification-induced errors, improving the final textured mesh.

5.3 Method Analysis

Effectiveness of Simplification Gradients.

We evaluate the effect of our gradients using the base reconstruction pipeline in Sec. 5.1 at K=500. We compare against Forward-only post-processing and three in-loop variants sharing our forward simplifier: Survivor grad propagates each output gradient only to its surviving input vertex, Cluster grad distributes it equally among all input vertices merged into that output vertex, and W/o quadric grad treats quadrics as constants while retaining direct vertex-position gradients. Following our progressive vertex-budget schedule, we measure optimization progress over three intervals: Ramp (iterations 1000–3250, budget reduction), Hold (3250–5000, fixed target budget), and Overall (1000–5000). At iterations 1000, 3250, and 5000, we evaluate rendering losses against ground-truth renderings using the unsimplified mesh (Raw) and its simplified version at K=500 (Deployed), regardless of the current vertex budget. We report relative changes ΔL/L=(L_end-Lₛₜₐᵣₜ)/Lₛₜₐᵣₜ.

Table 5 shows that all in-loop variants improve CD over Forward-only, while Cluster grad and Ours also improve F1, suggesting that optimizing through simplification can improve geometric fidelity. Cluster grad makes substantial progress during Ramp but largely stalls during Hold. Survivor grad yields limited gains, while removing quadric gradients worsens the deployed objective. In contrast, our method continues to reduce the deployed objective, achieving the greatest overall improvement and best geometric fidelity. These results highlight the importance of differentiating the geometric dependencies of simplification rather than relying on surrogate gradient propagation. Moreover, gradient-based optimization remains effective even as collapse histories are reselected at every iteration.

The raw and deployed objectives further expose the optimization–deployment mismatch. Forward-only reduces the raw objective without improving the deployed objective, whereas our method reduces the deployed objective even as its raw objective increases. This divergence shows that optimizing unsimplified geometry does not necessarily improve its budget-constrained output. Optimizing through simplification instead enables upstream geometry to compensate for errors introduced by the final complexity reduction.

Computational Efficiency.

We compare DiffSimp against QEM and a PyTorch autograd replay on Gaussian random-field meshes. As shown in Table 6, our forward pass is 61.3–319.1× faster than QEM, demonstrating the efficiency of parallel GPU execution. Under identical collapse histories, the order-of-magnitude backward speedups and fewer CUDA kernel launches reflect our factorized backward, which enables parallel collapse-local VJPs and avoids redundant face-level differentiation across rounds through the quadric reduction forest. For low-poly reconstruction in Table 1, DiffSimp incurs 1.25× the runtime of its base pipeline (205 versus 164 seconds). For inverse rendering in Table 4, its runtime remains comparable to the base pipeline (3,262 versus 3,255 seconds). Peak GPU memory increases by 11 and 59 MiB, respectively.

6 Conclusion

We present DiffSimp, integrating QEM-based mesh simplification into gradient-based geometry optimization as a differentiable layer. By differentiating the collapse map with the recorded collapse history fixed, our method enables upstream optimization to compensate for simplification-induced errors. Combining our improved forward simplifier with a factorized backward scheme, DiffSimp outperforms the evaluated post-processing simplification baselines in low-poly reconstruction and inverse rendering, with modest runtime and memory overhead. We further show that gradient propagation provides increasing gains under tighter vertex budgets, where simplification introduces larger geometric errors. These improvements extend across diverse geometry optimization frontends, demonstrating the effectiveness of optimizing through DiffSimp rather than applying simplification as post-processing.

We thank Xinyue Wei for insightful discussions and valuable feedback that helped shape and refine this work.

Supplementary Material

Contents

Appendix A Experimental Details

A.1 Low-Poly Mesh Reconstruction

For the low-poly mesh reconstruction experiments in Sec. 5.1, we build on the official FlexiCubes implementation, optimizing a randomly initialized SDF at grid resolution n=128 for T=5000 iterations using multi-view silhouette, depth, and normal supervision without ground-truth SDF. Our reconstruction objective is

L=λₘₐₛₖLₘₐₛₖ+λ_depthL_depth+λₙₒᵣₘₐₗLₙₒᵣₘₐₗ+λ_devL_dev+λ_signL_sign,(S1)

where L_dev and L_sign are the FlexiCubes deformation and sign regularizers. We set λₘₐₛₖ=5, λ_depth=400, λₙₒᵣₘₐₗ=1, and λ_dev=1. Following the official FlexiCubes implementation, we linearly decay λ_sign from 0.2 to 0.01 over the first 0.25T iterations. The other reconstruction pipelines in Table 3 use the same multi-view supervision scheme with frontend-specific settings. DiffMC follows our FlexiCubes reconstruction setup without L_dev. DMTet also omits L_dev, but uses λₘₐₛₖ=10, λ_depth=250, and λₙₒᵣₘₐₗ=1, while retaining the same sign regularization schedule. Large Steps uses the same rendering loss weights as DMTet, without deformation or sign regularization. Within each frontend, our method and the post-processing baselines share the same base reconstruction settings.

A.2 Inverse Rendering

For inverse rendering in Sec. 5.2, we follow the official nvdiffrec configurations for the eight NeRF-synthetic scenes, using FlexiCubes at n=128. Both stages run for 5,000 iterations with the original inverse-rendering objective,

L=L_image+Lₘₐₛₖ+λL_reg,

(S2)

where the regularization terms follow the official configurations. For the post-processing ADS baseline, which requires an initial simplified textured mesh, we apply TQEM to the final textured mesh obtained after both nvdiffrec stages. We then refine the TQEM output for 10,000 iterations at 2048² resolution, following the original ADS iteration count and resolution, using the final textured mesh as the reference.

Appendix B Implementation Details

We provide additional implementation details of the forward simplification in Sec. 4.1 and the closed-form derivatives underlying the backward formulation in Sec. 4.3.

B.1 Cost Threshold and Budget Control

We initialize the pass-wise cost threshold τₚ (Sec. 4.1) at τ₁=10⁻⁴ and set τₚ₊₁=√10 τₚ. Within each pass, parallel collapse rounds continue until no edge chosen by independent-region selection (Sec. 3.2) satisfies Cₑ≤τₚ. Let |V| be the current vertex count. If a round selects more than |V|-K edges, we collapse only the |V|-K lowest-cost candidates so that the target budget K is not overshot.

B.2 Placement Branches and Fallbacks

Consider a collapse e=(i,j)∈𝔼ᵣ within a pass. We omit round superscripts when unambiguous: vᵢ,vⱼ denote the positions vᵢ⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾,vⱼ⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾ before the collapse, and Qₑ,vₑ denote Qₑ⁽ʳ⁾,vₑ⁽ʳ⁾. As in Eq. (1), Qₑ=Qᵢ⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾+Qⱼ⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾ has blocks Aₑ,bₑ,cₑ.

Regularized QEM placement.

We select the regularized QEM branch when

(μ_\min(Aₑ))/(μ_\max(Aₑ))>κ, κ=10⁻³,

(S3)

where μ_\min and μ_\max are the extremal eigenvalues of Aₑ; we additionally require μ_\max(Aₑ)>0. The merged vertex is then placed at

vₑ=-(Aₑ+λₑI)⁻¹bₑ, λₑ=η\maxₖ|(Aₑ)ₖₖ|, η=10⁻⁶.

(S4)

Edge-segment fallback.

When the regularized QEM branch is not selected, we instead minimize the collapse error Eₑ (Sec. 3.1) along the edge. With δ=vⱼ-vᵢ, segment placement is used when

δ^⊤Aₑδ>εₛ, εₛ=10⁻⁷,

(S5)

and is given by

α^⋆=-(δ^⊤(Aₑvᵢ+bₑ))/(δ^⊤Aₑδ),(S6)
γₑ=clamp(α^⋆,0,1),
vₑ=vᵢ+γₑδ.

Clamping keeps vₑ on the edge, at an endpoint when α^⋆∉[0,1].

Midpoint fallback.

If Eq. (S5) is also not satisfied, we use vₑ=\tfrac12(vᵢ+vⱼ).

For each collapse, the forward pass also records the discrete choices required by the backward pass: the placement branch, the segment clamp state (interior or either endpoint), and the diagonal index kₑ attaining the maximum in Eq. (S4). These choices are part of the collapse history σ (Sec. 4.2) and remain fixed during differentiation. Across ten reconstruction samples, regularized QEM, edge-segment, and midpoint placements account for 63.1%, 35.6%, and 1.3% of in-loop collapses, respectively.

B.3 Gradients through Vertex Placement

We derive the collapse-local VJPs for the placement branches in Sec. B.2, writing gₓ for the gradient of the loss with respect to x. Given the incoming position gradient g_vₑ=g_vₑ⁽ʳ⁾, each branch produces direct position gradients g_vᵢ,g_vⱼ and a quadric gradient Gₑ=(∂vₑ/∂Qₑ)^⊤g_vₑ. Writing G_A and G_b for the gradients with respect to the independent blocks Aₑ and bₑ, we represent the symmetric quadric gradient as

Gₑ=\beginbmatrixG_A&\tfrac12G_b \tfrac12G_b^⊤&0\endbmatrix.

(S7)

The factors \tfrac12 account for the two symmetric occurrences of bₑ in Qₑ, and the zero block reflects that cₑ does not affect the placement. Let sym(M)=\tfrac12(M+M^⊤) denote the symmetric part of a matrix.

Regularized QEM placement.

On this branch, Eq. (S3) and μ_\max(Aₑ)>0 imply Aₑ\succ0. Its diagonal entries are therefore positive, and the absolute value in λₑ can be dropped. Differentiating (Aₑ+λₑI)vₑ+bₑ=0 with the recorded kₑ fixed gives

dvₑ=-(Aₑ+λₑI)⁻¹(dAₑ vₑ+dλₑ vₑ+dbₑ), dλₑ=η (dAₑ)_kₑkₑ.

(S8)

With u=(Aₑ+λₑI)⁻¹g_vₑ, the VJP is

G_A=-sym(uvₑ^⊤)-η (u^⊤vₑ) e_kₑe_kₑ^⊤,(S9)
G_b=-u, g_vᵢ=g_vⱼ=0,

where e_kₑ is the kₑ-th unit vector. This branch propagates the placement gradient entirely through the quadrics, including the dependence of λₑ on Aₑ.

Edge-segment placement.

For an interior solution γₑ=α^⋆∈(0,1), let ρ=δ^⊤Aₑδ, zₑ=Aₑvₑ+bₑ, and

βₑ=-(δ^⊤g_vₑ)/(ρ), hₑ=g_vₑ+βₑAₑδ.

(S10)

Differentiating Eq. (S6) gives

g_vᵢ=(1-α^⋆) hₑ-βₑzₑ,g_vⱼ=α^⋆hₑ+βₑzₑ,(S11)
G_A=βₑsym(δvₑ^⊤),G_b=βₑδ.

If the solution is clamped to an endpoint, vₑ coincides with that endpoint and does not depend on Qₑ:

(g_vᵢ,g_vⱼ)=\begincases(g_vₑ,0),&γₑ=0, (0,g_vₑ),&γₑ=1,\endcases Gₑ=0.

(S12)

Midpoint placement.

For vₑ=\tfrac12(vᵢ+vⱼ),

g_vᵢ=g_vⱼ=\tfrac12g_vₑ, Gₑ=0.

(S13)

In all branches, Gₑ is the placement term of Eq. (7) and is added to the quadric gradients of both endpoints. The direct gradients g_vᵢ and g_vⱼ form the position part of the round-wise VJP g⁽ʳ⁻¹⁾=Jᵣ^⊤g⁽ʳ⁾.

B.4 Face-Quadric Derivatives

At the beginning of a pass, let f=(i,j,k)∈Fₚ₋₁ be a nondegenerate face. We write vᵢ,vⱼ,vₖ for its pass-input positions vᵢ⁽⁰⁾,vⱼ⁽⁰⁾,vₖ⁽⁰⁾ and define

\begingathereds=(vⱼ-vᵢ)×(vₖ-vᵢ), n_f=s/∥s∥, d_f=-n_f^⊤vᵢ, p_f=\beginbmatrixn_f d_f\endbmatrix, w_f=(∥s∥)/(2ā), K_f=w_fp_fp_f^⊤,\endgathered

(S14)

so that w_f=a_f/ā as in Sec. 4.1. From Eq. (8), the incoming face-quadric gradient is g_K_f=g_Qᵢ⁽⁰⁾+g_Qⱼ⁽⁰⁾+g_Qₖ⁽⁰⁾. Differentiating K_f gives

g_p_f=2w_fsym(g_K_f)p_f, g_w_f=p_f^⊤g_K_fp_f.

(S15)

We partition g_p_f=(g_n_f^⊤,g_d_f)^⊤ into normal and offset parts. Since d_f also depends on n_f, the total gradient on n_f is g̃_n_f=g_n_f-g_d_fvᵢ, and the gradient with respect to s is

gₛ=(1)/(∥s∥)(I-n_fn_f^⊤)g̃_n_f+(g_w_f)/(2ā)n_f.

(S16)

The face contributions to the vertex-position gradients follow from the cross product:

g_vⱼ^f=(vₖ-vᵢ)×gₛ,(S17)
g_vₖ^f=gₛ×(vⱼ-vᵢ),
g_vᵢ^f=-g_d_fn_f-g_vⱼ^f-g_vₖ^f.

Summing these contributions over incident faces and adding the direct position gradients g_vᵢ⁽⁰⁾ yields the pass-input gradient in Eq. (8). As in Sec. 4.1, ā is held fixed during differentiation. Under a fixed collapse history, uniformly scaling all quadrics leaves the vertex placement unchanged in every branch.

Appendix C Additional Method Analysis

We further analyze the forward simplifier, the fixed-history backward pass, and iterative optimization. Unless stated otherwise, we follow the low-poly mesh reconstruction setup of Sec. 5.1 and use the same 79 shapes. We report squared Chamfer distance (CD) scaled by 10⁵.

C.1 Forward Simplifier

C.1.1 Component Ablation

We evaluate the contributions of area-weighted face quadrics, the cost-threshold schedule, and pass-wise quadric recomputation by removing each component from our forward simplifier. All variants simplify the original meshes of the same 79 shapes (33,228 vertices on average) to K=1000 without optimization. Base denotes our parallel QEM-based edge-collapse simplifier without these three improvements. As shown in Table S1, Base yields higher mean CD (1.879 vs. 1.774) and lower F1 (0.196 vs. 0.215) than sequential QEM, reflecting the quality–efficiency trade-off of parallel edge collapse. Our complete forward simplifier reduces mean CD to 1.250, while removing any component increases CD and decreases F1. Fig. S1 illustrates the qualitative effects of these components.

C.1.2 Comparison with Other Simplification Operators

Table S2 compares our forward simplifier with QEM, vertex clustering, and PaMO on the same 79 original meshes at K=1000 without optimization. These methods exhibit different trade-offs: vertex clustering is fast but introduces substantial geometric error due to spatial quantization, while PaMO ensures intersection-free outputs at higher computational cost. Sequential QEM achieves better geometric fidelity than both but requires considerably more time than ours. Our forward simplifier achieves the lowest CD, the highest F1 and NC, and the shortest simplification time (7.5 ms) among the evaluated methods, while maintaining SI and SR at levels comparable to QEM. This balance of approximation quality and efficiency makes it suitable for repeated application within gradient-based optimization.

C.2 Backward

C.2.1 Pass Count and Quadric Reduction-Forest Efficiency

Our factorized backward substantially reduces computation within each pass by propagating quadric gradients through the reduction forest, allowing face quadrics to be differentiated only once per pass across multiple collapse rounds. As shown in Table S3, even at K=250, simplification requires only 4.3 passes on average despite 101.3 collapse rounds. In contrast, recomputing quadrics after every round requires repeated face-quadric differentiation. Our pass-wise approach consequently achieves 5.5–8.8× faster backward execution, demonstrating the efficiency of reusing quadrics across collapse rounds. Note that the every-round variant still computes collapse-local VJPs in parallel, as described in Sec. 4.3.

C.2.2 Backward Work

The quadric reduction-forest formulation in Sec. 4.3 performs constant-size updates per collapse and differentiates each pass-input face once, yielding work proportional to W=∑ₚ(∑ᵣ₌₁^Rₚ|𝔼ᵣ|+|Fₚ₋₁|). Here, Rₚ denotes the number of collapse rounds in pass p, and the pass index of 𝔼ᵣ is omitted for brevity. As shown in Table S4, our launched GPU threads remain near 2.05–2.25 per unit of W across the tested input sizes. In contrast, an autograd replay of the same recorded history launches 501–772 threads per unit of W, while the normalized direct face-derivative count ∑ₑ|Fₑ|/W increases from 5.40 to 21.95. This increase reflects repeated differentiation of the same face-quadric contributions accumulated in vertex quadrics across successive collapses. These results support the linear-work structure of our factorized backward and demonstrate how the quadric reduction forest avoids redundant face-level differentiation across collapse rounds.

C.2.3 Gradient Correctness

We validate the factorized CUDA backward pass of DiffSimp against a PyTorch autograd replay of the same recorded collapse history. We randomly select ten of the 79 original meshes and perform a single forward and backward evaluation per mesh at K=1000, without optimization. For each mesh, we define a random linear loss on the simplified vertex positions. Let G and G_AD64 denote the input-vertex gradients computed by our double-precision CUDA backward and double-precision PyTorch autograd, respectively. We measure the relative L₂ error ∥G-G_AD64∥₂/∥G_AD64∥₂ over flattened vertex gradients. The mean and maximum relative L₂ errors are 4.7×10⁻¹² and 2.5×10⁻¹¹, respectively, demonstrating near-exact numerical agreement between our CUDA backward and the autograd reference.

C.3 Iterative Optimization

C.3.1 Training Loss Curves

Fig. S2 compares the training losses of DiffSimp and the unsimplified reference in low-poly mesh reconstruction (Sec. 5.1) and inverse rendering (Sec. 5.2). With T=5000, the warmup (t_w=0.2T) and budget-reduction (tᵣ=0.45T) schedules divide training into warmup (0–1000), ramp (1000–3250), and hold (3250–5000) phases. Both methods optimize the same dense geometry during warmup. During the ramp, our training loss increases as the vertex budget progressively decreases. Once the target budget is reached, our training loss continues to decrease throughout the hold phase, exhibiting a clear convergence trend despite repeated simplification during optimization.

C.3.2 Post-Simplification Fine-Tuning

An alternative is to simplify the dense reconstruction once and then optimize the simplified mesh with fixed connectivity. To construct this baseline, we apply our forward simplifier as post-processing and refine the resulting vertex positions for 2,000 additional iterations using Large Steps with its multi-view reconstruction objective described in Sec. A.1. Table S5 shows that, even after these additional 2,000 iterations, post-simplification fine-tuning fails to match the in-loop output of DiffSimp in both CD and F1 across all tested vertex budgets. The gaps in both metrics increase under tighter budgets, with the largest differences at K=500.

item.description:
一句话：已有方法要么依赖精心整理的源-风格训练对，要么需要额外视觉参考。

要点：

  • 任务：卡通着色（toon shading）把物体渲染成平整、风格化的外观；扩散模型提供了一条新路——把真实感视频转成动画风格
  • 两条现有路线的负担：大多**依赖精心整理的源-风格训练对**，或者**需要额外的视觉参考**
