为什么值得看：卡通/三渲二是国内最主流的风格之一，而「不依赖成对数据」意味着可以直接拿现有实拍或渲染素材转风格。从图像骨干换到视频扩散，直接对应的是长镜头下的时序一致性。

中文摘要：卡通着色把物体渲染成平整、风格化的外观；扩散模型为这项任务开了一条新路——把真实感视频转成动画风格。但现有方法往往依赖精心整理的「源—风格」训练对，或者需要额外的视觉参考。Diffutoon 通过结构引导与上色绕开了这些要求，但它建立在图像扩散骨干加短窗运动模块之上，需要反复重叠处理才能覆盖长视频。Diffutoon-2 因此改用视频扩散模型，目标是在不需要成对训练数据与风格参考的前提下，得到长程时序一致的卡通化结果。

主题：AI Rendering

来源：arXiv·cs.CV（English）

原文发布：2026-11-24

本期推送：2026-11-25

Diffutoon-2: Toon Shading with Video Diffusion Models

Abstract

Toon shading renders objects with a flat, stylized appearance. Diffusion models open a new route to this task by transforming photorealistic videos into an anime style. However, existing approaches often rely on curated source and style training pairs or additional visual references. Diffutoon avoids these requirements through structure guidance and colorization, but builds on an image diffusion backbone with short-window motion modules and repeated overlapping-window denoising. We present Diffutoon-2, a video diffusion framework that learns toon shading through animation reconstruction. Two complementary modules independently reconstruct animation clips from outlines and blurred colors, with the video backbone frozen. At inference, the modules jointly guide generation using the same types of conditions extracted from photorealistic footage, requiring neither cross-domain training pairs nor external style references. Extensive experiments demonstrate that Diffutoon-2 outperforms both general-purpose and domain-specific baselines, across quantitative metrics and human evaluation. All resources will be open sourced111https://github.com/modelscope/DiffSynth-Studio, including code and models.

1 Introduction

Toon shading is a non-photorealistic rendering task that gives objects a flat, stylized appearance and is widely used in animation production. With the rise of diffusion models, video stylization has provided ways to achieve this appearance from photorealistic footage by rendering it in anime style. The source video supplies the subjects, composition, and motion, while the model transforms texture and shading into the clean outlines and simplified color regions characteristic of anime rendering. This formulation brings toon shading to recorded scenes without requiring explicit 3D representation.

Existing approaches obtain the target appearance through paired supervision or visual references. EchoStyle [20] constructs source and style video pairs, while PickStyle [31] uses paired images to synthesize aligned training clips. The reference-guided formulation of Kiwi-Edit [25] uses reference images during training and inference, whereas AnyV2V [18] edits the first source frame and propagates its appearance through video generation. These routes introduce two dependencies. Paired supervision requires curated examples that change style while preserving content correspondence. Reference-based generation requires a suitable image whose quality and semantic coverage affect subsequent rendering. In particular, first-frame editing errors can propagate through a video, and scene changes can introduce content that the initial reference does not represent. Diffutoon [8] repurposes off-the-shelf modules designed for image generation from line art and image super-resolution to provide structure guidance and colorization. However, its image diffusion backbone relies on motion modules with windows of at most 32 frames, while repeated denoising of overlapping windows adds computational cost.

We present Diffutoon-2, a framework that renders photorealistic videos in an anime style by conditioning a video diffusion model on outlines and blurred colors extracted from the input video. The outline video constrains scene structure, while the blurred color video preserves spatial color information and suppresses photographic texture. Both types of supervision are readily available from animation footage itself, since line-art extraction and Gaussian blur each produce a condition paired with the original animation. We use these two forms of supervision to train the structure and colorization modules through animation reconstruction, avoiding the need to generate aligned photorealistic counterparts. The modules are optimized independently with the same backbone kept frozen and composed through residual fusion at inference. At inference, both conditions come directly from the source photorealistic video, eliminating external style references and a separate first-frame editing stage. Generated context supports continuation beyond a single generation window.

Our contributions are summarized as follows.

  • •

    We present Diffutoon-2, a technique for toon shading with video diffusion models that renders photorealistic videos in an anime style through structure guidance and colorization.

  • •

    We formulate complementary animation reconstruction tasks for structure and colorization, enabling independent training and joint control at inference without cross-domain paired supervision or external reference images.

  • •

    On extensive experiments, Diffutoon-2 outperforms both general-purpose and domain-specific baselines, including the closed-source Seedance2.5, across quantitative metrics and human evaluation.

    • 2 Related Work

    Cartoonization and animation colorization.

    Generative animation covers stylization, colorization, and motion [37]. Cartoonization models contours and simplified appearance [5, 39]; diffusion methods colorize animation line art from references [3, 49], propagate colors through grayscale videos [28], and render videos [9, 8]. FlowStyler [13] transports geometric and color fields. We learn outline and low-frequency color guidance through animation reconstruction.

    Video stylization and editing.

    Temporal propagation and synchronization support diffusion editing [43, 12, 18, 22, 40, 38], including local guidance for faces [11]. Stylization uses text [16, 46], visual references [27, 45, 48], or broader conditions and modalities [21, 44]. Paired supervision supports both stylization [31, 20] and editing [1, 30, 25]. Meet-in-Style and StructuReiser [19, 36] learn fast networks from stylized examples, with StructuReiser emphasizing structure preservation. We render directly with video diffusion trained through animation-only reconstruction.

    Controllable video generation.

    Video diffusion supports diverse controls [42], including spatial residuals [47], motion and appearance for image animation [14, 15, 41], and trajectories for anime synthesis [24]. DiTCtrl [2] controls attention across prompts; V-RGBX [10] edits intrinsic scene properties. RTR-DiT [29] enables streaming stylization with autoregressive distillation and reference-preserving caching. We combine outline and low-frequency color guidance with clean latent context for window continuation.

    3 Method

    Figure 2 provides an overview of our framework. We first formalize video toon shading as conditional video generation that renders photorealistic inputs in an anime style while preserving their content. We then describe the structure and colorization modules, which learn animation reconstruction from complementary conditions and jointly guide the video diffusion backbone. Finally, we introduce window continuation and prompt construction for rendering videos beyond a single generation window.

    3.1 Problem Formulation

    Given a photorealistic video with T frames X={xᵢ}ᵢ₌₁ᵀ, we aim to generate an output Y={yᵢ}ᵢ₌₁ᵀ in an anime style while preserving the source composition, colors, and motion. Let E denote a line-art extractor and G_σ a Gaussian blur. The two visual conditions are

    S=E(X),\hskip20.00003ptC=G_σ(X),

    		(1)

    where S is the outline video, C is the color video, and σ is the standard deviation of the Gaussian blur. A textual condition p specifies the target style and the content of the input.

    For a video partitioned into K generation windows indexed by k=0,…,K-1, let Xₖ, Sₖ, and Cₖ denote corresponding source and condition segments, pₖ the window-specific text, and Hₖ the generated context from the preceding window. The first window has H₀=∅. We denote the video generator by D_θ,φₛ,φ_c, where θ contains the backbone parameters and φₛ,φ_c belong to the structure and colorization modules. With Gaussian latent noise εₖ, generation and assembly are written as

    Yₖ=D_θ,φₛ,φ_c(εₖ,Sₖ,Cₖ,pₖ,Hₖ),(2)
    Y=A_T(Y₀,…,Y_K-1),

    where Yₖ is the generated output for window k and T is the source frame count. The assembly operator A_T merges each pair of overlapping frames into one blended frame, appends the non-overlapping frames, and retains the first T output frames. For a single window, this reduces to generation conditioned on the source outlines, colors, and text.

    3.2 Structure Module

    We use the line-drawing extractor of Informative Drawings [4] to obtain S=E(X) frame by frame. The extractor produces contours that convey scene geometry and semantics while suppressing surface texture. The extracted drawings are resized to the source frame dimensions.

    For training, an animation clip A provides the outline condition E(A) and the reconstruction target A, together with the structure-training text pₛ. We optimize the structure module with a flow-matching loss [26],

    Lₛ=𝔼_A,ε,τ[∥v_θ,φₛ(z_τ,τ,E(A),pₛ)-u∥₂²],

    		(3)

    where v_θ,φₛ is the velocity predicted by the frozen backbone conditioned by the structure module. The noisy latent is z_τ=(1-τ)z_A+τε, with z_A the encoded animation, ε∼ℕ(0,I) Gaussian noise, and τ∈[0,1] sampled according to the backbone scheduler. Here τ=0 corresponds to the clean animation latent and τ=1 to pure Gaussian noise. The target velocity is u=ε-z_A, and only φₛ is optimized.

    At inference, the trained module receives the source outlines and outputs F_φₛ^ℓ(z_τ,τ,S,p), the structural residual feature at backbone layer ℓ. Here z_τ is the current generation latent and p is the inference text. These features constrain the spatial structure of the rendered video.

    3.3 Colorization Module

    We construct the color video by applying spatial Gaussian filtering independently to each input frame,

    C⁽ⁱ⁾(q)=(K_σ*xᵢ)(q),(4)
    K_σ(δ)=1/2πσ²\exp (-(∥δ∥₂²)/(2σ²)),

    where C⁽ⁱ⁾ is the filtered frame corresponding to xᵢ, q is a spatial position, δ is a spatial offset, K_σ is the normalized Gaussian kernel, and * denotes spatial convolution. The resulting condition preserves broad color regions while attenuating photographic texture, without filtering across time.

    For training, we use the pair (G_σ(A),A) with colorization text p_c and optimize the flow-matching loss

    L_c=𝔼_A,ε,τ[∥v_θ,φ_c(z_τ,τ,G_σ(A),p_c)-u∥₂²],

    		(5)

    where v_θ,φ_c is the velocity predicted with the colorization module, using the same latent path and target velocity as in Eq. 3. Only φ_c is optimized in this run. The two modules are trained independently on the same animation dataset, with the backbone and encoders frozen. Each training run includes only one control module, avoiding the simultaneous storage of gradients and optimizer states for both modules. At inference, the colorization module receives the blurred input video C and outputs F_φ_c^ℓ(z_τ,τ,C,p), the color residual feature at layer ℓ.

    Joint inference.

    The structure and colorization modules jointly condition the video backbone on the outline video S and color video C. Both modules use the shared text p, and their residual features are combined at each controlled layer as

    r_ℓ=λₛF_φₛ^ℓ(z_τ,τ,S,p)+λ_cF_φ_c^ℓ(z_τ,τ,C,p),

    		(6)

    where r_ℓ is the combined residual injected into the backbone and λₛ,λ_c are the control strengths. For windowed rendering, the conditions and text are replaced by Sₖ, Cₖ, and pₖ.

    3.4 Window Continuation

    We process the video across K windows of at most W frames with overlap O and stride W-O. The first window (k=0) is generated from noise. For each subsequent window (k>0), we take the final O frames of the accumulated output Y as context Hₖ and retain their clean latent representation. Only the remaining region, corresponding to W-O new frames for a full window, is generated from noise.

    At every denoising step, the model receives clean context latents followed by the current latents of the new region,

    z̃=Concat(z_ctx,zⁿᵉʷ),(7)
    tⱼ=\begincases1,&j∈I_ctx, 1-τ,&j∈I_new.\endcases

    Here z̃ is the full-window latent input to the model, z_ctx denotes the clean encoded context, zⁿᵉʷ denotes the evolving new-region latent, and Concat concatenates them along the temporal dimension. The sets I_ctx and I_new index their video tokens after temporal VAE compression. The model timestep tⱼ uses the reverse convention, with tⱼ=0 denoting pure noise and tⱼ=1 the clean latent. Context tokens use tⱼ=1, while new tokens use tⱼ=1-τ. Only tokens in I_new are updated.

    Both modules receive the full current-window conditions Sₖ and Cₖ, including the overlap and new frames. Algorithm 1 summarizes the inference procedure. The descending noise schedule is τ₀,…,τ_N, with N denoising steps. The vector t contains the per-token model timesteps, and v[I_new] selects the predicted velocities for the new region.

    After denoising, we decode the full window latent into RGB frames Yₖ. For the first window (k=0), we initialize Y←Y₀. For k>0, the first O frames of Yₖ overlap with the context Hₖ. We merge each pair of overlapping RGB frames via linear blending,

    Ȳ_k,i=(1-αᵢ)H_k,i+αᵢY_k,i,(8)
    αᵢ=\begincasesi/(O-1),&O>1, 1/2,&O=1.\endcases

    Here H_k,i and Y_k,i denote frame i of Hₖ and Yₖ, respectively, and Ȳ_k,i is the blended frame, with i=0,…,O-1. The coefficient αᵢ is the blending weight of the current-window frame. We then update Y by replacing its last O frames with {Ȳ_k,i}ᵢ₌₀^O-1 and appending the remaining new frames of Yₖ.

    3.5 Prompt Construction

    We use Qwen3.8-27B [33] to describe video content from sampled frames. For a video that fits within one generation window (T≤W), its caption d is combined with a fixed anime-style instruction p_style to form the generation prompt,

    p=Concat(p_style,d),

    		(9)

    where Concat denotes text concatenation.

    For longer videos (T>W), we first describe the whole video and then generate a local caption for each window using the global description as a reference,

    d_global=ℚ_g(X),(10)
    d_local,k=ℚₗ(Xₖ,d_global),
    pₖ=Concat(p_style,d_local,k),

    where ℚ_g and ℚₗ are the global and local Qwen captioning procedures. The global caption d_global provides consistent subject names across windows, while d_local,k describes the appearance and actions visible in the current segment. Only the local caption is included in pₖ. Captioning details and examples of improved naming consistency with global guidance are provided in the supplementary material.

    4 Experiments

    4.1 Implementation Details

    We train separate structure and colorization modules on a private dataset of 15,605 animation clips. We use MiniMax-H3 as the backbone. Both modules adopt a ControlNet architecture [47], with nine control blocks corresponding to backbone block IDs 0,5,10,15,20,25,30,35,40. Each module is trained for 5,000 steps on eight PPU-ZW810s with 96 GB of memory each, taking approximately 36 hours. We use a batch size of 8, a learning rate of 10⁻⁵, and 39-frame clips. Training resolutions preserve the input aspect ratio and are scaled as large as possible without exceeding one million pixels.

    At inference, source videos are resampled to 24 fps. For structure guidance, each frame is resized to a short side of 512 pixels before line-art extraction, and the extracted outlines are resized back to the source dimensions. Gaussian filtering of the input video uses σ=20. Both control strengths are set to 0.5, with a maximum window length of 328 frames and one frame of overlap. We use a LoRA accelerated through distribution matching distillation (DMD) from LightX2V [23] for four-step denoising. More details are provided in the supplementary material.

    4.2 Evaluation Protocol

    Evaluation data and baselines.

    We evaluate Diffutoon-2 on 70 photorealistic videos against both open-source and closed-source systems. We randomly select 30 videos from PixaBay100 [9] and 40 from the combined training and validation sets of DAVIS2017 [32]. The comparisons include open-source toon shading and video stylization methods (Diffutoon[8], EchoStyle[20], and PickStyle[31]), open-source video editing and reference-conditioned generation methods (Kiwi-Edit[25], AnyV2V[18], and MiniMax-H3-Ref2VA), and a general-purpose closed-source model (Seedance2.5). We provide MiniMax-H3-Ref2VA with the same outline and color videos as references, allowing us to assess the benefit of our trained modules over direct reference-conditioned generation. All methods target an anime style and are evaluated on corresponding source intervals.

    Evaluation metrics.

    We report nine metrics grouped into content preservation, style and text alignment, and visual and temporal coherence.

    Content preservation.Line-art Boundary F1-score (Line-F1) measures agreement between outlines extracted from aligned source and generated frames, using binarized line maps and a spatial matching tolerance. Chroma adapts CIEDE2000 by removing lightness differences and applying Gaussian smoothing to the chroma channels. This formulation permits changes in luminance associated with cel shading while measuring the spatial agreement of color. UnifiedReward-Edit (UR-E)[6] jointly evaluates editing-instruction adherence and source-content preservation.

    Style and text alignment.CLIP score[34] measures agreement between generated frames and the evaluation text. UnifiedReward-2 Style (UR2-S)[7] assesses aesthetic appeal, while UnifiedReward-2 Alignment (UR2-A)[7] measures agreement with the described content.

    Visual and temporal coherence.CSD[35] measures style consistency between subsequent output frames and the first frame. VBench Motion Smoothness (Smooth)[17] evaluates motion smoothness on continuous output videos, while UnifiedReward-2 Coherence (UR2-C)[7] assesses within-frame visual coherence and distortions. For a fair comparison, outputs from all methods are resized to 480p and resampled to 8 fps for evaluation. Details of baseline implementations and metric computation are provided in the supplementary material.

    4.3 Comparison with Existing Methods

    Quantitative results.

    Table 1 reports results across three categories. Content preservation. Diffutoon-2 and Diffutoon rank first and second in Line-F1 and UR-E, consistent with their explicit structure guidance and colorization design. Diffutoon-2 also achieves the lowest Chroma error of 4.86, improving color preservation over Diffutoon’s 9.30.

    Style and text alignment. Diffutoon-2 leads all three metrics, supporting effective anime stylization with content alignment and aesthetic quality. AnyV2V and MiniMax-H3-Ref2VA obtain the lowest CLIP and UR2-A scores, consistent with their limited transformation of the source’s photographic appearance.

    Visual and temporal coherence. Diffutoon-2 achieves the highest CSD and UR2-C scores and ties Seedance2.5 in motion smoothness at the reported precision. These results support coherent rendering within and across frames, consistent with the video backbone’s temporal prior and framewise source guidance.

    Qualitative results.

    Figures 1 and 3 show that Diffutoon-2 produces convincing anime renderings while preserving source outlines and colors. Seedance2.5 does not consistently stylize the entire scene, sometimes transforming only foreground objects or retaining a non-anime appearance throughout. EchoStyle, PickStyle, and Kiwi-Edit generate anime-style outputs but introduce larger changes to the source content and lose fine details. Diffutoon preserves source outlines well, but its image-based generation backbone provides weaker color consistency across frames, an observation consistent with its strong Line-F1 and lower CSD scores in Table 1. AnyV2V and MiniMax-H3-Ref2VA largely retain the original photographic appearance, as shown in Fig. 3.

    4.4 Ablation Studies

    Structure guidance and colorization.

    Both ablation studies use Line-F1 for outline preservation, Chroma for color preservation, CLIP for text alignment, and CSD for consistency. Table 2 and Fig. 4 examine the two modules. Structure guidance primarily improves Line-F1, while colorization reduces Chroma error. Their combination at (0.5,0.5) achieves the best outline preservation, color preservation, alignment, and consistency. We find that scale combinations near (0.5,0.5) yield similar results, with further analysis provided in the supplementary material. Figure 4 shows that increasing the structure scale preserves more details, whereas increasing the colorization scale produces colors closer to the source. Without Gaussian filtering during training and inference, the RGB-conditioned variant still retains source colors reasonably well, with a Chroma error of 9.65, but its CLIP score drops from 30.5 to 21.8. Its outputs retain a photographic appearance rather than the desired anime style, supporting the use of low-frequency color conditions.

    Consistency across video segments.

    We evaluate overlap length on the 21 videos in our 70-video evaluation set that exceed 328 frames after resampling to 24 fps. Table 3 favors O=1. Larger overlaps weaken outline preservation, color preservation, and consistency, with independent generation performing worst in all three. Figure 5 compares latent-context continuation with overlap lengths O=1,22,56,90 against independent-window generation. We align the first new source timestamp and fix the prompt, control strengths, resolution, and random seed across variants. Independent generation introduces abrupt appearance changes at the boundary. Longer contexts make the following window appear increasingly washed out with lower contrast, whereas a one-frame context better preserves the transition’s appearance.

    4.5 Human Evaluation

    We randomly select 10 videos from the evaluation set and recruit 30 participants, yielding 300 pairwise comparisons in total. For each video, each participant is shown the output of Diffutoon-2 alongside that of a randomly selected baseline, without revealing the method identities, and rates both results on a scale from 1 to 5. As shown in Table 4, Diffutoon-2 outperforms all baselines in human preference and achieves the highest mean rating and the lowest standard deviation.

    5 Conclusion

    We presented Diffutoon-2, a video diffusion framework for toon shading that combines structure guidance from outlines with colorization from low-frequency appearance. Both modules are trained independently through animation reconstruction, enabling anime rendering without cross-domain training pairs or external style references. Across 70 photorealistic videos, Diffutoon-2 achieves leading results in content preservation, style and text alignment, and visual and temporal coherence against specialized methods and general-purpose baselines. Human evaluation further favors Diffutoon-2 over every baseline. Ablation studies confirm that complementary structure and low-frequency color guidance preserve source content while enabling anime rendering.

    Diffutoon-2: Toon Shading with Video Diffusion Models
    Supplementary Material

    Appendix A Training and Inference Details

    Training.

    We train the structure and colorization modules separately on the same private dataset of 15,605 animation clips. Each clip is paired with its extracted outlines for structure training and its Gaussian-filtered version for colorization training. The original animation is the reconstruction target in both cases. Each run updates one module with flow matching while keeping the MiniMax-H3 backbone and encoders frozen; the other module is absent. Both modules use nine control blocks corresponding to backbone layers 0,5,10,15,20,25,30,35,40.

    We use 39-frame clips, a batch size of 8, and a learning rate of 10⁻⁵. Training preserves the source aspect ratio and uses the largest supported resolution below one million pixels. Each module is trained for 5,000 steps on eight PPU-ZW810s with 96 GB of memory each, taking approximately 36 hours.

    Preprocessing and sampling.

    Input videos are resampled to 24 fps. Output dimensions preserve the input aspect ratio under a budget of 1,032,192 pixels and are aligned to multiples of 32. The structure condition is extracted with Informative Drawings [4], using a short side of 512 pixels before resizing the outlines back to the source dimensions. The color condition uses a spatial Gaussian filter with σ=20 in source pixels. Both control strengths are 0.5. We use the four-step DMD LoRA supplied by LightX2V [23].

    Window continuation.

    We use an overlap of O=1 frame. The final window is rounded up to the smallest supported length 17n+5, where n≥1, and excess output frames are discarded. MiniMax-H3 encodes each 17-frame block into five temporal latent positions, with one for the first frame and one for each subsequent group of four frames. Our one-frame overlap therefore corresponds to a single temporal latent position.

    Appendix B Textual Conditions and Caption Generation

    We use Qwen3.8-27B [33] to describe video content and combine the descriptions with task instructions. Training uses the respective text conditions pₛ and p_c for structure and colorization. At inference, a fixed style instruction is combined with the description of the current video window. Prompts B and B specify the two training tasks, and Prompt B gives the inference text wrapper.

    Training descriptions.

    The training metadata uses a fixed wrapper for each module, with only {clip_caption} changing between clips. Prompt B treats the outlines as the complete specification of scene content and motion. Prompt B asks for clean anime appearance while retaining the blurred video’s composition and temporal structure.

    Global and local inference captions.

    For the global description, we uniformly sample up to 12 frames across the source video. For each local description, we sample up to 12 frames from the corresponding window, excluding the retained overlap in later windows. Sampling follows the output timeline at 24 fps, with output frame k mapped to source frame round(kfₛ/24) for source rate fₛ. Sampling stops at the source endpoint, so padded generation frames are never captioned. Images with a short side above 560 pixels are downscaled while preserving their aspect ratio.

    Prompt B supplies the common system instruction. Prompt B establishes the subjects, setting, and major changes. The local instruction in Prompt B receives the current frames and is extended with the position and reference blocks in Prompts B and B. The latter provides a common naming reference; local appearance and actions must still be supported by the current frames. Qwen receives a shared system instruction followed by the images in temporal order and the user prompt. We use bfloat16, medium reasoning effort, and a maximum of 2,048 new tokens. The global and local prompts request at most 150 words. The parsed local description fills Prompt B; the global description is used only to guide local captioning.

    The numbered prompt templates below preserve the training wrappers and inference instructions. Braced fields are substituted with the relevant descriptions or video metadata. Punctuation is reproduced verbatim.

    Appendix C Baseline Implementation Details

    Before computing any metric, we resize videos from every method to 480p and sample frames at 8 fps to ensure a fair comparison. Source-dependent metrics use source and generated frames aligned at the same timestamps and spatial coordinates. Whenever a baseline uses a VLM for caption generation, we use Qwen3.8-27B [33]. All other components and settings follow the original methods. Evaluation text and metric-model settings are shared across methods. MiniMax-H3-Ref2VA receives the outline and blurred color videos as dual video references and uses four denoising steps. Its spatial budget and frame rate match ours. Diffutoon uses ten denoising steps in its main toon-shading pipeline. Table 6 summarizes model sizes and generation settings.

    Appendix D Evaluation Metrics

    Let xᵢ and yᵢ denote the aligned source and generated frames, respectively, and let N be the number of evaluated frames in a video.

    Line-art Boundary F1-score (Line-F1).

    We extract source and output line drawings with the same Informative Drawings detector [4]. Each line-art video is binarized using its own Otsu threshold, estimated from sampled frames and held fixed across the sequence. For frame i, we compute boundary precision and recall with a spatial tolerance,

    Pᵢ=(|{q∈Bᵢʸ:d(q,Bᵢˣ)≤δ}|)/(|Bᵢʸ|),(11)
    Rᵢ=(|{q∈Bᵢˣ:d(q,Bᵢʸ)≤δ}|)/(|Bᵢˣ|),
    Line-F1=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^N2PᵢRᵢ/Pᵢ+Rᵢ.

    Here Bᵢˣ and Bᵢʸ are the source and generated boundary-pixel sets, q is a pixel location, |·| counts pixels, and d(q,B) is the Euclidean distance to the nearest pixel in set B. We set δ=1.5 pixels, so a boundary pixel can match the same location or any of its eight immediate neighbors, including diagonal neighbors at distance √2. Pᵢ and Rᵢ are the resulting precision and recall. A frame receives zero when Pᵢ+Rᵢ=0 or only one boundary map is empty; it receives one when both maps are empty. Higher scores indicate better outline preservation.

    Chroma.

    We adapt CIEDE2000 by smoothing the CIELAB chroma channels and removing the lightness difference. Define

    Ψ(x)=[50, G_σ_c(a(x)), G_σ_c(b(x))],(12)
    Chroma=(1)/(N|Ω|)∑ᵢ₌₁^N∑_q∈ΩΔE₀₀(Ψ(xᵢ)_q,Ψ(yᵢ)_q).

    Here Ψ is the transformed Lab representation, a(x) and b(x) are its chroma channels, and G_σ_c is a spatial Gaussian filter with standard deviation σ_c. Both lightness channels are set to the same constant, chosen here as 50. Any common value produces the same score because the CIEDE2000 lightness-difference term vanishes; 50 serves only as a placeholder for this channel. The set Ω contains the evaluated pixel positions, |Ω| is their count, and ΔE₀₀ denotes CIEDE2000 between two transformed pixel colors. The subscript q selects a pixel. This score preserves sensitivity to spatial color changes while allowing cel shading to change luminance. Lower values are better. The evaluation smoothing scale σ_c is separate from the blur used to construct the model’s color condition.

    UnifiedReward-Edit (UR-E).

    We use the pointwise editing evaluator with the source frame, generated frame, and editing instruction. It returns two scores from 0 to 25 for editing success and source preservation against unnecessary changes. UR-E is their arithmetic mean, averaged over evaluated frames. The preservation component assigns higher scores to better preservation.

    CLIP score.

    We use CLIP-ViT-H-14 with the laion2B-s32B-b79K weights [34]. The implemented score is

    CLIP=1/N∑ᵢ₌₁^Ne^ℓ(f_I(yᵢ)^⊤f_T(pᵢ))/(∥f_I(yᵢ)∥₂ ∥f_T(pᵢ)∥₂),

    		(13)

    where f_I and f_T are the image and text encoders, pᵢ is the evaluation text associated with frame i, and ℓ is the checkpoint’s learned logit-scale parameter. The transpose and ∥·∥₂ denote the inner product and Euclidean norm. We retain the checkpoint’s scale e^ℓ, so the reported score is a scaled similarity rather than a probability. Text is tokenized with a maximum length of 77 tokens.

    UnifiedReward-2 Style (UR2-S), Alignment (UR2-A), and Coherence (UR2-C).

    UnifiedReward-2 [7] evaluates each generated frame together with its text description in a single VLM call. The three outputs are scored separately from 1 to 5. UR2-S measures aesthetic appeal, UR2-A measures content agreement with the text, and UR2-C measures within-frame visual coherence, including object distortions and visual glitches. We report each axis separately without combining them into a total. UR2-C evaluates individual frames, not temporal consistency.

    CSD.

    We use the official CSD descriptor [35] to compare each evaluated output frame with the first frame,

    CSD=1/N-1∑ᵢ₌₂^N(f_S(y₁)^⊤f_S(yᵢ))/(∥f_S(y₁)∥₂ ∥f_S(yᵢ)∥₂),

    		(14)

    where f_S is the CSD style encoder, y₁ is the initial generated frame, and N>1. Each term is the cosine similarity of two style descriptors. The first frame’s self-similarity is excluded. This measures consistency of the rendered style within a video and requires no external style reference.

    VBench Motion Smoothness (Smooth).

    We use the official VBench frame-interpolation evaluator [17]. It retains alternate frames, reconstructs the intermediate frames with its interpolation model, and compares them with the actual held-out frames,

    Smooth=1-1/255M∑ₘ₌₁^MMAE(y_iₘ,ỹ_iₘ),

    		(15)

    where M is the number of reconstructed intermediate frames, iₘ is the corresponding frame index, and ỹ_iₘ is its interpolated prediction. MAE averages the absolute difference over pixels and RGB channels on the 0 to 255 intensity scale. Higher scores indicate greater agreement with the interpolation model’s motion prediction. The evaluator receives the complete ordered 8 fps sequence after the common preprocessing.

    Appendix E Consistency of Global and Local Captions

    Figures 6 and 7 compare descriptions of two adjacent windows with and without a global reference. Our procedure reuses names for recurring subjects and settings, while allowing each window to describe its own events. In these examples, global guidance retains “heathland” and “tall tapering skyscraper” across windows. Independently generated captions vary the scene description or introduce a specific landmark name in the second window. These excerpts illustrate greater naming consistency; differences in wording alone do not establish incorrect scene content. We show the full global descriptions and the relevant opening sentences of the local captions.

    Appendix F Sensitivity to Control Scales

    Figure 8 shows combinations of structure and colorization scales from 0.3 to 0.8 in increments of 0.1. Rows vary the structure scale λₛ, and columns vary the colorization scale λ_c. Combinations near (0.5,0.5) produce similar overall appearance, supporting our default setting without requiring precise tuning. Increasing structure guidance generally retains more source details, while stronger colorization brings the palette closer to the input.

    Appendix G Sensitivity to Gaussian Blur Strength

    We vary the Gaussian blur standard deviation at inference over σ∈{5,8,12,15,20,25}. Figure 9 shows that small values lead to insufficient stylization, with smooth color gradients rather than the distinct, flat color regions characteristic of cel shading. Excessively large values produce a softer, slightly blurred appearance. Table 7 compares the six settings on all 70 evaluation videos using all nine metrics from the main evaluation.

    Appendix H Seventy-Video Evaluation Manifest

    Table 8 lists the 30 PixaBay100 and 40 DAVIS2017 source videos used for evaluation. Resolution, frame rate, duration, and frame count describe the source files before generation and evaluation resampling. DAVIS videos are selected from the combined training and validation sets.
